The replies should either be created with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` (matching the imported topic) or converted to Markdown. As written, imported Disqus replies will be double-processed and likely display broken markup. Also, `Date.parse(p[:created_at])` will raise on malformed dates, aborting the whole import with no error handling.

Embed route has no rate limiting and is unauthenticated

`get 'embed/best' => 'embed#best'` is a public, unauthenticated route with no rate limit. Combined with the job-enqueue-per-miss behavior and the TopicView construction on hit, it's an easy DoS/amplification vector: an attacker can request /embed/best?embed_url=<unique-string> with a spoofed Referer matching embeddable_host, each request enqueuing a Sidekiq job and (for existing topics) building a full TopicView. There is no RateLimiter usage in EmbedController. The endpoint should be rate limited per IP (and per embed_url), and the referer check should be supplemented with a per-IP limiter since the Referer is trivially spoofable.

Feed item id used as URL without any validation enables file:// and internal URL fetch

`url = i.link; url = i.id if url.blank? || url !~ /^https?\:\/\//`. When an RSS item has no link (or a non-http link), the item's `id` (often a GUID, which in many feeds is a URN like `urn:uuid:...`, a tag URI, or — in attacker-controlled feeds — an arbitrary string such as `file:///etc/passwd` or `http://169.254.169.254/`) is used as the URL and passed to TopicEmbed.import → import_remote → `open(url)`. TopicEmbed.import line 11 does check `url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` and returns nil otherwise, which blocks file:// at that layer — but only for the import path; the regex is also loose (matches `https://` anywhere at the start, accepts `https://` followed by anything). The deeper issue is that poll_feed hands unvalidated feed data to a URL fetcher; the id fallback should be removed or strictly validated, and the fetch layer must enforce scheme/IP restrictions regardless (defense in depth).

Loading page reloads unconditionally every 30s with no cap, hammering the server for never-imported URLs

The loading view does `setTimeout(function() { document.location.reload(); }, 30000)` with no maximum retry count and no backoff. If the URL can never be imported (host not actually embeddable, fetch fails, user not found — TopicRetriever.fetch_http returns silently if embed_by_username is blank), the iframe reloads forever, each time enqueueing another RetrieveTopic job (see the controller finding). A single abandoned embed tab generates 2 requests/minute indefinitely plus a Sidekiq job each time. The reload should stop after N attempts and show a permanent message with a link to start the discussion on the forum.

PollFeed spec requires the wrong dependency and never tests poll_feed itself

The spec requires `jobs/regular/process_post` (line 2) — an unrelated job — instead of `jobs/scheduled/poll_feed`, and all four tests only exercise the `execute` guard conditions by mocking `poll_feed`. There is no test that poll_feed actually parses a feed, handles a missing user, handles a malformed feed, or calls TopicEmbed.import with the right arguments. The require of process_post suggests a copy-paste error and means the spec may not even load the class under test in some configurations. The spec should require the correct file and include tests for poll_feed's behavior (using a stubbed SimpleRSS.parse / fakeweb, both of which are available in the Gemfile).

Raw HTML from external feeds stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`. In app/models/post.rb (lines 130-137), `cook` short-circuits and returns `raw` unchanged when cook_method is raw_html, bypassing the entire Markdown pipeline and Sanitize-based HTML cleaning that normally applies to all user content. The `contents` come straight from an external RSS/Atom feed (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35: `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) or from a remote page fetched by ruby-readability (import_remote, line 48). Any script, event handler, or iframe in the feed content is persisted verbatim into `posts.cooked` and rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19 and in the standard topic view. This allows a compromised or malicious feed (feed_polling_url is an admin setting, but embed_url values come from third-party sites via the public /embed/best endpoint) to inject arbitrary JavaScript into the forum — a stored XSS. Imported HTML must be passed through Sanitize with a whitelist before being stored.

Referer host comparison doesn't handle missing port/scheme normalization and is case-sensitive

`URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host` — URI#host returns a downcased host without port, but SiteSetting.embeddable_host is compared as a raw string. If the admin enters `Eviltrout.com` or `eviltrout.com:80` or `http://eviltrout.com` in the setting, the comparison fails for every request and the feature is entirely broken (all requests raise InvalidAccess). The setting should be normalized once (downcase, strip scheme/port) before comparison, or the comparison should parse the setting as a URI too. The spec (embed_controller_spec.rb) only tests with an exact lowercase match, so this misconfiguration is untested.

RetrieveTopic job is enqueued on every cache miss with no deduplication, enabling job flooding

When no TopicEmbed exists for the embed_url, the controller enqueues `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` and renders the loading page, which auto-reloads every 30 seconds (app/views/embed/loading.html.erb line 10). Each reload re-enters `best`, finds no embed (the job may still be running or throttled), and enqueues another RetrieveTopic job. TopicRetriever has a 60-second Redis throttle (`retrieved_recently?`), but that only prevents the actual fetch — the jobs still pile up in Sidekiq, and each one performs DB queries and, for staff users (`no_throttle: user.try(:staff?)`), bypasses the throttle entirely. A popular embed (or a bot hitting /embed/best?embed_url=... directly with a valid Referer) can enqueue thousands of jobs. The controller should check the throttle key (or use a single enqueue-per-URL lock) before enqueueing, and the loading page should back off.

Script assumes #discourse-comments exists; throws if the host page lacks it

`document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` can return null if the host page doesn't include the expected div (typo, different embed snippet version, CSP-modified DOM), and `comments.appendChild(iframe)` on line 12 then throws a TypeError, breaking the entire script. The embed snippet should be documented as requiring the div, but the script should guard: `if (!comments) { return; }`. Low severity (host-page integration issue), but it silently breaks embedding with no error message.

TopicRetriever spec never tests the actual retrieval, throttling, or host validation logic end-to-end

All tests mock `perform_retrieve` or `retrieved_recently?`, so the spec verifies only the wiring of `retrieve` (that it calls perform_retrieve unless invalid_host?/retrieved_recently?). It never tests that invalid_host? correctly parses URIs, that retrieved_recently? actually uses Redis setnx/expire correctly (the throttle could be broken and no test would catch it), that perform_retrieve checks TopicEmbed existence, or that fetch_http looks up the embed user. The Redis throttle in particular is concurrency-sensitive logic that deserves a real test (mock_redis is available in the Gemfile).

TopicView is built with current_user, leaking private topic data into the public embed

`TopicView.new(topic_id, current_user, {best: 5})` passes the current user. The embed endpoint is meant to be loaded in an iframe on a third-party site; the iframe request will typically carry the Discourse session cookie of whatever user happens to view the host page (cookies are sent on iframe requests depending on SameSite settings). If that user is a staff member or a member of a restricted category, TopicView will include posts/topics they can see but anonymous visitors cannot, and the rendered HTML (including post content from restricted categories) is served to the third-party page. The embed view must always be built as an anonymous/system user (e.g. `TopicView.new(topic_id, nil, ...)` or a dedicated embed user) and should verify the topic is publicly visible before rendering. As written, restricted/private post content can be exfiltrated by embedding a URL.

URL validation regex is too loose and inconsistent with the rest of the codebase

`return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` accepts strings like `https://` (nothing after), `https://?x`, `https:// evil.com`, and `https://example.com/redirect?to=javascript:...`. It also uses escaped colons (`\:`) which are unnecessary in a regex. Elsewhere the codebase uses the same loose pattern (poll_feed.rb line 33), so the inconsistency is systemic, but the import path is the security boundary: a URL like `https://eviltrout.com@evil.com/` (userinfo trick) passes the regex and URI parsing will treat evil.com as the host — which then fails invalid_host? in TopicRetriever, but TopicEmbed.import is also called directly from PollFeed with feed-supplied URLs that bypass TopicRetriever's host check entirely. The URL should be parsed with URI() and validated: scheme in [http, https], host present, and host matching the expected domain.

Update path revises the post but never updates the topic title

When content changes, import revises the post via PostRevisor with the new contents, but the topic title (from the feed item's `i.title`) is never updated — only the initial creation uses `title`. A feed that renames an article leaves the Discourse topic with the stale original title forever. Additionally, `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` skips validations/callbacks (acceptable here) but if the PostRevisor revision fails silently (revise! returns false when raw is unchanged — though sha1 differs so raw differs — or raises), the sha1 is still updated only after revise! returns, which is correct, but there is no transaction wrapping the revise + update_column, so a crash between them leaves the post updated but the sha1 stale, causing a redundant re-revision next poll (harmless but noisy). The title update is the real gap: PollFeed passes `i.title` on every run but import ignores it on the update path.

Update-path spec doesn't verify the content_sha1 changed or that a revision was created

The "Supports updating the post" test only asserts `post.cooked.should =~ /new contents/`. It doesn't verify that the TopicEmbed's content_sha1 was updated (so the next poll with the same content won't re-revise), that a PostRevision was created, or that the returned post is the same post (same id) as the original. A regression where import creates a second topic on update (the race condition described in the concurrency finding) would still pass this test as long as cooked contains the new text. The test should assert `post.id == original_post.id`, `TopicEmbed.count == 1`, and the updated sha1.

X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value and disables framing protection

The controller sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. ALLOWALL is not a recognized X-Frame-Options directive (valid values are DENY and SAMEORIGIN); browsers ignore unknown directives, so this header provides no protection and, worse, signals intent to allow framing from anywhere. Since the endpoint renders user-generated post content (including the unsanitized raw_html posts created by TopicEmbed), any site can embed it. If framing from the configured host only is intended, the correct approach is to omit X-Frame-Options and rely on CSP `frame-ancestors`, or set it conditionally. At minimum the invalid value should be removed or replaced with a real mechanism.

absolutize_urls only handles root-relative URLs and mishandles protocol-relative and default ports

absolutize_urls rewrites only hrefs/srcs that `start_with?('/')`. Protocol-relative URLs (`//cdn.example.com/x.jpg`) and scheme-relative paths (`http://other.com/...` is fine, but `//host/path` is left as-is and will resolve against the Discourse origin when rendered, breaking images/links). Also, the port logic `prefix << ":#{uri.port}" if uri.port != 80 && uri.port != 443` appends the port for https URLs on port 80 or http URLs on port 443 incorrectly (e.g. `https://host:80/` would get `:80` appended even though URI normalizes... actually URI keeps explicit ports, so `https://eviltrout.com:80/` yields prefix `https://eviltrout.com:80` which is wrong-ish but functional). More importantly, relative URLs like `images/foo.jpg` (no leading slash) are not absolutized at all and will 404 when rendered from the Discourse origin. The method should use URI.join semantics for all relative references, not just root-relative ones.

cook_method default of 1 does not match Post.cook_methods enum ordering

The migration sets `default: 1, null: false` for posts.cook_method. Post.cook_methods is `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` (app/models/post.rb lines 63-65). Discourse's Enum assigns values starting at 1 in declaration order (regular=1, raw_html=2) — so default 1 = regular, which is correct. However, this is fragile: the migration hardcodes the integer 1 instead of referencing the enum, and the schema comment in post.rb doesn't list cook_method at all (the annotate block at the bottom of post.rb is missing the new column). If the enum order ever changes, existing rows silently change meaning. The migration should use a comment documenting the mapping, and the model's schema annotation should be regenerated to include cook_method. More importantly, `Post#cook` (line 133) compares `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` — for legacy rows defaulted to 1 this is regular, fine, but there's no DB check constraint tying the value to the enum, so a bad value (0, 3) silently falls through to the regular cook path.

cook_method raw_html bypasses all cooking/sanitization with no guard on who can set it

`cook` returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. The only setter is PostCreator line 216 (`post.cook_method = @opts[:cook_method] if @opts[:cook_method].present?`), and PostCreator is a public API used by controllers with user-supplied opts in many places. Any code path that passes user-controlled opts through to PostCreator (e.g. a plugin, the API, or a future controller) can set cook_method to raw_html and store arbitrary unsanitized HTML. There is no Guardian check restricting raw_html to staff/import contexts. The raw_html path should be gated (e.g. only settable when the acting user is staff or via an explicit import flag checked against the guardian), and the value should be validated against the enum on assignment.

discourse_expires_in 1.minute is applied even to the loading page, causing rapid re-fetch churn

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` sets a 1-minute HTTP cache on both the rendered topic view and the loading page. For the loading page this is mostly harmless, but combined with the 30-second auto-reload in loading.html.erb, a shared/CDN cache could serve a stale loading page for up to a minute after the topic has actually been imported, making the embed appear stuck. More importantly, caching the rendered best view for only 1 minute means every embed impression after the first minute hits the Rails stack and rebuilds a TopicView (an expensive operation) — for a high-traffic embed this is a significant load multiplier. The cache duration should be longer for the success path (the content changes only when the topic changes) and the loading page should send no-cache headers so the reload actually re-queries.

feed_key is defined but never used — Last-Modified/ETag caching is dead code

The job defines `feed_key` (a Redis key `feed-modified:<sha1 of url>`) but nothing in the file ever reads or writes it. The apparent intent was to send If-Modified-Since / track the feed's Last-Modified header and skip re-parsing unchanged feeds, but `poll_feed` unconditionally does `SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` every hour and re-imports every item (TopicEmbed.import does dedupe by content_sha1, so it's not catastrophic, but every item's content is re-hashed and compared each hour, and the HTTP fetch always happens). Either implement the conditional GET using feed_key or remove the dead method; as written it misleads maintainers into thinking conditional requests are happening.

fetch_http performs an unvalidated server-side request to a user-influenced URL (SSRF surface)

fetch_http calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, @embed_url)`, which does `open(url).read` (app/models/topic_embed.rb line 48). The URL originates from the `embed_url` query parameter of the public `/embed/best` endpoint (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb line 9). The only validation is `invalid_host?`, which checks `URI(@embed_url).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. This still allows SSRF-style abuse within the allowed host (e.g. `http://eviltrout.com:22/`, `http://eviltrout.com/admin/internal-endpoint`, `http://user:pass@eviltrout.com/`, or `file://` if the host string is ever misconfigured to match), and `open()` follows redirects by default, so a URL on the allowed host that redirects to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` (cloud metadata) or an internal service will be fetched and its content imported as a post. open-uri must be restricted: validate scheme is http/https, resolve and reject private/loopback/link-local IPs, disable redirects or re-validate each hop, and set timeouts.

import mutates the caller's contents string via <<

Line 13 does `contents << "\n<hr>..."`, which mutates the String object passed in by the caller. In app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35 the content is `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` — a fresh string, so it's mostly harmless there, but in app/models/topic_embed.rb import_remote line 52, `doc.content` (the Readability result) is passed and then mutated; any caller reusing the string (e.g. computing the sha1 before/after, or the Disqus importer in lib/tasks/disqus.thor) will see the appended footer. Note also that `content_sha1` on line 16 is computed AFTER the mutation, so the stored hash includes the footer — meaning an update comparison is consistent, but the mutation of a caller-owned object is a hidden side effect that can corrupt data if the same string is reused (e.g. the spec at spec/models/topic_embed_spec.rb line 40 calls import twice with different literals, masking the issue). Use `contents = contents + ...` or `<<` on a dup.

import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs with open() — no scheme, redirect, or private-network restrictions

`Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)` uses Kernel#open (open-uri) on a URL that, via TopicRetriever/RetrieveTopic, is ultimately derived from the public embed_url parameter, and via PollFeed from feed item links/ids (`url = i.id if url.blank? || url !~ /^https?\:\/\//` in poll_feed.rb line 33 — note this fallback accepts ANY string as a URL, including `file:///etc/passwd`, which open-uri will happily open). There is no scheme whitelist, no redirect limit, no timeout, and no protection against requests to internal/private IP ranges. This is a full SSRF primitive: an attacker who can influence a feed item id/link (or an embed_url on the allowed host that redirects) can make the server read local files (`file://`) or internal HTTP services and import the response body as a forum post, leaking internal data. The fetch must be hardened (scheme whitelist, redirect re-validation, IP range blocking, timeouts).

import_remote fetches the full page with no timeout, size limit, or redirect limit

`Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)` reads the entire response body into memory with open-uri defaults: no open_timeout/read_timeout, no redirect limit (open-uri follows up to 10 redirects by default), and no maximum size. A slow or huge page on the allowed host (or an allowed-host URL redirecting to a multi-GB file) will hang the Sidekiq worker and consume unbounded memory. The fetch should use explicit timeouts, a redirect cap with re-validation, and a maximum content length.

invalid_host? returns true when embeddable_host is blank, but comparison is exact-host and case-sensitive

`SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host` compares the configured host string directly to the URI host. If embeddable_host is configured as `http://eviltrout.com` (with scheme) or `Eviltrout.com` (mixed case) or `eviltrout.com/` (trailing slash), the comparison fails for perfectly valid embed URLs and retrieval is silently skipped; conversely `www.eviltrout.com` vs `eviltrout.com` mismatches. The setting is documented as "Host that can embed the comments" (config/locales/server.en.yml), so it should be normalized (strip scheme, downcase, strip port) before comparison, and the embed_url host should be compared as a suffix of the configured registrable domain. As written, misconfiguration silently disables the entire feature.

no_throttle is granted based on the user_id passed from the controller, which is the iframe viewer's identity

`TopicRetriever.new(args[:embed_url], no_throttle: user.try(:staff?))` — the user_id comes from `current_user.try(:id)` in the embed controller, i.e. whichever Discourse user's browser loaded the third-party page. Any staff member who visits a page containing an embed (or an attacker who socially engineers a staff member to a page with many distinct embed_urls) gets the 60-second throttle disabled, allowing unbounded fetch/import of arbitrary URLs on the allowed host. The throttle bypass should not be tied to the viewer's identity at all; if staff bypass is desired it should be a server-side decision, and the throttle key should also incorporate the URL (it does) but the bypass should be removed or gated on a server-controlled flag.

raw post.cooked rendered in embed view The view renders `
<%= raw post.cooked %>
`. In the main Discourse UI, cooked post HTML is produced by the Markdown pipeline which sanitizes dangerous markup; here `raw` bypasses any escaping. For posts created through TopicEmbed this cooked content is entirely unsanitized external HTML (see the TopicEmbed raw_html finding), so any script in an imported article executes in the context of the Discourse origin inside the embed iframe. Even for normal cooked posts, re-rendering with `raw` in a separate layout that lacks the standard CSP/onebox protections weakens the XSS posture. The embed view should render cooked content through the same sanitization used elsewhere, and imported raw_html posts must never reach this template unsanitized.

skip_validations option now skips post validations on revise, but the raw_html cook_method is never re-applied on revision

The diff changes `@post.save` to `@post.save(validate: !@opts[:skip_validations])`, which is needed for the import update path. However, when TopicEmbed.import revises a raw_html post (topic_embed.rb line 36), PostRevisor.update_post sets `@post.raw = @new_raw` and saves; the before_save callback in post.rb (line 321) recomputes `self.cooked = cook(raw, ...)` only `unless new_record?` — for an existing raw_html post, cook returns raw, so cooked is correctly set to the new raw. That part works. The subtle issue: `skip_validations` now bypasses Validators::PostValidator for ALL revisions when the option is passed, including length/entropy/spam checks — acceptable for the import path, but the option is a general-purpose footgun now available to any caller of PostRevisor. It should be named/scoped to the import use case or documented. Low severity since only TopicEmbed passes it today.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Flexbox added to .small-action but child floats not cleared — mixed float/flex layout causes misalignment

The diff adds `@include flexbox()` and `@include align-items(center)` to `.small-action` (lines 264-265), making it a flex container. However, its children still use `float: left`: `.topic-avatar` has `float: left` (line 270), `.small-action-desc .avatar` has `float: left` (line 298), and the `button` has `float: right` (line 309). In a flex container, `float` is ignored on flex items — the computed value of `float` becomes `none` for flex items per the CSS Flexbox spec. This means: (1) the `float: right` on the button no longer pushes it to the right edge; it becomes a flex item placed in DOM order, likely appearing to the left of where it should be; (2) the `float: left` on avatars is neutralized, which may be fine for layout but changes the intended wrapping behavior; (3) the trailing `clear: both` (line 312) on `.small-action` itself is meaningless on a flex container. Additionally, the diff changes `.small-action-desc` padding from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (which reserved space for the floated avatar) to `0 1.5%`, and removes `padding-top: 4px` from `> p` — these spacing changes were tuned for the old float-based layout and will produce incorrect spacing now that the avatar is a flex item without its reserved left padding. The `.custom-message p` margin change from `5px 0` to `0` (line 292) further removes vertical spacing that was compensating for the old layout.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`align-items` mixin emits both `-ms-flex-align` and `-ms-align-items` — `-ms-align-items` is invalid

The `align-items` mixin (lines 117-123) emits `-ms-flex-align` (correct for IE10) and `-ms-align-items` (line 121). The property `-ms-align-items` is not a valid CSS property — IE10 only supports `-ms-flex-align` for the 2012 flexbox spec; there is no `-ms-align-items` prefixed property. This invalid property will be ignored by browsers, adding dead weight to the compiled CSS. It should be removed. Additionally, the mixin emits `-webkit-box-align` (for old 2009 flexbox) which expects different keyword values (e.g., `start`, `end`, `center`, `baseline`, `stretch`) — passing `center` works for both old and new specs, but `baseline` in old Webkit flexbox has different behavior; however, since the only usage in this PR is `align-items(center)` and `align-items(baseline)`, the `baseline` value in `-webkit-box-align` (line 118) may render differently in old Safari (6.0) versus modern browsers, potentially causing vertical misalignment of bullet badges in `badges.css.scss` line 57.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:

The diff adds `@include flexbox()` and `@include align-items(center)` to `.small-action` (lines 264-265), making it a flex container. However, its children still use `float: left`: `.topic-avatar` has `float: left` (line 270), `.small-action-desc .avatar` has `float: left` (line 298), and the `button` has `float: right` (line 309). In a flex container, `float` is ignored on flex items — the computed value of `float` becomes `none` for flex items per the CSS Flexbox spec. This means: (1) the `float: right` on the button no longer pushes it to the right edge; it becomes a flex item placed in DOM order, likely appearing to the left of where it should be; (2) the `float: left` on avatars is neutralized, which may be fine for layout but changes the intended wrapping behavior; (3) the trailing `clear: both` (line 312) on `.small-action` itself is meaningless on a flex container. Additionally, the diff changes `.small-action-desc` padding from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (which reserved space for the floated avatar) to `0 1.5%`, and removes `padding-top: 4px` from `> p` — these spacing changes were tuned for the old float-based layout and will produce incorrect spacing now that the avatar is a flex item without its reserved left padding. The `.custom-message p` margin change from `5px 0` to `0` (line 292) further removes vertical spacing that was compensating for the old layout.

Replacing raw `display: inline-flex` with `@include inline-flex()` adds old-spec fallbacks that change rendering in legacy browsers

The diff replaces `display: inline-flex; align-items: baseline;` (raw modern CSS) with `@include inline-flex()` and `@include align-items(baseline)` (lines 55-57). The `inline-flex()` mixin (mixins.scss lines 108-114) emits `display: -webkit-inline-box; display: -webkit-inline-flex; display: -moz-inline-box; display: -ms-inline-flexbox; display: inline-flex;`. The old-spec fallbacks `-webkit-inline-box` and `-moz-inline-box` use the 2009 flexbox model, which has different sizing and alignment behavior than modern flexbox. In old Safari (6.0) and old Firefox (pre-22), the badge wrapper will render using the 2009 box model, where `align-items: baseline` (via `-webkit-box-align: baseline`) behaves differently — specifically, baseline alignment in old flexbox aligns to the first line of text, which may cause the bullet badge's colored dot and category text to misalign vertically compared to modern browsers. Since the original code used unprefixed `inline-flex` (which old browsers simply ignore, falling back to the `display: inline-block` from `.badge-wrapper` line 22), the visual result in old browsers was a simple inline-block badge. The mixin change makes old browsers attempt flexbox layout with the old spec, potentially introducing visual bugs in legacy browsers that were previously rendering correctly with inline-block fallback.

`@include order(2)` applied to `.extra-info-wrapper` without a flex container parent — order property has no effect and may cause layout regression

The diff adds `@include order(2)` to `.extra-info-wrapper` (line 30), but the `order` CSS property only applies to flex items or grid items. There is no `@include flexbox()` applied to any ancestor of `.extra-info-wrapper` in this file or in the provided diff — its parent (`#topic-title` or the topic header container) is not converted to a flex container. Without a flex/grid parent, `order: 2` (and all its prefixed variants emitted by the mixin) is completely ignored by browsers. Meanwhile, the diff removes the `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` rule from `.badge-wrapper` inside `.extra-info-wrapper` (lines 33-35), which was providing vertical spacing for bullet-style category badges. The net effect is that the intended reordering does nothing, and the removed margin-top causes bullet badges in the extra-info area to lose their top spacing, misaligning them vertically with adjacent content. The change is both ineffective (order without flex parent) and harmful (removed margin).

`@include order(3)` on `.panel` assumes sibling order values 1 and 2 exist, but no other flex items have explicit order — visual order may not match DOM order intent

The diff adds `@include order(3)` to `.panel` (line 39) and relies on `margin-left: auto` to push it right. In flexbox, `order` changes the visual ordering of flex items. The default `order` value is 0 for all flex items. By setting `.panel` to `order: 3`, it will be placed after all items with `order: 0` (the default) — which includes `.title`, `.icons`, `.login-button`, etc. — regardless of their DOM position. This means `.panel` will always render last among the flex items, which may be the intent (pushing the user panel to the right). However, combined with `margin-left: auto`, the behavior is redundant and potentially conflicting: `margin-left: auto` on a flex item absorbs free space and pushes the item (and subsequent items) to the right, but `order: 3` already places it last. If there are other flex items after `.panel` in the DOM with default `order: 0`, they would appear BEFORE `.panel` visually despite being after it in the DOM — this is an accessibility concern (visual order ≠ DOM order, confusing screen reader users) and may cause unexpected layout if the header DOM structure changes. The `order` property should be used sparingly; using `margin-left: auto` alone would achieve the right-alignment without reordering.

`order` mixin emits invalid prefixed properties: `-ms-flex-order` and `-webkit-order` are not valid CSS

The `order` mixin (lines 125-131) emits five properties: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group`, `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, `-ms-flex-order`, `-webkit-order`, and `order`. Two of these are invalid: (1) `-ms-flex-order` — the correct IE10 flexbox property is `-ms-flex-order` only in the context of the old 2009/2012 IE flexbox implementation, but the standard IE10 property for the 2012 spec is `-ms-flex-order` is actually correct for IE10... however, `-webkit-order` (line 129) is NOT a valid property — WebKit never shipped a prefixed `order` property; Safari supported unprefixed `order` from the start of its flexbox implementation (Safari 6.1+/7 with `-webkit-flex`). Similarly, `-moz-box-ordinal-group` is for the old 2009 Firefox flexbox (`display: -moz-box`), which is fine as a fallback, but `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` correctly maps to old WebKit flexbox. The real issue: `-webkit-order` is invalid and will be dropped by browsers, and more importantly, `-ms-flex-order` expects an integer but the mixin passes `$val` directly — for the header use case `@include order(3)`, IE10's `-ms-flex-order` uses 1-based ordinal groups where the default is 0, so `order(3)` in IE10 would place the panel after items with default order 0, which may not match the intended visual order of 1,2,3 in modern browsers. The mixin also lacks `-ms-flex-item-align` or other IE10-specific corrections. Invalid properties in the output CSS increase stylesheet size and can confuse CSS validators/linters; the IE10 ordinal mismatch can cause the header panel to appear in the wrong position in IE10.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is not a predicate method, so the attribute is always serialized

The method is named `include_website_name` (without a trailing `?`), but ActiveModel::Serializers only calls `include_<attr>?` predicate methods to decide whether to include an attribute. Because no `include_website_name?` method exists, the serializer falls back to always including `website_name`. This means `website_name` is serialized even when `website` is blank/nil, producing a JSON payload with `website_name: null` for every user with no website. The guard `website.present?` inside the method is dead code in this context. The method should be renamed to `include_website_name?` (matching the pattern used by `include_email?`, `include_stats?`, etc. in the same file).

false_positives.candidate:
JSDoc comment for profileBackground was incorrectly changed from websiteName

The diff changed the JSDoc `@property` annotation from `websiteName` to `profileBackground` on the `profileBackground` computed property. This appears to be an accidental edit — the original `@property websiteName` was already wrong (it should have been `profileBackground` for this method), but the change in this PR is unrelated to the website_name feature. While the fix is technically correct (the doc now matches the method name), it's an unrelated change bundled into this PR. More importantly, the original code had a `websiteName` computed property in the controller (removed in this PR) that had no JSDoc, and this model file never had a `websiteName` property — so the original `@property websiteName` on `profileBackground` was a pre-existing copy-paste error. The fix is correct but should have been a separate commit/PR.

No test for website_name when website is blank or nil

The spec only tests `website_name` when a website is filled out (line 67+). There is no test verifying that `website_name` is absent (or null) when `user_profile.website` is blank. Given the `include_website_name` predicate bug (it's not a real predicate), this case is important to test — it would catch the bug where `website_name` is always serialized even for users with no website. A test like `expect(json).not_to have_key(:website_name)` when website is nil would be appropriate.

URI(website.to_s) is parsed multiple times in website_name

The `website_name` method calls `URI(website.to_s)` three separate times (lines 138, 143, 146, 149) to extract the host and path. Each call re-parses the URL string. This is wasteful — the parsed URI object should be computed once and reused. While the performance impact is negligible for a single serialization, it's called for every user in list views (e.g., user directory, admin user list), so the redundant parsing adds up. Extract `uri = URI(website.to_s) rescue nil` once at the top and use `uri.host` and `uri.path` throughout.

Untrusted attributes test does not include website_name, so the TL0/anonymous privacy leak is not caught

The test on line 11 defines `untrusted_attributes` as `%i{bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background}` but does NOT include `:website_name`. Since `website_name` was added to the `untrusted_attributes` list in the serializer (line 109 of user_serializer.rb), it should be included in this test to verify that TL0 users' website names are hidden from anonymous viewers. Without this, the test passes even if the `untrusted_attributes` mechanism is broken for `website_name`, and a privacy regression (leaking a TL0 user's website path to anonymous users) would go undetected. Additionally, because `include_website_name` is not a proper predicate (see separate finding), the attribute may be serialized even when `website` is blank, which this test also fails to catch.

Website link uses unescaped href attribute that could allow javascript: URLs

The template renders `<a href={{model.website}} ...>` where `model.website` comes directly from user profile data (user-controlled input). While the server-side `website` field is presumably validated on save, the serializer returns the raw `user_profile.website` value without any scheme validation. If a user can set their website to `javascript:alert(1)` (depending on server-side validation in the user profile update path, which is not shown in this PR), clicking the link would execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the Discourse site. The `website_name` display text is safely derived from the host, but the `href` uses the raw URL. The server should enforce http/https scheme on the website field, or the serializer should sanitize it. At minimum, this is a defense-in-depth concern — the href should be validated to start with `http://` or `https://`.

website_name logic is incorrect for subdomain relationships and can produce wrong display text

The `website_name` method attempts to show the full path when the website host matches the instance host, but the branching logic is flawed. In the `elsif` branch (line 144), it compares `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')` with `discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')` — this strips the first label from both hosts and compares the remainders. For `website_host = 'forums.example.com'` and `discourse_host = 'example.com'`, the lengths differ (3 vs 2) so this branch is skipped, but for `website_host = 'a.b.example.com'` and `discourse_host = 'c.b.example.com'` (both length 4), it would incorrectly treat them as the same site. More importantly, the final `else` branch (line 149) checks `discourse_host.ends_with?('.' + website_host)`, which correctly handles `forums.example.com` ending with `.example.com`, but the middle branch's length-equality requirement means cases like `website_host = 'www.example.com'` (3 labels) vs `discourse_host = 'example.com'` (2 labels) fall through to the else branch and are handled correctly only by accident. The logic is convoluted and the comment on line 148 ('example.com == forum.example.com') describes the else branch but the condition actually tests the reverse (instance is subdomain of website). Consider simplifying to a single check: show the path when `website_host == discourse_host || discourse_host.ends_with?('.' + website_host)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Pagination offset calculation is wrong — next page offset can exceed user_count

In the `next` action: `offset = Math.min(group.get("offset") + group.get("limit"), group.get("user_count"))`. This caps the offset at `user_count`, but the correct next-page offset should be `offset + limit` capped at `user_count - limit` (or simply `offset + limit` without capping, letting the server return empty results). Capping at `user_count` means if `user_count = 100` and `limit = 50`, starting at offset 0, next gives offset 50 (correct). But if `user_count = 75` and `limit = 50`, starting at offset 0, next gives `Math.min(50, 75) = 50`, which returns members 50-74 (25 members) — correct. However, if `user_count = 100` and `limit = 50`, at offset 50, next gives `Math.min(100, 100) = 100`, which requests offset 100 — an empty page. The `showingLast` check (`currentPage == totalPages`) should prevent this, but `totalPages` is `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` which for 100/50 = 3 pages (0-49, 50-99, and a phantom page 100+). The formula `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` is wrong for exact multiples: 100/50 = 2 pages, not 3. It should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`. This causes an extra empty page to be shown and the "next" button to be enabled when it shouldn't be. Same bug in `totalPages` at line 13.

true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

Using `:put` in the test will not match the DELETE route — it will either 404 or route to a different action. The test is therefore not actually testing the remove_member endpoint; it may be passing for the wrong reason (e.g., routing error returning 422 coincidentally, or the test framework matching loosely). The test should use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, ...`. Additionally, as noted in the controller finding, the parameter should be `id`, not `group_id`. This test as written does not validate the intended behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages formula is incorrect for exact multiples of limit

`totalPages` computes `Math.floor(this.get("user_count") / this.get("limit")) + 1`. For `user_count = 100` and `limit = 50`, this yields `Math.floor(2) + 1 = 3` pages, but there are only 2 pages of data (offsets 0 and 50). The correct formula is `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`. This causes the UI to show "page 3 of 3" when only 2 pages exist, and enables the "next" button on page 2, leading to an empty page 3. The `showingLast` computed property (`currentPage == totalPages`) will be true on page 3 (the empty page), but page 2 will incorrectly show as not-last.

true_positives.golden_comment: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined
true_positives.matched_candidate:
findMembers returns undefined instead of a promise when name is empty

When `this.get('name')` is empty, `findMembers` executes `return ;` which returns `undefined`, not a Promise. Callers like `admin_group_route.js` line 13 (`model.findMembers()`) and `group-members.js.es6` line 11 (`model.findMembers()`) do not chain on the result, so this is currently harmless. However, `removeMember` and `addMembers` both call `self.findMembers()` inside `.then()` without handling the return value, which is fine. But any future caller that does `group.findMembers().then(...)` will crash with "Cannot read property 'then' of undefined" when the group has no name (e.g., a newly created group before the name is set). The previous implementation returned `Ember.RSVP.resolve([])` which was a proper Promise. This is a regression in the method's contract — it should consistently return a Promise. Fix: `return Ember.RSVP.resolve();` or `return Ember.RSVP.resolve([]);`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
add_members and remove_member use params.require(:group_id) but routes define member routes without :group_id segment

The routes in config/routes.rb define `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` and `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` inside `resources :groups`. This generates URLs like `/admin/groups/:id/members` where `:id` is the group id, NOT `:group_id`. However, the controller actions call `params.require(:group_id)`. This will raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing` because the route parameter is named `id`, not `group_id`. The frontend model (`group.js`) calls `/admin/groups/' + this.get('id') + '/members.json'` which maps to the `:id` param. The controller must use `params.require(:id)` or the routes must be changed to use `:group_id`. As written, every add/remove member request will 500 with ParameterMissing. This is a critical functional break — the feature does not work at all.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.

false_positives.candidate:
Error handler assumes e.responseText is valid JSON — crashes on network errors or non-JSON responses

In the `save` action's error callback: `var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors;`. If the server returns a non-JSON response (e.g., a 500 HTML error page, or a network timeout where `responseText` is empty), `$.parseJSON` will throw a SyntaxError, masking the original error and leaving the UI in a broken state (disableSave was set to true and the finally block may not execute if the exception propagates). The error handler should be defensive: check that `e.responseText` exists and parse it safely, or use `e.responseJSON` if available. This is a robustness issue that will produce confusing behavior when the server errors unexpectedly.

SQL injection via ILIKE search parameter

The `index` action interpolates the user-supplied `search` parameter directly into a SQL string: `groups.where("name ILIKE ?", "%#{search}%")`. While the `?` placeholder protects against classic injection of the value itself, the surrounding `%` wildcards are part of the interpolated string, and more importantly this pattern is fragile: if the code is later changed to `"name ILIKE '%#{search}%'"` (a common mistake), it becomes a direct SQL injection. The safe form is `groups.where("name ILIKE ?", "%#{search}%")` — which is what is written — but the value is still being embedded with wildcards in Ruby rather than passed as a bound parameter with wildcards appended by the database layer. More concretely: the previous code used lowercase `ilike` which fails on PostgreSQL (case-sensitive operator name), and the fix to `ILIKE` is correct, but the interpolation of `search` into the SQL fragment via string formatting inside the `where` argument is a code-smell that invites injection if refactored. The robust fix is `groups.where("name ILIKE :q", q: "%#{search}%")` or `Group.where("name ILIKE ?", "%#{search}%")` with the wildcards in the bound value only. As written, the bound parameter is safe, but the pattern should be tightened to prevent future regressions.

Stray closing div tag inside table row breaks HTML structure Line 19 contains `` inside the `{{#each}}` loop within a `` element. There is no corresponding opening `
` — the `
` is opened at line 7 and closed at line 18. This stray `` is invalid HTML inside a table context and will be ignored or cause rendering issues by the browser's HTML parser. It should be removed.

`usernames.split(",")` does not strip whitespace from each username. If the client sends `"alice, bob"` (with a space after the comma, which is natural for a comma-separated user selector), the lookup `User.find_by_username(" bob")` will fail silently because usernames cannot contain spaces. The member is silently not added, and the endpoint still returns success. The fix is `usernames.split(",").map(&:strip).each` or equivalent. This is a data-integrity issue: an admin believes members were added but they were not.

create action does not set alias_level, defaulting to 0 (nobody) which may not be intended

The `create` action sets `name` and `visible` but does not set `alias_level`. The `update` action sets `alias_level` if present. For a new group, `alias_level` defaults to the database default (likely 0). The admin UI (`group.hbs`) shows an alias level combo box, but on create, the selected alias_level from the UI is sent via `save()` which calls `group.create()` — but `asJSON()` includes `alias_level`, so it IS sent. However, the controller's `create` action ignores `params[:alias_level]` entirely. The `asJSON()` method sends `alias_level`, but the controller only reads `params[:name]` and `params[:visible]`. This means the alias_level selected by the admin during group creation is silently discarded. The controller should also set `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i if params[:alias_level].present?` in the `create` action, matching the `update` action's behavior.

The template iterates `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}`. The controller (`admin-group.js.es6`) no longer has a `members` property (it was removed in the diff). In Ember, `members` in the template resolves via the controller, which proxies to the model (since it's an `ObjectController`). The model (`group.js`) sets `members` via `setProperties` in `findMembers`. So `members` resolves to `model.members`. This works, but it's implicit. The `itemView="group-member"` references the view `admin/views/group-member.js.es6` which has `templateName: "admin/templates/group_member"`. The template `group_member.hbs` uses `{{#unless automatic}}` — `automatic` also proxies to the model. This is functional but fragile; if the controller ever defines a `members` property it would shadow the model's. Not a bug per se, but worth noting the implicit dependency.

`offset = Math.min(this.get("user_count"), Math.max(this.get("offset"), 0))` clamps the offset to be at most `user_count`. But a valid offset for pagination should be at most `user_count - limit` (or the server should handle it). Clamping to `user_count` allows requesting an offset equal to the total count, which returns an empty page. This is related to the pagination formula bug in the controller. The clamp should be `Math.min(this.get("user_count") - this.get("limit"), ...)` or simply pass the offset through and let the server handle bounds. As written, it permits an empty page request.

`total = group.users.count` executes a COUNT query, then `members = group.users.order(:username_lower).limit(limit).offset(offset)` executes another query. The `group.users` association is being queried twice. This could be optimized by using a single query with a window function or by using `group.users.count` once and reusing the relation. However, since `group.users` is an association, calling `.count` and then `.limit().offset()` on it separately does generate two SQL queries. This is a minor performance issue for large groups but not critical. A better approach would be to use `group.users.order(:username_lower).limit(limit).offset(offset)` and get the total from a separate count only if needed, or use `group.users.size` if the association is loaded. As written, it's two queries where one might suffice with proper SQL.

`removeMember` and `addMembers` construct URLs using `this.get('id')` (`/admin/groups/' + this.get('id') + '/members.json'`), while `findMembers` uses `this.get('name')` (`/groups/' + this.get('name') + '/members.json'`). This is intentional since admin routes use id and public routes use name. However, after a group is renamed via the admin UI (the `update` action sets `group.name = params[:name]`), the model's `name` property is updated locally, but if the user navigates away and back, or if the rename fails server-side, the cached `name` may be stale. More importantly, `findMembers` is called after `removeMember`/`addMembers` resolve, and it uses `this.get('name')` — if the group was just renamed in the same session, the name is correct. The real issue is that `findMembers` uses the public `/groups/:name/members.json` endpoint which requires the group to be visible (`guardian.ensure_can_see!`), whereas the admin is managing the group and should use the admin endpoint or the group should be visible to admins. If the group is not visible (`visible: false`), the public members endpoint will raise `Discourse::InvalidAccess` for non-admin users, but admins can see it. However, the admin UI calls `findMembers` which hits the public route — this works for admins but is semantically wrong; it should use an admin-specific endpoint or the existing admin show route. This is a design inconsistency that could cause permission errors if the public route's visibility check changes.

`group.users.delete(user_id)` will silently succeed even if the user_id does not exist or is not a member of the group. The endpoint returns success_json regardless. Additionally, if `user_id` refers to a non-existent user, the delete is a no-op but the response is still 200. This is misleading API behavior. More importantly, `group.users.delete(user_id)` followed by `group.save` is an odd pattern — `delete` on a has_many :through association already removes the join record immediately (it issues a DELETE), so calling `group.save` afterwards is unnecessary and may not do what the author expects. The correct approach is `group.users.delete(user)` after fetching the user, or `group.remove(user)` if such a method exists. As written, passing an arbitrary user_id will delete the membership if it exists, which is fine, but the silent success on non-members is a contract issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! has a race condition: check-then-act on @loaded_locales without the LOAD_MUTEX

The new `ensure_loaded!(locale)` method does `@loaded_locales ||= []` then `load_locale locale unless @loaded_locales.include?(locale)`. The `load_locale` method acquires `LOAD_MUTEX` and re-checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` inside the mutex, so concurrent calls to `load_locale` are safe. However, `ensure_loaded!` itself reads `@loaded_locales` without any synchronization. In a multi-threaded server (Puma, Passenger threaded mode), two threads can both observe `@loaded_locales` as nil or both pass the `unless` check before either calls `load_locale`. The `@loaded_locales ||= []` is also a non-atomic read-modify-write on a shared array. Worse, `translate` (line 68) also does `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)` without the mutex — this pre-existing pattern is now amplified because `ensure_loaded!` is called from `ApplicationController#set_locale` on every request. Consequence: duplicate locale loading (wasted work, potential `I18n::InvalidLocale` data races on the backend's translations hash), and in the worst case, concurrent mutation of `@loaded_locales` (an Array) during `include?` iteration causing `Concurrent::Ruby` errors or MRI crashes under heavy concurrency. The fix is to make `ensure_loaded!` delegate entirely to `load_locale` (which is already mutex-protected and idempotent) without the unsynchronized pre-check, e.g. `def ensure_loaded!(locale); load_locale(locale); end` — `load_locale` already returns early if loaded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
FallbackLocaleList#[] returns an Array, but I18n::Backend::Fallbacks expects a hash-like mapping of locale => fallbacks

`I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new` assigns a Hash subclass whose `#[]` returns an Array of locales (e.g. `[:fr, :en]`). The `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` module (from the i18n gem) expects `I18n.fallbacks` to respond to `[](locale)` returning the fallback chain for that locale — which an Array does satisfy — but it also calls `fallbacks[locale]` internally via `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` and maps over the result; more importantly, the standard Fallbacks implementation computes `fallbacks[locale]` and expects it to be an enumerable of locales, which works, BUT the Fallbacks module also relies on `I18n.fallbacks` being a `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` instance for methods like `ensure_loaded!` delegation and for computing defaults (`@map`). Overriding `#[]` on a plain Hash without populating the underlying hash means `I18n.fallbacks.map`, `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` in contexts expecting the stored mapping, and `I18n.fallbacks.defaults` will behave incorrectly or return empty. Additionally, `ensure_loaded!` defined on FallbackLocaleList shadows/conflicts with `I18n.ensure_loaded!` semantics. The implementation should either use `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks.new` with a custom mapping block, or properly implement the Fallbacks interface. As written, fallback resolution is fragile and likely broken when the Fallbacks module iterates the mapping.

FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded! calls I18n.ensure_loaded! with a locale argument, but I18n.ensure_loaded! takes no arguments in the i18n gem

`FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` does `self[I18n.locale].each { |l| I18n.ensure_loaded! l }`. However, the translate_accelerator patch (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb, line 62) defines `I18n.ensure_loaded!(locale)` as a class method on `I18n` that takes a locale argument — this is a custom extension, not part of the standard i18n gem. The standard `I18n.ensure_loaded!` (from the i18n gem) takes no arguments and ensures all configured locales are loaded. The custom `ensure_loaded!(locale)` in the accelerator shadows/extends this. This works only because the accelerator patch is loaded. But the initializer's `ensure_loaded!` method name on `FallbackLocaleList` conflicts conceptually with `I18n.ensure_loaded!`, and the call `I18n.ensure_loaded! l` relies on the accelerator's custom signature. If the accelerator patch is ever removed or refactored, or if the standard i18n gem's `ensure_loaded!` is called elsewhere expecting no arguments, this breaks. More concretely, `I18n.ensure_loaded!` in the standard gem is `def ensure_loaded!; backend.ensure_loaded!; end` — calling it with an argument raises `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (1 for 0)`. The accelerator's version accepts an argument, so it works, but this tight coupling between the initializer and the freedom patch is fragile and undocumented. The initializer should call `I18n.load_locale(l)` or the accelerator's method explicitly rather than overloading `ensure_loaded!`.

Fallbacks module included into wrong class, breaking I18n fallback resolution

The initializer does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)`. At initializer time, `I18n.backend` is an instance of `I18n::Backend::Simple`, so this includes Fallbacks into `I18n::Backend::Simple` itself. However, the translate_accelerator patch (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb) aliases `I18n.translate` to `translate_no_cache` and defines its own `translate` that calls `translate_no_cache(key, *args)`. The Fallbacks module works by overriding `translate` on the backend to walk the fallback chain; because the accelerator's `I18n.translate` calls the backend's `translate` directly (via the aliased original), and the Fallbacks module's `translate` override is defined on `I18n::Backend::Simple` while `I18n::Backend::Base#translate` is what actually gets invoked through the alias chain, the fallback chain (`I18n.fallbacks[locale]`) is never consulted during translation lookups. The `ensure_loaded!` calls in ApplicationController#set_locale and FallbackLocaleList only pre-load locale files into the backend; they do not make missing translations fall back to the site default locale or English. Consequence: any translation key missing from the user's locale will render as a 'translation missing' string instead of falling back, which is the entire purpose of this PR. The correct approach (as done in the actual Discourse codebase) is `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` — including into the Simple class, matching how the pluralization module is included on line 5 — and ensuring the backend chain composes with the accelerator.

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! called on every request in set_locale before_filter

`set_locale` is a `before_filter` that runs on every request. The added line `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` calls `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, which does `self[I18n.locale].each { |l| I18n.ensure_loaded! l }`. This iterates the fallback chain (up to 3 locales) and calls `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each, which delegates to the translate_accelerator's `ensure_loaded!` → `load_locale` → mutex acquisition + `include?` check. While `load_locale` short-circuits if already loaded, the method call overhead, array construction in `FallbackLocaleList#[]` (`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`), and `SiteSetting.default_locale` lookup (a DB-backed setting, potentially cached but still a method call) happen on every single request. For high-traffic endpoints this adds measurable per-request overhead. The `ensure_loaded!` call is only needed when the locale changes or on first use; it could be memoized per-locale or moved to only run when `I18n.locale` actually changes. Consequence: unnecessary per-request latency, especially since `set_locale` already sets `I18n.locale` and the translate_accelerator's `translate` method already lazily loads the current locale on demand (line 68).

Initializer ordering comment references a file that may not guarantee load order

The first line is `# order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb`. Discourse initializers in `config/initializers/` are loaded alphabetically by Rails unless explicitly ordered. The comment suggests the author believes this controls load order, but Rails does not parse `# order:` comments — that is a convention used by some Discourse-specific loaders or by `config/initializers` in certain plugin systems, but standard Rails `config/initializers/*.rb` files are loaded via `Dir.glob` in alphabetical order. The file is named `i18n.rb`, which sorts after `02-freedom_patches.rb` alphabetically (digits sort before letters in ASCII), so it likely works by accident. However, if the freedom patches are loaded via a custom mechanism (e.g., `lib/freedom_patches` required from `application.rb`), the `I18n::Backend::Simple` class may not yet be patched when this initializer runs, meaning `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` could include into the wrong class or the accelerator's `translate` override may not yet be in place. The dependency on `translate_accelerator.rb` being loaded first is implicit and fragile. Consequence: if load order changes, the Fallbacks module may be included before or after the accelerator patches, leading to broken translation caching or missing fallbacks.

Removal of config.i18n.fallbacks = true from environment configs is an API/contract change for deployments relying on Rails-level fallbacks

The PR removes `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` from `production.rb`, `profile.rb`, and `config/cloud/cloud66/files/production.rb`. These lines enabled Rails' built-in I18n fallback mechanism (`config.i18n.fallbacks = true` sets `I18n.fallbacks = I18n::Locale::Fallbacks.new` during initialization). The replacement is a custom initializer (`config/initializers/i18n.rb`) that sets `I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new`. However, Rails' `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` also triggers `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` and `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)` via the Rails I18n railtie during initialization, and sets up `I18n.fallbacks` with default mappings. By removing these lines and relying solely on the custom initializer, any code path that depends on `I18n.fallbacks` being a proper `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` instance (e.g., `I18n.fallbacks.defaults`, `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` returning a `Fallbacks` chain object, or `I18n.fallbacks.map`) will break. Additionally, the custom `FallbackLocaleList` does not implement the full `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` interface. This is a contract break for any plugin or external code that expects standard I18n fallback behavior. The initializer should either use `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` properly or ensure full interface compatibility.

SiteSetting.default_locale may be nil or a string, causing invalid fallback locale entries

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` calls `.to_sym` on `SiteSetting.default_locale` without a nil guard. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil (e.g., during early boot, in a fresh install before the setting is seeded, or in certain test environments), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'to_sym' for nil:NilClass`, which would crash the initializer and prevent the application from booting. The `.compact` on the array suggests the author intended to handle nils, but `.to_sym` is called before `compact` can remove it. This should be `SiteSetting.default_locale && SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` or use `Array(SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym)` with a safe navigation. Consequence: boot failure or request-time 500 errors in environments where the site setting is not yet populated.

translate reads @loaded_locales without synchronization, racing with load_locale mutations

`def translate(key, *args)` on line 68 does `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`. The `@loaded_locales` array is mutated inside `load_locale` under `LOAD_MUTEX` (line 58: `@loaded_locales << locale`), but the `include?` check on line 68 is performed outside any mutex. In MRI, Array#<< and Array#include? are individually atomic-ish due to the GVL, but the check-then-act pattern means a thread can pass the `unless` check (locale not yet loaded) and then call `load_locale`, which is fine due to the internal re-check. However, `@loaded_locales` may be nil on the very first call if `ensure_loaded!` or `load_locale` hasn't run — line 68 would raise `NoMethodError: undefined method 'include?' for nil:NilClass` because unlike `ensure_loaded!` (line 63), `translate` does not initialize `@loaded_locales ||= []` before the `include?` check. This is a latent nil-dereference bug that can surface on the first translation call in a fresh process before any `ensure_loaded!` has run. The `reload!` method (line 39) also resets `@loaded_locales = []` without the mutex, which can race with concurrent `translate` calls.

The new guard has two problems: (1) during re-authentication (prompt=login) the user IS already set in the context, so the condition is true and fillContextForm runs — but the intent of the original code was to enable the conditional UI on the username form when NO user is known yet; (2) more importantly, the companion change in challenge(context, error, field) (line 137) uses the same isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()) guard, so after a failed password attempt during re-authentication the WebAuthn conditional-UI attributes are re-populated only when a user is set — which is the re-authentication case — but the initial challenge path and the UsernameForm skip logic interact such that the passkey conditional UI is not offered where it should be. This inverts the original behavior and will suppress the passkey conditional UI on the first-step login form in flows where the user is pre-set (e.g. organization authenticator or IdP brokering sets the user before the username/password form), preventing passwordless passkey login for those users. New shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() indirection is a no-op refactor that obscures the original condition

The change replaces `if (user != null)` with `if (shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context))` where the new protected method (lines 128-130) simply returns `context.getUser() != null`. The constant is an implementation detail of the username/password form authenticators; it should either remain in the browser package and be accessed via a public method on AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator (e.g. a static helper `isUserAlreadySetBeforeUsernamePasswordAuth(context)` which already exists as a protected instance method at line 257), or be moved to a neutral location. The PR changed both assertions (lines 200 and 211) to `MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), Matchers.notNullValue())`, so NoSuchElementException is no longer referenced anywhere in the file. The import `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` (line 51) is now unused. This is a minor cleanliness issue (unused import) that will cause checkstyle/IDE warnings; it should be removed. Note that PasskeysUsernameFormTest still uses NoSuchElementException (line 202) so its import is still needed there.

WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse() now calls AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context) on every passkey error. That utility (AuthenticatorUtils.java lines 125-133) sets LoginFormsProvider.USERNAME_HIDDEN=true and REGISTRATION_DISABLED=true only when the auth note USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH is 'true'. The note is set in UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate() only when context.getUser() != null (line 102). However, this authenticator is also used from UsernameForm flows and potentially other flows where the note may be stale: the note is removed in UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate() only in the `else` branch (line 104), but if a previous authentication attempt in the same authentication session set the note (e.g. user was identified, then the flow restarted or a different authenticator ran), the note can persist and cause the username field to be hidden on a subsequent error page even though the current challenge is for a fresh login where the user must type their username. More concretely: in the UsernameForm flow (PasskeysUsernameFormTest), after the user submits a username, the PasswordForm runs; if a passkey error occurs there, createErrorResponse() is invoked and — because the note was never set in that flow (UsernameForm does not set USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH) — the utility correctly does nothing. But in the UsernamePasswordForm flow, if the user first fails a password (note set, username hidden), then the passkey conditional UI errors, the error page keeps the username hidden — which is intended. The risk is that the note is session-scoped and not cleared when the authentication session restarts the flow (e.g. after a 'try again' or restart), so a stale 'true' note can hide the username on a fresh login form. The utility should be defensive, but more importantly the note lifecycle is not reset when the user is cleared (context.clearUser() in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.badPasswordHandler clears the user but not the note), so a user who fails password (note set), then somehow gets the user cleared and re-enters a username, would see a hidden username field with no way to correct it.
