The PR adds 7 new keys (`cache_status`, `cache_last_updated`, `delete_cached_data`, `cache_deleted_successfully`, `error_deleting_cache`, `confirm_delete_cache`, `yes_delete_cache`) only to the English locale file. Cal.com's i18n setup (next-i18next with `ADD_NEW_STRINGS_ABOVE_THIS_LINE_TO_PREVENT_MERGE_CONFLICTS`) expects translations to be contributed for other locales, typically via the `translate-locales` script or Crowdin. Until other locales are updated, non-English users will see either the English fallback or the raw key (depending on `fallbackLng` config). This is a known workflow in the repo, but the PR should either run the translation pipeline or note that translations are pending. At minimum, verify the fallback behavior so users don't see raw keys like `cache_deleted_successfully`.

Script writes a public tunnel URL into ../.env, potentially committing a webhook endpoint that exposes the local Google Calendar webhook to the internet

The script sets `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` in `../.env` to a public `*.tunnelmole.net` URL. The Google Calendar webhook handler at `/api/integrations/googlecalendar/webhook` is protected by `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_TOKEN`, but this script's purpose is to expose a local dev server to Google's push notifications. Risks: (1) the tunnel URL is written into a file that developers may accidentally commit (`.env` is typically gitignored, but `../.env` relative to `scripts/` is the repo-root `.env` — verify it is ignored); (2) the tunnel stays alive for the whole script session, leaving a public route into the developer's machine; (3) the script reuses an already-running tmole (`pgrep -f "tmole $TM_PORT"`) without verifying it belongs to this project, potentially overwriting `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` for an unrelated tunnel. At minimum the script should warn that the tunnel is public and ensure `.env` is gitignored.

Stale TODO comment says updatedAt 'doesn't exist yet in CalendarCache table' but the column was just added by this PR

Line 116 contains `// TODO: For better tracking we could also want to use updatedAt directly which doesn't exist yet in CalendarCache table`. This PR adds the `updatedAt` column to CalendarCache (schema.prisma + migration). The TODO is now obsolete: `updatedAt` exists and is exactly what `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` uses. The ordering logic in `getCachedAvailability` (orderBy `expiresAt: "desc"`) could now also consider `updatedAt`, or the TODO should be removed/updated so future readers are not misled into thinking the column is missing.

Unrelated refactor of findMany (removing satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs) is bundled into this PR

The diff changes `findMany` from building `const args = { where, select, orderBy } satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs; return await prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany(args);` to a direct `return await prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany({ where, select, orderBy });`. This change is unrelated to the calendar-cache feature (it removes a type-safety assertion). It is not needed for the feature and slightly reduces type checking strictness; it should be reverted or split into its own PR so reviewers can evaluate it independently.

cacheUpdatedAt prop is typed as Date but tRPC serializes dates as strings over the wire with superjson disabled or as Date with superjson — type may mismatch at runtime

The prop is `cacheUpdatedAt?: Date | null` and the component does `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` before formatting, which works for both Date and string. However, the tRPC `RouterOutputs` type for `connectedCalendars` will type `cacheUpdatedAt` according to the transformer. Cal.com uses superjson, which preserves Date instances, so the type is likely correct. But the defensive `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` suggests uncertainty. If the transformer ever changes or the platform atoms package consumes this without superjson, the `Date` type would be a lie and `Intl.DateTimeFormat.format()` would receive a string (which `new Date()` handles, so it works). This is a minor robustness note: either trust the type and drop the `new Date()` wrapper, or type the prop as `Date | string | null` to be explicit. Low severity because the current code handles both.

connectedCalendars now always instantiates CalendarCacheRepository and runs an extra groupBy query even when calendar-cache is disabled

The handler unconditionally constructs `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds)` on every `connectedCalendars` query. The codebase has a `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` used precisely when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (the mock logs "Skipping ... due to calendar-cache being disabled"), and `CalendarCache.init(null)` elsewhere selects mock vs. real based on configuration. Here the real repository is always used, so every connectedCalendars call — including for users/teams without the calendar-cache feature — pays for an extra `groupBy` DB query. This adds latency to a frequently-called query (it is used with `suspense: true` in the settings UI and onboarding). The handler should use the same feature-detection used by `CalendarCache.init` (e.g. check the team feature flag / `getCalendarCacheRepository()` factory) and skip the query entirely when the feature is disabled, returning `cacheUpdatedAt: null`.

credentialIds may contain in-memory delegation credential ids (negative numbers) which are passed to a DB groupBy query

`connectedCalendars.map((cal) => cal.credentialId)` can include negative in-memory delegation credential ids (the codebase uses negative ids for in-memory delegation credentials, see `isInMemoryDelegationCredential` and `assertCalendarHasDbCredential` which throws for `credentialId < 0`). These ids are passed straight into `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy({ where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } } })`. Prisma will happily query with negative integers (no rows match), so this is not a crash, but it is wasted work and signals the handler does not account for delegation credentials. The `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` call should filter to DB-backed credential ids (e.g. `credentialIds.filter(id => id > 0)`) or the repository should guard, consistent with `assertCalendarHasDbCredential` used elsewhere in the same package.

deleteCache authorization check misses delegation credentials, allowing cache deletion for credentials the user does not own

The handler verifies ownership with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. In cal.com, delegation credentials (service-account based Google Calendar connections) are stored as Credential rows whose `userId` is null (they are linked via `delegatedToId` / `delegationCredentialId`), so this check correctly rejects them. However, the inverse problem exists: a regular user credential can be *delegated to* another user (credential.delegatedToId set, credential.userId still set to the owner). More importantly, the UI passes `connectedCalendar.credentialId` which for delegation-credential-connected calendars is a negative in-memory credential id or a credential belonging to the org, and the `connectedCalendars` query returns calendars the logged-in user can see but does not own. The ownership check only covers `userId`, not team/org membership or delegation relationships, so any authenticated user who can obtain a credentialId (e.g. via the connectedCalendars response of a shared/team context, or by guessing sequential ids combined with a leaked id) can delete another user's calendar cache. Cache deletion forces expensive re-fetches and can be used to degrade availability data (a denial-of-service vector on the calendar-cache feature). The check should verify the credential belongs to the user OR to a delegation credential the user is authorized to manage, and should reject in-memory (negative) credential ids explicitly.

deleteCache input schema is defined inline instead of a dedicated schema file, inconsistent with sibling procedures

The router defines `deleteCache` with an inline `z.object({ credentialId: z.number() })`, while `connectedCalendars` and `setDestinationCalendar` import dedicated schemas (`ZConnectedCalendarsInputSchema`, `ZSetDestinationCalendarInputSchema`) from `./connectedCalendars.schema` and `./setDestinationCalendar.schema`. The codebase convention (visible in the same file) is one schema file per procedure. This inconsistency makes the input schema harder to discover/reuse (e.g. for platform API parity or client-side validation) and will drift from the handler's `DeleteCacheOptions` type, which is declared separately in `deleteCache.handler.ts` with no compile-time link to the zod schema. Create `deleteCache.schema.ts` exporting `ZDeleteCacheInputSchema` and use it in both the router and the handler type (`z.infer<typeof ZDeleteCacheInputSchema>`).

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, so the cache status UI stays stale after deletion

The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls `onSuccess?.()`. The `disconnectMutation` explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`, but the delete-cache mutation does not. After a successful cache deletion, the `connectedCalendars` query still returns the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show "Cache Status: Last updated ..." and the "Delete cached data" option even though the cache rows were deleted. The component relies on the parent's `onChanged` callback to refetch, but `onChanged` is optional and in `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` it is passed through from props without any guaranteed invalidation. The mutation should invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (at minimum) in `onSettled`, mirroring the disconnect mutation.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds does not guard against an empty credentialIds array, issuing a pointless groupBy query

When `connectedCalendars` is empty (a user with no connected calendar apps, or all filtered out by `_ensureNoConflictingNonDelegatedConnectedCalendar`), `credentialIds` is `[]` and the handler still calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds([])`, which issues `SELECT credentialId, MAX(updatedAt) FROM CalendarCache WHERE credentialId IN () GROUP BY credentialId`. Prisma translates `IN ()` to a `FALSE`/`0 = 1` condition, so the query is cheap but still a round-trip to the DB on every connectedCalendars call for users with no calendars. The repository method (or the handler) should early-return `[]` when `credentialIds.length === 0`.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds includes expired cache rows, so the UI shows a stale 'last updated' timestamp for expired caches

The `groupBy` query filters only by `credentialId: { in: credentialIds }` and takes `_max: { updatedAt: true }`. It does not filter on `expiresAt >= now()`, unlike `getCachedAvailability` which requires `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`. Consequence: after a cache entry expires (CACHING_TIME = 30 days), the connectedCalendars handler still reports a `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the UI shows "Cache Status: Last updated <date>" and offers "Delete cached data" for a cache that is no longer being served. Deleting it is harmless but misleading; worse, the displayed timestamp suggests fresh data when the cache is actually dead, which can mislead users debugging availability issues. The query should add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to the `where` clause.

updateManyByCredentialId accepts Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput but the only caller passes {}, hiding the fact that it can update arbitrary fields across all of a credential's calendars

The new method signature is `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId: number, data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput)`. `SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` allows updating any scalar field (externalId, integration, userId, eventTypeId, googleChannelId, etc.) across every SelectedCalendar row for a credential. That is a broad, potentially dangerous primitive (e.g. it could reassign calendars to another userId or change externalId en masse). The only current caller passes `{}`, so the method's real purpose is "touch updatedAt". The signature should be narrowed to reflect actual intent — e.g. `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId: number)` that internally sets `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`, or accept a restricted `Pick<Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput, "updatedAt">` — so future callers cannot accidentally mass-modify integrity-sensitive fields.

updateManyByCredentialId is called with an empty data object, relying on Prisma @updatedAt side effect with no explicit intent

`await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes an empty `data` object. The only effect is that Prisma touches `updatedAt` (because the schema has `@updatedAt` on SelectedCalendar). This is obscure: a reader cannot tell whether the empty object is a bug or intentional. The PR description itself notes "Consider if SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update should be removed." Either make the intent explicit with a comment or pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` explicitly, or remove the call if the timestamp is not consumed anywhere (the frontend uses `cacheUpdatedAt` from CalendarCache, not SelectedCalendar.updatedAt).

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation calls are not awaited, so the booking-cancel request can complete before reminders are marked cancelled

The block `updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => { booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { ... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); ... }) })` calls the async `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` functions without `await` and without collecting the promises. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` performs a Prisma `update` (setting `cancelled: true`) and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` performs a Twilio cancel plus a Prisma `delete`. Because these promises are not awaited, the handler proceeds to `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and returns a 200 while the reminder updates may still be in flight or may fail silently (both functions swallow errors with `console.log`). If the process is under load or the DB write is slow, the response can be sent before `cancelled: true` is persisted; a crash or early return leaves scheduled emails unsuppressed. The promises must be collected and awaited (the previous code did this via `remindersToDelete` / `PrismaPromise` array).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true cancels the SendGrid send but never deletes or marks the WorkflowReminder row

In `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminderId, referenceId, immediateDelete)`, when `immediateDelete` is true the function calls SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `status: "cancel"` and then `return`s — it never deletes the `WorkflowReminder` database row nor sets `cancelled: true`. Callers that pass `immediateDelete: true` are `handleNewBooking.ts` (reschedule path, line 968) and `workflows.tsx` (workflow deleted / step deleted, lines 214 and 521). Consequence: after a booking is rescheduled, the old booking's reminder rows remain in the DB with `scheduled: true` and the old `referenceId`. The CRON job `scheduleEmailReminders` only deletes rows with `scheduledDate <= now`, so these stale rows persist; worse, the `unscheduledReminders` query filters on `scheduled: false`, but any code path that re-reads these rows (e.g. a later cancel of the same booking) will attempt to cancel an already-cancelled batch id. The reminder row must be deleted (or marked cancelled) in the `immediateDelete` branch as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New 'cancelled' column is nullable with no default, so existing and new rows have NULL instead of false

The migration adds `"cancelled" BOOLEAN` with no `NOT NULL` and no `DEFAULT false`. The Prisma schema declares `cancelled Boolean?` (nullable). All existing rows get NULL, and new `workflowReminder.create` calls in `emailReminderManager.ts` / `smsReminderManager.ts` do not set `cancelled`, so new rows are also NULL. The CRON query in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` filters `cancelled: true`, which works, but any future query filtering `cancelled: false` (a natural way to express 'not cancelled') will silently miss all NULL rows, and the `unscheduledReminders` query (which needs to exclude cancelled reminders, see related finding) cannot simply use `cancelled: false`. The column should be `BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false` with a backfill (`UPDATE "WorkflowReminder" SET "cancelled" = false WHERE "cancelled" IS NULL`) and the schema should be `cancelled Boolean @default(false)`.

false_positives.candidate:
A single failed SendGrid cancellation aborts the whole loop and skips deletion of remaining cancelled reminders

The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop awaits `client.request(...)` inside a single `try/catch` that wraps the entire loop. If the SendGrid call for the first reminder throws (network error, invalid batch_id, expired batch), the catch swallows it and the loop exits, so no further reminders are cancelled and none of the `workflowReminder.delete` promises (collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete`) are awaited. Cancelled reminders whose scheduled date is within the hour will then remain in the DB with `cancelled: true` and, because the earlier `deleteMany` only removes reminders with `scheduledDate <= now`, they can be re-processed on the next run — but more importantly, reminders later in the list never get their SendGrid scheduled send cancelled, so the emails are still sent. Each reminder's cancellation should be individually try/caught, and the DB delete should only happen after a successful SendGrid cancel (or be retried).

CRON cancellation query does not filter by method, so SMS reminders are also picked up and 'cancelled' via SendGrid

The new query `prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(1, "hour") } } })` selects ALL cancelled reminders regardless of `method`. For SMS reminders, `referenceId` is a Twilio message SID, not a SendGrid batch_id, so the subsequent `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: reminder.referenceId` will either fail or, worse, attempt to cancel an unrelated SendGrid batch if a SID collides with a batch id. The query must include `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` (and ideally `scheduled: true` / `referenceId: { not: null }`), otherwise SMS reminders marked cancelled are never actually cancelled in Twilio and are deleted from the DB by this job, leaving the scheduled SMS to still be delivered.

Multiple reminder-cancellation loops in the update mutation are not awaited

In the `update` mutation there are three separate `forEach` loops that call the async `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting them: (1) `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach(...)` around line 376 (event types disabled), (2) `remindersToUpdate.forEach(async (reminder) => {...})` around line 574 (edited steps — the callback is async but forEach still doesn't await it), and (3) the deleted-step branch around line 519. None of the returned promises are collected or awaited, and the mutation proceeds to delete workflow steps / update the workflow and returns. Consequences: the HTTP response can be sent before the Prisma `update({cancelled: true})` / `delete` and Twilio cancels complete; failures are swallowed by the `console.log` inside the manager functions; and because `workflowStep.delete` runs right after, the `workflowReminder` rows (which have `onDelete: Cascade` to the step) may be cascade-deleted by Prisma before the manager's own `delete`/`update` executes, causing the manager's DB writes to fail on a missing row while the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation may or may not have happened — leaving provider-side scheduled sends alive with no DB record to retry. All cancellation promises must be gathered (e.g. `await Promise.all(reminders.map(...))`) before deleting steps.

Reschedule path does not await reminder cancellations and uses immediateDelete which leaves stale DB rows

In the reschedule branch, `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); ... })` is not awaited (the functions are async and perform SendGrid/Prisma/Twilio calls), and the surrounding `try/catch` only catches synchronous errors — any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Additionally, per the `emailReminderManager.ts` finding, the `immediateDelete: true` path never deletes or marks the `WorkflowReminder` row, so the old booking's reminders stay in the DB with `scheduled: true`. Since the old booking is not deleted on reschedule (it is kept for history), these stale rows are never cleaned up by the `scheduledDate <= now` deleteMany in the CRON (they only get removed once their scheduled date passes), and any later operation iterating `workflowReminders` of the old booking will try to cancel an already-cancelled SendGrid batch. The calls must be awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`) and the reminder rows must be removed.

Sender ID input is now rendered for EMAIL actions, allowing users to set an SMS sender ID on email steps

The refactor changed the wrapper condition from `{(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded) && (...)}` to a separate `isPhoneNumberNeeded` block plus an unconditional `<div className="mt-2 rounded-md bg-gray-50 p-4 pt-0">` that renders either the Sender ID input (when `isSenderIdNeeded`) or the Sender Name input. `isSenderIdNeeded` is initialized to `true` when `step?.action === SMS_NUMBER || step?.action === SMS_ATTENDEE`, but it is only ever set to `false` in the action `onChange` handler — for an existing EMAIL step loaded from the DB, `isSenderIdNeeded` stays `false`, so this is mostly fine; however the sender block is now always rendered even for actions where neither sender ID nor sender name is relevant, and the `isSenderIdNeeded` state is not re-synced when `step` changes (component reuse across steps), so switching between steps in the UI can show the wrong sender field. This is a UI-state regression introduced by the restructuring; the sender block should be gated on `isSenderIdNeeded || !isEmailSubjectNeeded` (or equivalent) and the state should be derived from the current action.

The 'unscheduled reminders' query can pick up reminders that were just marked cancelled, causing emails for cancelled bookings to be scheduled and sent

The query for `unscheduledReminders` filters on `method: EMAIL, scheduled: false, scheduledDate <= now + 72h`. It does not exclude rows with `cancelled: true`. A reminder that was created with `scheduled: false` (scheduled date more than 72h out, see `emailReminderManager.ts` line 184) and later cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (which only sets `cancelled: true` and leaves `scheduled: false`) will match this query on the next CRON run. The job will then create a SendGrid batch, send the email with `sendAt`, and set `scheduled: true` — resurrecting a reminder for a cancelled/rescheduled booking. The query must add `cancelled: { not: true }` (or `cancelled: false` / `OR: [{cancelled: null}, {cancelled: false}]` since the column is nullable).

The initial deleteMany removes past-due reminders regardless of cancelled/scheduled state, deleting rows that the new cancellation logic depends on

The first statement `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` deletes every EMAIL reminder whose scheduled date has passed, including rows with `cancelled: true` that have not yet been processed by the new cancellation block (which runs after this delete). If a reminder was marked cancelled but its scheduled date is already in the past (e.g. the booking was cancelled after the reminder's scheduled send time but before SendGrid actually delivered it, or the CRON was down), this deleteMany removes the row before the cancellation loop can call SendGrid to cancel the scheduled send — so the email is never cancelled at the provider and will still be delivered. The deleteMany should exclude cancelled rows (`cancelled: { not: true }`) or the cancellation block should run before it.

WorkflowReminder rows are deleted even when the SendGrid cancellation was never confirmed, and reminders without a referenceId are deleted without any provider call

The code unconditionally pushes `prisma.workflowReminder.delete({ where: { id: reminder.id } })` into `workflowRemindersToDelete` right after issuing the SendGrid cancel request, without checking the response and without handling reminders that have `cancelled: true` but `referenceId: null` (e.g. reminders that were never scheduled with SendGrid because they were beyond the 72h window and `scheduled: false`). For those, `batch_id: null` is sent to SendGrid. Deleting the DB row removes the only record that the email still needs to be cancelled, so if the SendGrid request silently fails or the row had no referenceId, the scheduled email will be sent and there is no longer any state to retry the cancellation. The delete should only occur after a successful provider cancellation, and rows without a referenceId should be handled explicitly.

deleteScheduledSMSReminder deletes the DB row even when the Twilio cancellation fails

`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` wraps both `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` in a single try/catch. If `cancelSMS` throws (Twilio API error, already-completed message, invalid SID), the catch logs the error and the Prisma `delete` is never executed — that part is fine — but the inverse is also true: there is no verification that the Twilio cancellation succeeded before the row is removed, and more importantly the function gives callers no signal of failure (it always resolves). Combined with the un-awaited call sites, a failed Twilio cancel is indistinguishable from success, and because the row is deleted on success while the CRON has no equivalent SMS-cancellation path (the new CRON logic only handles EMAIL), a missed Twilio cancellation means the SMS will still be delivered with no DB record left to retry. The function should rethrow or return a status so callers can react, and the CRON should also process cancelled SMS reminders.

requestReschedule does not await reminder cancellation calls

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` invokes async functions without `await` and discards the returned promises. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` performs a Prisma `update` setting `cancelled: true` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` performs a Twilio cancel plus a Prisma `delete`; both swallow errors internally. Because they are not awaited, the mutation can return success before the reminders are actually cancelled/marked, and any failure is silently lost (only a console.log). If the DB update hasn't committed when the request finishes, the CRON job may not see `cancelled: true` in time and the scheduled email/SMS for the old booking slot will still be sent. The promises must be collected and awaited before the mutation returns.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getVideoAdapters silently skips apps whose dynamic import rejects, with no error handling

`const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore];` at line 26 awaits a dynamic import inside a `for` loop with no try/catch. If the dynamic import fails (e.g. chunk load error, network failure in production, or a missing/renamed app directory), the entire `getVideoAdapters` promise rejects. Callers like `createMeeting` (line 52) call `await getVideoAdapters([credential])` outside of any try/catch that would handle this specific failure — the `try` block in `createMeeting` starts at line 70, after `getVideoAdapters` at line 52. So a failed chunk load will cause `createMeeting` to throw an unhandled error instead of falling back to Cal Video (the fallback logic at lines 86-97 only catches errors from `firstVideoAdapter?.createMeeting`, not from `getVideoAdapters`). Same for `updateMeeting` (line 111) and `deleteMeeting` (line 144). Consequence: a transient chunk-loading failure breaks meeting creation entirely instead of degrading to the Cal Video fallback. Add a try/catch around the `await appStore[...]` (or around the whole loop) that logs and skips the credential, matching the previous behavior where a missing app simply produced no adapter.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions before sending reschedule email

The code uses `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await the promises returned by its callback, so the `await getCalendar(...)` and the subsequent `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` calls run as fire-and-forget. The function proceeds immediately to `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` (line 143) and returns `true` before the external calendar events and video meetings have actually been deleted. Consequences: (1) the reschedule email can be sent while the old event still exists on the provider's calendar, causing double-booking; (2) errors thrown inside the async callback are not caught by the surrounding `try/catch` (which only catches synchronous throws), so deletion failures are silently swallowed and never logged; (3) the outer `try/catch` around a `forEach` is effectively dead code for async errors. The same pattern exists in `packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts` line 125 and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 553. These should be rewritten with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` so deletions complete (or fail loudly) before the email is sent.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests cover the async appStore contract; consumers that forget to await will fail silently at runtime

The PR converts every `appStore` entry from an eagerly-imported module namespace into a dynamic-import `Promise`. This is a breaking change to the shape of the default export, and the safety of the migration depends entirely on every call site remembering to `await` the indexed value before accessing `.lib` / `.config`. The PR updates the known call sites, but there is no test that exercises `appStore` access patterns (e.g. a unit test asserting `await appStore.googlecalendar` exposes `lib.CalendarService`, or a type-level test that `appStore` values are promises). A consumer that does `const app = appStore[x]; if ("lib" in app)` without `await` will silently skip the integration (the `"lib" in app` check on a Promise is false) with no error. Recommend adding a test that iterates all appStore entries, awaits them, and asserts each resolves to a module with the expected shape, plus a type test ensuring consumers must await.

Warn message interpolates the module object instead of the app type string

Line 18: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — `paymentApp` is now the awaited module namespace (an object), so the log will render the app type as `[object Module]` instead of the actual dirName. This makes the warning useless for debugging which payment app is misconfigured. Use `paymentAppCredentials?.app?.dirName` in the message. Same issue in `packages/lib/payment/handlePayment.ts` line 28 and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 969.

Warn message interpolates the module object instead of the app type string

Line 28: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — `paymentApp` is the awaited module namespace object, so the message prints `[object Module]` rather than the payment app's dirName. This obscures which app failed. Interpolate `paymentAppCredentials?.app?.dirName` instead. Same defect in `packages/lib/payment/deletePayment.ts` line 18, `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts` line 591, and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 969.

Warn message interpolates the module object instead of the app type string

Line 969: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — after `const paymentApp = await appStore[...]`, `paymentApp` is the resolved module namespace object, so the warning prints `[object Module]` instead of the payment app's dirName, making it impossible to tell which app is unimplemented. Use `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` in the template string.

Warn message logs the awaited module object instead of the app type when PaymentService is missing

After the change `const paymentApp = await appStore[paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName as keyof typeof appStore];`, the guard at line 590 checks `"PaymentService" in paymentApp.lib`, and the warning at line 591 is `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);`. Since `paymentApp` is now the resolved module namespace object (not a string), the log message will print `[object Module]` or similar instead of the app's dirName/type. The same wrong-message pattern exists in `packages/lib/payment/deletePayment.ts` line 18, `packages/lib/payment/handlePayment.ts` line 28, and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 969. The message should reference `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` (the string) so operators can identify which payment app failed to load.

appStore values are now dynamic-import Promises, breaking all synchronous consumers and the exported type contract

The module now exports an object whose every value is a `Promise<typeof import(...)>` (e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`), whereas previously the values were the resolved module namespaces. The default export's type has silently changed from `{ applecalendar: typeof import("./applecalendar"), ... }` to `{ applecalendar: Promise<typeof import("./applecalendar")>, ... }`. Every consumer that does `appStore[key]` and then accesses `.lib`, `.config`, etc. without `await` will now receive a Promise and fail at runtime (e.g. `"lib" in app` on a Promise is false, so integrations will be silently skipped). The PR updates some call sites (`getCalendar.ts`, `videoClient.ts`, payment handlers) but the type contract of the default export is broken for any consumer not updated, and TypeScript may not catch this if consumers use `keyof typeof appStore` indexing with `await` inconsistently. Additionally, `import("./applecalendar")` at module top-level means all app modules are still referenced at build time (defeating some bundling benefits unless the bundler code-splits), and any circular-import or side-effect ordering that previously relied on eager `import * as` evaluation may change. The maintainers should ensure every `appStore[...]` access site is audited and `await`ed, and consider exporting a typed async accessor function instead of a raw object of promises to make misuse a compile error.

forEach callback pushes deleteMeeting promises without awaiting them

In the legacy video-credential fallback branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach((credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deleteMeeting(credential, uidToDelete)); })` (lines 505-511) pushes the promises returned by `deleteMeeting` into `apiDeletes` synchronously. That part is fine because `apiDeletes` is later awaited via `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 — however, note that `deleteMeeting` is now `async` and internally awaits `getVideoAdapters`, so the promise is correctly deferred. The real issue is that this `forEach` is not awaited itself, but since it only pushes promises (no `await` inside), it is actually safe. On review, this specific block is correct; the concern is only the adjacent async `forEach` at line 460. No change needed here beyond verifying `apiDeletes` is awaited, which it is at line 652.

forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions before sending reschedule email

Identical to the vital reschedule issue: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` at line 125 does not await the async work. The `await getCalendar(...)` and `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` calls are fire-and-forget, so `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` at line 143 runs before external events are deleted, and any rejection inside the callback escapes the surrounding `try/catch` (which cannot catch async errors from `forEach`). This can cause the reschedule email to be sent while the old calendar event still exists (double-booking) and silently swallow deletion failures. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions in requestReschedule

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` (line 553) does not await the async callback. The `await getCalendar(...)` at line 556 and the `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` calls are fire-and-forget: the mutation proceeds to `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` (line 570) and then sends webhooks (line 618) without waiting for the old calendar events and video meetings to be deleted. Consequences: the reschedule confirmation email and BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks can fire while the old event still exists on the external provider (double-booking window), and any error thrown inside the async callback is not caught (there is no try/catch here at all), producing unhandled promise rejections. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

forEach with async callback does not await per-credential calendar deletions for recurring bookings

In the recurring-event cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... await calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... })` (lines 460-470) uses `forEach` with an async callback. The promises are never awaited, so `apiDeletes` may be populated after `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 has already run (or the deletions may still be in flight when the handler returns). Consequences: external calendar events for recurring bookings may not be deleted before the response is sent, deletion errors become unhandled rejections, and the booking can be reported as cancelled in the DB while the provider-side events remain. Replace with `await Promise.all(credentials.map(async (credential) => { ... }))` and push results into `apiDeletes`, or collect promises and await them before line 652.

getCachedResults awaits all calendar module loads serially with Promise.all before starting availability fetches, adding latency

`const calendars = await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)));` at line 142 now awaits all dynamic imports before any `getAvailability` call begins. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous so this was instant. Now, on a cold start (first request after deploy, or when chunks are not cached), every calendar credential's module must be fetched and evaluated before availability fetching starts, serializing module-load latency ahead of the actual work. This is partially mitigated by `Promise.all` (loads happen in parallel), but the availability fetches (the expensive part) cannot start until all modules are loaded. A better pattern would be to interleave: map each credential to an async function that awaits `getCalendar` and then immediately calls `getAvailability`, all within a single `Promise.all`, so module loading and availability fetching overlap. As written, cold-start latency for the busy-times endpoint increases by the full module-load time.

getCalendar result awaited but deleteEvent call not awaited inside updateAllCalendarEvents merge path

In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, the merge path (when `newBookingId` is set) does `const calendar = await getCalendar(calendarCredential);` at line 488 followed by `await calendar?.deleteEvent(oldCalendarEvent.uid, event, oldCalendarEvent.externalCalendarId);` at line 489. The `await` on line 489 is present, so this specific call is fine. However, note that `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` — if `calendar` is `null` (e.g. unknown credential type or failed dynamic import), the expression short-circuits to `undefined` and `await undefined` resolves immediately, silently skipping the deletion of the old calendar event during a booking merge. There is no log or error when the old event fails to be deleted, so a merge can leave an orphaned event on the external calendar. Consider logging when `calendar` is null in this path.

getCalendarCredentials calls async getCalendar without await, storing a Promise instead of a Calendar instance

`getCalendar` was changed to be `async` (returns `Promise<Calendar | null>`), but `getCalendarCredentials` (line 23-36) is still a synchronous function that does `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` at line 28 without `await`. As a result, `calendar` is a `Promise`, not a `Calendar` instance, and it is stored in the returned objects as `{ integration: app, credential, calendar }`. Downstream, `getConnectedCalendars` (line 48) does `const calendar = await item.calendar;` which happens to unwrap the promise, masking the bug there — but any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` that treats `calendar` as a `Calendar` (e.g. calling `calendar.listCalendars()` or `calendar.createEvent(...)` directly without awaiting) will break at runtime with "calendar.listCalendars is not a function" or operate on a Promise. The function must either become `async` and `await getCalendar(credential)`, or callers must be audited. This is a latent type-safety/runtime break introduced by the async conversion.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check in checkIfIsAvailable uses wrong start/end values, making the check ineffective

In the newly added working-hours validation inside `checkIfIsAvailable`, both `start` and `end` are computed identically as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` (lines 141-142). The `end` should be the slot end time (`slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`), not a copy of the start. As written, the condition `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` only rejects slots whose start minute-of-day falls outside the working-hours window; it never rejects a slot that starts inside working hours but extends past the end of the working-hours window (e.g. a 60-minute event starting at the last 30 minutes of an availability block). This means the new working-hours guard — which is the mechanism that makes fixed-host date overrides restrict round-robin slots — fails to block slots that overrun the override/working-hours end, so round-robin events can still be booked at times when the fixed host is unavailable. Fix: compute `end` from `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date-override containment checks in checkIfIsAvailable compare instants with `===` on Dayjs objects and mis-handle blocked (zero-length) overrides

In the new date-override block, `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` (line 114) compares two distinct Dayjs object instances with `===`, which is always `false` — object identity, not value equality. The intent (per the surrounding logic: a zero-length override means 'blocked/unavailable all day') is to detect a blocked day, but the comparison never fires, so an all-day 'unavailable' override (start === end) falls through to the range checks and the slot is treated as available during the blocked day. The correct check is `.isSame(...)` (or comparing the underlying timestamps). Additionally, the containment logic returns `true` from the `find` callback when the slot is entirely before the override start or entirely after the override end, which makes `dateOverrides.find(...)` truthy and causes `return false` ('slot is not within the date override') — i.e. any slot on a day that has any override but falls outside the override window is rejected, which is correct only if the override replaces the whole day; combined with the broken zero-length check, blocked days and partial overrides interact incorrectly. The comparisons should use `.isSame()`/`.isBefore()`/`.isAfter()` consistently and the zero-length (blocked) case must be handled explicitly.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override activation window uses UTC day boundaries of the invitee day, mismatching overrides stored in organizer-local dates

`activeOverrides` is computed as overrides where `dayjs.utc(override.start).isBetween(startOfInviteeDay, startOfInviteeDay.endOf("day"), null, "[)")`. `startOfInviteeDay` is the invitee's local midnight converted to an instant, and `override.start` is a UTC instant derived from an organizer-local date/time. An override created for '2023-05-10 14:00–18:00' in the organizer's timezone is stored as the corresponding UTC instant; whether it falls inside the invitee-day window `[inviteeMidnight, inviteeMidnight+24h)` depends on the invitee's timezone offset relative to the organizer. For invitees whose day window does not contain the override's UTC start instant (e.g. invitee far behind/ahead of the organizer), the override is silently dropped and the normal working hours are used, so the date override has no effect for those timezones — precisely the timezone bug (#8329) this PR claims to fix. The activation check should be based on the override's calendar date in the organizer's timezone (using `override.timeZone`, now available on `TimeRange`) compared against the invitee day converted to the organizer's timezone, not on raw UTC instants against the invitee-day window.

Date-override day matching in checkIfIsAvailable uses organizer offset with a sign error and ignores the override's own timeZone

The new date-override logic computes `const utcOffset = organizerTimeZone ? dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1 : 0;` and then compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` against the slot's UTC day. Two problems: (1) `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset()` already returns the offset of that instant in the organizer zone; negating it and adding it to the UTC instant shifts the date in the wrong direction, so the 'which day does this override belong to' comparison is off by the offset (e.g. an override stored as 2023-05-10T00:00:00Z for a UTC+5:30 organizer is treated as belonging to 2023-05-09). (2) The override objects now carry their own `timeZone` (added to the flattened `dateOverrides` at line 410-416 and to the `TimeRange` type), but `checkIfIsAvailable` never reads `date.timeZone`; it only uses the passed `organizerTimeZone`, which for per-user schedules is `schedule.timeZone`/`userSchedule.timeZone` — the user's profile timezone, not necessarily the schedule's timezone the override was created in. Consequences: overrides can be matched to the wrong calendar day (slots wrongly excluded or wrongly allowed), and the day-boundary logic is inconsistent with the timezone-correct conversion added in `packages/lib/slots.ts` (which uses `override.timeZone`). The day-matching should use the override's own `timeZone` (falling back to `organizerTimeZone`) and the correct offset sign, consistent with the slots.ts conversion.

Fixed-host availability check spreads the whole per-user schedule object, so dateOverrides/workingHours are not scoped to that host

The fixed-host filter does `checkIfIsAvailable({ time: slot.time, ...schedule, ...availabilityCheckProps, organizerTimeZone: schedule.timeZone })` where `schedule` is the per-user availability object `{ timeZone, workingHours, dateOverrides, busy, user }`. Because `...schedule` spreads `workingHours` and `dateOverrides` from that user's availability, the new working-hours/date-override checks inside `checkIfIsAvailable` are applied per fixed host — which is the intent — but note that `workingHours` from `getUserAvailability` is the user's raw working hours in minutes-since-midnight in the user's timezone, while `checkIfIsAvailable` compares them against `slotStartTime.hour()*60 + slotStartTime.minute()` where `slotStartTime = time.utc()` — i.e. UTC minutes-of-day, not organizer-local minutes-of-day. Unless the organizer is in UTC, the working-hours comparison is shifted by the organizer's UTC offset, so the guard rejects/accepts the wrong slots. The minutes-of-day must be computed in the organizer's timezone (`slotStartTime.tz(schedule.timeZone)`), consistent with how the override day-matching attempts to use the organizer timezone.

New timezone test only asserts identical UTC output and does not cover a case where the invitee timezone changes the override day

The added test `scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone` requests the same UTC window with `timeZone: Timezones["+6:00"]` (Asia/Dhaka, 30 minutes ahead of the organizer's Asia/Kolkata) and asserts the exact same UTC slot list, with the comment 'it should return the same as this is the utc time'. Because the requested `startTime`/`endTime` window is identical and the override (14:00–18:00 'UTC' in the fixture, interpreted via the schedule timezone) does not cross a day boundary between +5:30 and +6:00, this test cannot detect the day-window/offset bugs described in the slots.ts and slots.ts findings — the override start instant still falls within the invitee-day window and the offset math happens to cancel. A meaningful regression test would use an override near midnight in the organizer's timezone (so that a +6:00 or negative-offset invitee sees it on a different calendar day) and assert the slots shift accordingly, and would also cover a blocked (zero-length) override and a fixed-host round-robin scenario, none of which are present in the added tests.

Override-to-invitee offset conversion in getSlots uses the override start instant's offsets, which is wrong across DST boundaries and for multi-day offsets

The new override conversion computes `organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` and `inviteeUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(timeZone).utcOffset()`, then shifts both `override.start` and `override.end` by the same `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` minutes. The offsets are sampled at the override's start instant only; if the override spans a DST transition in either the organizer's or the invitee's timezone, the end time is shifted by the wrong amount, producing slots at the wrong UTC times (off by the DST delta, typically 60 minutes) for part of the override window. Additionally, `dayjs(override.start.toString())` stringifies a Date in the runtime's local timezone before re-parsing, which can shift the instant depending on the server's TZ — it should operate on the Date/UTC value directly (e.g. `dayjs.utc(override.start).tz(...)`). The conversion should compute the offset per endpoint (start and end separately) using `dayjs(override.start).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` style calls on the actual instants.

Selected-slot filtering returns false for users with no selected slot when seats are not enabled, inverting the intended logic

In the selectedSlots filtering block, the per-user filter does: `if (!busy?.length && eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot === null) { return false; }`. `busy` here is the list of that user's reserved (non-seat) selected slots. For a round-robin/team event without seats (`seatsPerTimeSlot === null`), a user who has no reserved slot is filtered out (`return false`), so `slot.userIds` ends up empty and the slot is dropped by the following `.filter((slot) => !!slot.userIds?.length)` — even though the user is perfectly available. The condition appears inverted: a user with no busy/selected time should be kept (subject to `checkIfIsAvailable`), and it is users with conflicting selected slots who should be removed. As written, whenever any selected slot exists for the event, all slots whose `userIds` include users without a reservation are removed, which can suppress valid availability (or, conversely, fail to suppress users whose reserved slot conflicts, since those users are still passed to `checkIfIsAvailable` with the reduced `busy` list). This directly affects the round-robin fixed-host scenario this PR targets.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
User mismatch check crashes with KeyError when integration metadata lacks 'sender'

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. However, `sender` is only populated in `build_integration` when `state.get("sender")` is present (line 376-377), and `build_integration` is only called when the Integration does not yet exist. For an Integration that already exists in the database (created via webhook or a previous partial flow) but whose metadata was stored without a `sender` key — or where `metadata["sender"]` exists but lacks a `login` key — this raises an unhandled `KeyError`, producing a 500 error instead of the intended graceful failure. The code path is reachable: the `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` at line 494 succeeds for pre-existing integrations, and nothing guarantees `metadata["sender"]["login"]` exists. This should use `.get()` with a safe default (e.g., `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`) so a missing sender is treated as a mismatch and renders the error page.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
GitHubInstallation reads installation_id from request.GET without validating pipeline state, allowing cross-pipeline state confusion

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, `installation_id = request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))` prefers a request-supplied `installation_id` over the pipeline-bound state. Because `PipelineAdvancerView` has `auth_required = False` and `csrf_protect = False` (src/sentry/web/frontend/pipeline_advancer.py lines 25-27), and the pipeline is looked up from a cookie/Redis keyed by pipeline name, an attacker who knows (or guesses) a valid pipeline identifier could craft a request to `sentry-extension-setup` with an arbitrary `installation_id` query parameter. The OAuthLoginView step binds `github_authenticated_user` to the pipeline, but GitHubInstallation then trusts a fresh `installation_id` from GET — meaning the user-mismatch check at line 501 compares the OAuth-authenticated user against the `sender` of a *different* installation than the one whose OAuth flow was completed. While the mismatch check still requires the authenticated user to match the sender of whatever installation_id is supplied, this breaks the intended binding between the OAuth step and the installation step: the `installation_id` validated in OAuthLoginView (line 397-399) is not necessarily the one checked in GitHubInstallation. The installation_id should come exclusively from pipeline state (`pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id")`), with the GET parameter only used to *initialize* the pipeline on the first entry, not to override it on subsequent steps.

OAuth access token may be logged or leaked via exception traces

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the `access_token` obtained from GitHub's token endpoint (line 431-434) is passed to `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])`. If `get_user_info` raises an exception (unhandled, per the related finding), the exception traceback — and potentially the request URL or headers containing the token — could be logged by Sentry's error reporting or appear in server logs. Additionally, the token is stored in the pipeline state only as the derived `login` string (line 438), which is good, but the raw token exists in local variables (`payload`, `data`) for the duration of the request. While this is largely unavoidable in an OAuth flow, the lack of exception handling around `get_user_info` increases the risk that the token-bearing request context is captured in an error report. Wrapping the token-exchange and user-info calls in try/except (returning the generic error page) would prevent token leakage through unhandled exception traces.

OAuth authorize redirect URL parameters are not URL-encoded

The redirect to GitHub's authorize endpoint is built via f-string interpolation: `f"{ghip.get_oauth_authorize_url()}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. The `redirect_uri` value (produced by `absolute_uri(reverse(...))`) and potentially `state` are not URL-encoded with `urlencode`. If `redirect_uri` contains characters like `&`, `=`, `+`, or spaces (e.g., from a customer-domain URL prefix or unusual host configuration), the query string will be malformed — parameters can be injected or truncated, potentially causing the OAuth flow to use an incorrect redirect_uri or allowing parameter manipulation. This should use `urllib.parse.urlencode` to safely construct the query string.

OAuth state comparison is not constant-time, allowing timing side-channel

The pipeline signature (a security token acting as OAuth `state`) is validated with a plain string equality check: `if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature:`. String comparison in Python short-circuits on the first differing character, creating a timing side-channel that could theoretically allow an attacker to recover the signature byte-by-byte. Since `pipeline.signature` is a secret used to authenticate the OAuth callback (and the pipeline state in Redis is keyed by it), it should be compared using `hmac.compare_digest()` (or `secrets.compare_digest()`). This is a defense-in-depth issue — the signature is high-entropy so practical exploitation is difficult — but comparing secrets with `==` is a recognized anti-pattern for exactly this reason.

OAuth token exchange failure is not handled, causing unhandled exception instead of user-facing error

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called without any exception handling. If GitHub's token endpoint returns a non-2xx status (e.g., invalid/expired/replayed `code`, rate limiting, or network error), `safe_urlopen` raises an exception that propagates up as a 500 error rather than the intended user-facing 'Invalid installation request' error page. The PR description explicitly states the pipeline should fail gracefully when 'GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code (wrong or attempt of re-use of code)', but a GitHub error response (which is the normal way GitHub signals a bad code) will crash instead of rendering the error template. The subsequent try/except only wraps `safe_urlread(req).decode('utf-8')` and `parse_qsl`, not the `safe_urlopen` call itself, so HTTP error statuses from the token endpoint are unhandled.

assert_setup_flow hardcodes response call index, making it brittle to unrelated stub changes

In `assert_setup_flow`, the assertion `auth_header = responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` (line 257) relies on the exact ordering and count of HTTP requests made by `responses`. The index was changed from `calls[0]` to `calls[2]` to account for the two new requests made by OAuthLoginView (the token exchange POST and the `/user` GET). This is brittle: any future change that adds or reorders a stubbed HTTP call (e.g., adding a rate-limit check, changing the order of operations in OAuthLoginView, or adding a request in `determine_active_organization`) will silently break this assertion or, worse, assert against the wrong request's headers. A more robust approach would be to find the relevant call by URL (e.g., `next(c for c in responses.calls if "/app/installations/" in c.request.url and c.request.method == "POST")`) rather than by positional index.

get_user_info API failure is unhandled, causing 500 instead of graceful error

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called without exception handling. `get_user_info` makes an HTTP request to GitHub's `/user` endpoint (as evidenced by the test stub at tests line 123). If that request fails (network error, GitHub 401/403 because the token is invalid or lacks `user` scope, rate limiting, or returns a non-JSON body), the exception propagates as an unhandled 500 error rather than the intended 'Invalid installation request' error page. The very next line defensively checks `if "login" not in authenticated_user_info`, showing the author intended to handle bad responses gracefully, but only handles the case where the response parses successfully yet lacks a `login` field — not the case where the request itself fails. This should be wrapped in try/except and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path

The test `test_installation_not_found` stubs a 404 for `GET /app/installations/{installation_id}` (line 381-383), but then makes requests that never reach `build_integration`/`get_installation_info`. The first request (line 385-387) hits `setup_path` with only `installation_id` — this enters GitHubInstallation (the second pipeline view) which redirects to the GitHub app URL because... actually with the new pipeline, the first view is OAuthLoginView which redirects to GitHub authorize (no state param). The second request (line 388-395) supplies a `state` value of `"ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` which does NOT match the pipeline signature (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` used elsewhere), so OAuthLoginView returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error at the state-mismatch check (integration.py line 412-413) — before any call to `get_installation_info`. true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutable default evaluated once at import time for `queued` field

The `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` default is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, not per-instance. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value (which is every call site, including `from_integration`) will share the exact same timestamp — the process start time. The field is named `queued` and typed as a datetime, strongly implying it records when the assignment was queued, but it actually records when the Python module was first loaded. This makes the field useless for its apparent purpose (e.g., detecting stale/delayed sync tasks, ordering, or debugging sync loops) and is misleading. Fix: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`assignment_source.to_dict()` embeds a `datetime` in Celery task kwargs without guaranteed serializability

`sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` (which includes the `queued` datetime via `asdict`) directly into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`. Celery's default JSON serializer cannot serialize `datetime` objects and will raise a `TypeError`/`SerializationError` at enqueue time — meaning any inbound webhook assignment (the exact scenario this PR targets) would fail to enqueue the outbound task entirely, or the deployment must be using a serializer that handles datetimes (pickle, or a custom one). If the serializer rejects it, the exception propagates out of `GroupAssignee.objects.assign`/`deassign` inside the `affected` block, after the DB write and activity record — a data-integrity-adjacent failure where the local assignment succeeds but the outbound sync task is never queued and the error surfaces to the webhook caller. `to_dict()` should serialize `queued` to an ISO-8601 string (and `from_dict` should parse it back), making the payload JSON-safe by construction.

false_positives.candidate:
Cycle guard compares `org_integration.integration_id` but `AssignmentSource.integration_id` is the Integration id — verify these are the same id space

`should_sync` suppresses outbound sync when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. `AssignmentSource.from_integration` sets `integration_id=integration.id` where `integration` is an `Integration`/`RpcIntegration` (src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:24). The comparison is against `self.org_integration.integration_id`, which is the FK from `OrganizationIntegration` to `Integration`. These should be the same id space, but the guard's correctness — the entire point of the PR — depends on it, and nothing in the tests exercises a mismatched-id scenario or documents the invariant. If any code path constructs `AssignmentSource` with an `OrganizationIntegration` id or an external id instead of the `Integration` id, the guard silently fails and the sync loop returns. The test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only covers the happy path; there is no test that a *different* integration's source still allows syncing (i.e., that the guard is not over-broad), nor a test pinning down which id is stored.

No test that a *different* integration's assignment source still syncs outbound (guard is not over-broad)

`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` verifies the guard suppresses sync when the source integration matches the target. But the PR description explicitly states the intent: "This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward" (comment in mixins/issues.py:388-389). There is no test with two integrations (or a source integration whose id differs from the external issue's integration) asserting that `sync_assignee_outbound` IS still called. Without it, a regression that suppresses ALL outbound syncs whenever any `assignment_source` is present (e.g., comparing against the wrong id field, or an inverted condition) would pass the test suite. This is the positive case that proves the fix breaks the cycle without breaking legitimate cross-integration propagation.

Outbound sync enqueued inside `assign` without the assignment row being committed/visible to the task

`sync_group_assignee_outbound` is called synchronously within `GroupAssigneeManager.assign` (line 192-194), which enqueues `sync_assignee_outbound` via `apply_async`. The task, when it runs, reads `ExternalIssue`/`GroupLink` but relies on the `GroupAssignee` state having been written. `assign` performs its writes with `get_or_create`/`update` but the outbound task is enqueued before the surrounding transaction commits (the `issue_assigned` signal is deferred via `transaction.on_commit`, but the sync call is not). If the task executes before the transaction that created/updated the `GroupAssignee` row commits (possible under async workers with fast queues or in tests with eager tasks), the outbound sync may run against a group whose assignee is not yet visible, or the enqueue itself can be lost if the transaction rolls back after the task was queued (Celery has no transactional outbox here). The `issue_assigned` signal is correctly deferred with `on_commit`, but the integration sync is not — an inconsistency that can cause lost or premature outbound syncs under transaction rollback or worker race.

`IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` signature diverges from `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`

`IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync(self, attribute, sync_source=None)` returns `False` unconditionally and ignores `sync_source`, while the subclass `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` implements the cycle guard. Any caller that holds an `IssueBasicIntegration` reference (rather than `IssueSyncIntegration`) and passes a `sync_source` will get `False` regardless — which is safe for cycle prevention but means the base-class signature promises behavior it does not implement. More importantly, `where_should_sync` (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:48) calls `.should_sync(key)` without a source, so inbound status sync paths are unaffected — fine — but the asymmetry between the two signatures (one typed `-> bool`, the other untyped) is a latent contract break for any third-party integration subclass that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-argument signature: calls that now pass `sync_source` positionally/keyword will raise `TypeError`. The PR changes a public-ish method signature without a compatibility shim; existing external integration subclasses overriding `should_sync(self, attribute)` will break when `sync_assignee_outbound` task calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)`.

`sync_assignee_outbound` installation method is called with `assignment_source` kwarg that the abstract signature does not declare

The task calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` (line 59-61), but the abstract method in `IssueSyncIntegration` (src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:396-408) declares only `(self, external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs)`. Concrete implementations (Jira, GitHub, etc., not shown in this PR) that define `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs` will raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'` at runtime. The abstract base should declare `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` explicitly (as was done for `sync_status_outbound`) so the contract is clear and implementations are forced to accept it. This is exactly the kind of break that only surfaces in production when a webhook-triggered assignment flows through the task.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler now inherits abstract methods it does not implement, making it impossible to instantiate

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` (line 11-12) is changed from `DetectorHandler` to `StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]` with just `pass`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract methods: `counter_names` (property, line 142-148), `get_dedupe_value` (line 150-156), `get_group_key_values` (line 158-164), and `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (line 166-170). Because `StatefulDetectorHandler` uses `abc.ABC` (via `DetectorHandler(abc.ABC, Generic[T])` at line 114), attempting to instantiate `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` — which happens in `Detector.detector_handler` property (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86, `return group_type.detector_handler(self)`) — will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. The class needs stub implementations of the abstract methods (even if they raise `NotImplementedError` or return empty values) or the `detector_handler` property needs to handle instantiation failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

In `test_state_results_multi_group` (lines 174-222), the data packet is `DataPacket("1", {"dedupe": 2, "group_vals": {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}})` (line 177), so `group_2` has value 10.
