The real regression is in RolePermissions.canMapRole as reported separately.

V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission matches resources by type 'Group' but V2 resources use type 'Groups', and name-prefix stripping is fragile

GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (lines 313-317) iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Group", ...)` and strips the 'group.resource.' prefix from resource names to recover group ids. This is the V1 evaluator, but MgmtPermissionsV2 now overrides groups() to return GroupPermissionsV2, so this V1 method is only used in V1 mode; however, the type string 'Group' (singular) versus the V2 schema's GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE ('Groups') shows the two evaluators use different resource type conventions, and any code path that mixes them (e.g. a realm migrated from V1 to V2 where resources were created with type 'Group') will silently return an empty set, breaking the group-based user visibility filter. The consequence is that admins lose visibility of users in groups they can view members of. The resource type lookup should be consistent (use AdminPermissionsSchema constants) or both types should be handled.

V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set when user can manage but not view, changing semantics from previous getGroupsWithViewPermission

The old V1 method getGroupsWithViewPermission() returned an empty set when `root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()` (i.e. full access). The new getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (line 298) only checks `root.users().canView()`, omitting the canManage() case. An admin with manage-users but not view-users would previously get an empty set (meaning 'no group filter, see all users'), but now gets a set of group ids derived from view-members/manage-members permissions, which is likely empty — and an empty set is treated by callers (UsersResource.searchForUser: `if (!groupIds.isEmpty()) session.setAttribute(...)`) as 'no filter', so the outcome may be the same by accident, but the intermediate semantics differ and any future caller that distinguishes empty-set from null will misbehave. More importantly, in V1, canViewMembers(group) was true when `root.users().canView()`; the new canViewMembers also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE, which is a deliberate change, but getGroupIdsWithViewPermission's guard should mirror the old condition (canView() || canManage()) to preserve behavior for manage-only admins.

V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission strips 'group.resource.' prefix from resource name, but if a resource name does not have the prefix (e.g. all-groups resource), substring produces garbage

In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 313-317), the code iterates resources of type 'Group' and does `resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())` to recover the group id. If a resource of type 'Group' has a name shorter than the prefix or without the prefix (e.g. manually created, or the all-groups resource if it were typed 'Group'), the substring produces a garbage string or throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The all-groups resource in V1 is named 'Users' for users (UserPermissions.USERS_RESOURCE) but for groups, the V1 initialize method creates resources named 'group.resource.<id>' with type 'Group' (line 117), so all type-'Group' resources have the prefix. However, the V2 schema creates resources named with the group id (no prefix) and type 'Groups'. If a realm has both V1 and V2 resources (migration scenario), the V1 method would encounter V2 resources (type 'Groups', not 'Group') and skip them (type mismatch), so no crash. But if any resource of type 'Group' lacks the prefix, the substring is unsafe. A length check or startsWith check should be added.

V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE and MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE but resource names use 'group.resource.' prefix; if V2 resources coexist, type mismatch causes empty results

The V1 GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 313) iterates resources of type 'Group' (singular) and strips the 'group.resource.' prefix. In a realm where V2 was enabled and group resources were created with type 'Groups' (GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and names equal to group ids (no prefix), this V1 method (if ever invoked in a mixed state) would find no resources of type 'Group' and return an empty set. An empty set is interpreted by callers as 'no group filter' (see UsersResource.searchForUser: `if (!groupIds.isEmpty())`), meaning the admin would see ALL users instead of only group members — a data exposure bug in mixed V1/V2 states. However, since MgmtPermissionsV2 overrides groups() to return GroupPermissionsV2, the V1 method is not used in V2 mode. The risk is during migration or if any code path constructs GroupPermissions directly. The type constant should be unified.

V2 canView()/canManage() omit the isAdminSameRealm check, enabling cross-realm access for admins with realm-management roles

UserPermissionsV2.canView(user) (line 47-53) and canManage(user) (line 55-62) check `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` and return true immediately, without verifying `root.isAdminSameRealm()`. The V1 base class UserPermissions.canView() (line 297-307) explicitly returns false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()` before evaluating permissions. In Keycloak, an admin from the master realm (or another realm) with the manage-users/view-users role in their own realm should NOT automatically have those rights in a different realm they are managing (unless they are realm-admin of that realm). hasOneAdminRole checks the admin's roles, which for a master-realm admin include master realm roles; if the admin has 'manage-users' in master, hasOneAdminRole returns true, and V2 canView() returns true even when managing a different realm. This bypasses the cross-realm protection that V1 enforces. The consequence: a master-realm admin with manage-users (a common setup for realm management) gains view/manage access to all users in every realm they can access, even without being admin of those realms. The isAdminSameRealm() check (or an equivalent adminsRealm == realm check) must be added to UserPermissionsV2.canView(), canManage(), canMapRoles(), canManageGroupMembership(), and canImpersonate() before the role check returns true.

V2 canView/canManage removed AdminRoles.ADMIN from the role check

In UserPermissionsV2.canView(user) and canManage(user) (lines 47-62), the role check was changed from `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.ADMIN, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (removing AdminRoles.ADMIN). AdminRoles.ADMIN is the 'admin' role in the master realm; hasOneAdminRole typically already accounts for realm-admin composite roles, but if an admin has only the 'admin' role (master realm admin managing another realm), the isAdminSameRealm() check would return false anyway, so the removal may be intentional. However, if hasOneAdminRole(ADMIN) was previously needed for same-realm admins with the 'admin' role (unusual but possible in custom setups), removing it could lock out such admins in V2. This should be verified against hasOneAdminRole semantics; if hasOneAdminRole already expands composites, the change is safe.

V2 group canView()/canManage() omit isAdminSameRealm check, enabling cross-realm group access

GroupPermissionsV2.canView() (line 47-53), canView(group) (line 55-62), canManage() (line 64-71), and canManage(group) (line 73-80) all check `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (or MANAGE_USERS) and return true without verifying `root.isAdminSameRealm()`. The V1 GroupPermissions.canView(group) (line 254-264) explicitly returns false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()`. As with the UserPermissionsV2 finding, a master-realm admin with manage-users/view-users roles would get canView()/canManage() = true in any realm they manage, bypassing the cross-realm restriction. This grants cross-realm group visibility and management. The isAdminSameRealm() check must be added before the role-based early return in all four methods (or in hasPermission, but the role check returns before hasPermission is reached).

canImpersonate does not check isAdminSameRealm before evaluating fine-grained permission

UserPermissionsV2.canImpersonate(user, requester) (line 65-74) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(ImpersonationConstants.IMPERSONATION_ROLE)` and returns true, then evaluates hasPermission(user, context, IMPERSONATE). The private hasPermission (line 94-97) does check `root.isAdminSameRealm()` and returns false if not same realm. However, the role check at line 66 returns true before hasPermission is called, so a cross-realm admin with the impersonation role gets impersonation rights in any realm. The V1 UserPermissions.canImpersonate() (line 411-421) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(ImpersonationConstants.IMPERSONATION_ROLE)` and then `if (!root.isAdminSameRealm()) return false;` before evaluating. The V2 override omits the isAdminSameRealm check entirely. This is a cross-realm impersonation bypass: an admin with the impersonation role in their home realm can impersonate users in any realm they can access. The isAdminSameRealm() check must be added.

canList() reordered but semantics changed: QUERY_GROUPS alone no longer implies list when canView() is false in V2

GroupPermissions.canList() was changed from `canView() || root.hasOneAdminRole(VIEW_USERS, MANAGE_USERS, QUERY_GROUPS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()`. Logically these are equivalent for the role check, but in V2, canView() is overridden by GroupPermissionsV2.canView() which additionally checks fine-grained permissions, so the behavior is preserved. However, the reordering means the fine-grained canView() is evaluated after the role check; this is fine. No concrete bug, but note that in V2, an admin with only a fine-grained 'view' permission on all groups (no admin roles) can now list groups — this is intended per the interface javadoc. Not reported as a defect; see other findings.

canManageMembership accepts MANAGE scope on the group, but manage-membership is a distinct, narrower capability

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership(group) (line 102), the permission check is `hasPermission(group.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP)`. This means an admin with the 'manage' scope on a group (full group management) can also manage membership (add/remove users). This is consistent with the interface javadoc ('MANAGE the group or MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP of the group'). However, the V1 GroupPermissions.canManageMembership (line 358-366) checks `canManage(group)` first (which includes global manage) and then MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP_SCOPE only — it does NOT accept the group's MANAGE scope as sufficient for membership management when the admin lacks the global role. Wait, V1 canManage(group) returns true if canManage() (global role) OR per-group MANAGE_SCOPE; so in V1, having per-group 'manage' scope also grants manage-membership. So V2 is consistent with V1. The semantic question: should 'manage' on a group imply 'manage-membership'? The interface javadoc says yes. Not a defect, but worth noting that 'manage' is a powerful scope that includes membership management, which may surprise admins who expect manage to only cover group attributes.

canManageMembership checks MANAGE_USERS role without isAdminSameRealm guard

GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership(group) (line 96-103) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` and returns true without an isAdminSameRealm check. The V1 GroupPermissions.canManageMembership (line 358-366) checks `canManage(group)` first (which includes the isAdminSameRealm check via canManage(group) -> canManage() -> role check + isAdminSameRealm in hasPermission path... actually V1 canManage(group) checks canManage() which is role-only, then isAdminSameRealm, then hasPermission). In V1, canManage() is role-only (no isAdminSameRealm), but canManage(group) checks `if (!root.isAdminSameRealm()) return false;` before hasPermission. So V1 denies cross-realm. V2 canManageMembership returns true for cross-realm admins with manage-users role. This allows a master-realm admin to manage group membership in any realm. The isAdminSameRealm check must be added.

canMapRole now requires MANAGE_USERS role directly, removing V1 fine-grained users manage fallback

In RolePermissions.canMapRole (line 302), the check was changed from `root.users().canManageDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)`. canManageDefault() was exactly `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` in UserPermissions (removed in this PR), so for V1 the behavior is identical. However, in V2, UserPermissionsV2.canManage() additionally grants manage when the admin has a fine-grained 'manage' permission on users (all-users or per-user). By bypassing root.users().canManage() and checking only the role, V2 admins who were granted fine-grained manage-users permission (but not the manage-users role) can no longer map roles, even though they can manage users. This is an inconsistency introduced by the refactor: role mapping should use root.users().canManage() (the evaluator), not the raw role check, so that V2 fine-grained permissions are honored.

canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership check MANAGE_USERS role without isAdminSameRealm guard

UserPermissionsV2.canMapRoles(user) (line 77-83) and canManageGroupMembership(user) (line 85-92) check `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` and return true without an isAdminSameRealm check. The V1 UserPermissions.canMapRoles (line 442-451) checks `canManage(user)` first (which includes isAdminSameRealm via canManage -> hasPermission path... actually V1 canManage(user) = canManage() || canManageByGroup(user); canManage() checks isAdminSameRealm at line 238-240). So V1 denies cross-realm. V2 allows cross-realm admins with manage-users role to map roles and manage group membership in any realm. The isAdminSameRealm check must be added.

canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership now accept MANAGE scope in addition to their specific scope, widening V2 permissions

In UserPermissionsV2, canMapRoles(user) (line 82) was changed from `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES)` to `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user)`, and canManageGroupMembership(user) (line 91) similarly now accepts MANAGE. Previously (in the base diff), canMapRoles checked `canManage(user)` first (which includes MANAGE), so accepting MANAGE is consistent with the old behavior; the change actually restores the 'manage implies map-roles' semantics that the intermediate version had removed. However, the interface javadoc for UserPermissionEvaluator.canMapRoles says 'MANAGE the user or MAP_ROLES of the user', so this is consistent. The concern: canManageByGroup(user) is now also OR-ed in, meaning an admin with manage-members on a group containing the user can map roles for that user. The interface javadoc explicitly documents this ('Or if it has a permission to MANAGE_MEMBERS of the group chain'), so it is intended. Not a defect per se, but the combination means 'manage-members' on a group grants role-mapping rights on all users in that group, which is a significant capability; this should be verified as intended by the security team.

canView() and canManage() use hasPermission(null, ...) which falls back to all-groups resource, but the policyStore.findByResource check may return empty for resource-type permissions

In GroupPermissionsV2.canView() (line 52) and canManage() (line 70), hasPermission(null, scopes) is called with groupId=null. In hasPermission (line 141), when groupId is null, resource is null, so the code goes to the fallback: it loads the all-groups resource via getResourceTypeResource and checks `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` (line 147). This checks for policies directly associated with the all-groups resource. However, scope permissions in Keycloak are policies of type 'scope' that reference resources; findByResource should return them. If the permission was created with resourceType='Groups' (as the tests do via createAllPermission), the policy is associated with the 'Groups' resource, so findByResource returns non-empty. This seems correct. But note: if the admin has a permission on a specific group resource (not all-groups), canView() (global) returns false, which is correct. No concrete bug, but the interplay between per-group and all-groups fallback in hasPermission (lines 141-150) means that when a per-group resource exists but has no granting permission, the all-groups fallback is NOT consulted (the code returns the per-group resource and evaluates it, and if no permission matches, returns false at line 164). This means a specific group resource's existence 'shadows' the all-groups permission: an admin with view on all-groups loses view on any group that has its own resource (even if that resource has no policies granting the admin). This is the same shadowing issue noted for UsersResource; it should be verified as intended or fixed by also evaluating the all-groups resource when the per-group evaluation yields no permission.

canViewByGroup now uses canViewMembers which includes MANAGE_MEMBERS, widening V1 user visibility via group permissions

In UserPermissions (V1), canViewByGroup(user) previously used `root.groups().getGroupsWithViewPermission(group)` which required VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE only. It now uses `root.groups()::canViewMembers`, and GroupPermissions.canViewMembers was simultaneously changed (line 340) to also accept MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE. The net effect in the V1 path: an admin with only 'manage-members' permission on a group (no view-members, no view-users role) can now see all users that are members of that group through the users search endpoint. This is a privilege widening in the legacy evaluator that was not part of the V2 feature; if manage-members is intended to imply viewing members, it should be an explicit, documented decision applied consistently, otherwise V1 behavior has silently changed for existing deployments.

canViewMembers and canManageMembers do not check isAdminSameRealm before evaluating permissions

In GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers(group) (line 83-87) and canManageMembers(group) (line 89-94), the methods check `root.users().canView()` / `root.users().canManage()` first, then call hasPermission(group.getId(), ...). The private hasPermission method (line 130-133) does check `root.isAdminSameRealm()` and returns false if not same realm. So cross-realm admins are correctly denied. However, the V1 GroupPermissions.canViewMembers (line 330-341) explicitly checks `root.isAdminSameRealm()` before evaluating, and returns false early. The V2 methods rely on hasPermission's internal check, which is fine. But note: canViewMembers first checks `root.users().canView()` — in V2, UserPermissionsV2.canView() checks admin roles and fine-grained permissions but does NOT check isAdminSameRealm() (the base UserPermissions.canView does check isAdminSameRealm at line 302-304, but UserPermissionsV2.canView() overrides it and does not call super, so the isAdminSameRealm check is skipped!). Wait, UserPermissionsV2.canView() (line 47-53) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(MANAGE_USERS, VIEW_USERS)` — hasOneAdminRole presumably checks the admin's roles in the admins realm; for cross-realm admins, this could return true if the admin has manage-users in their own realm but is managing a different realm. The base UserPermissions.canView() explicitly returns false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()`. UserPermissionsV2.canView() omits this check, meaning a cross-realm admin with manage-users role in the master realm could get canView()=true in a managed realm, and then GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers would return true for any group, leaking member lists cross-realm. This is a potential cross-realm authorization bypass in V2. The isAdminSameRealm check must be added to UserPermissionsV2.canView()/canManage() or to hasPermission (which does check it, but canView() returns true before reaching hasPermission when the role check passes).

canViewMembers now also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope, changing V1 semantics

In GroupPermissions.canViewMembers(GroupModel) (line 340), the permission check was changed from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)`. This means an admin granted only 'manage-members' on a group (without 'view-members') can now list group members via GroupResource.getMembers (which calls requireViewMembers). Whether this is intended is unclear — the V2 GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers does the same — but it is a behavioral change to the V1 evaluator that widens access: manage-members was previously not sufficient to view the member list. If the intent is that manage implies view, it should be documented; otherwise this is an unintended privilege widening in the legacy (non-V2) permission path.

canViewMembers/canManageMembers rely on root.users().canView()/canManage() which in V2 lack isAdminSameRealm check

GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers(group) (line 83-87) returns true if `root.users().canView()` is true. In V2, root.users() is UserPermissionsV2, whose canView() (as reported separately) lacks the isAdminSameRealm check. Therefore, a cross-realm admin with view-users role gets canViewMembers=true for all groups in the managed realm, leaking member lists. Similarly canManageMembers (line 89-94) uses root.users().canManage(). The V1 GroupPermissions.canViewMembers (line 330-341) checks `root.users().canView()` (V1 UserPermissions.canView which HAS the isAdminSameRealm check) and then explicitly checks isAdminSameRealm. The V2 chain loses both guards. This is a cross-realm member-list disclosure. Fixing UserPermissionsV2.canView()/canManage() to include isAdminSameRealm (as reported) resolves this, but an explicit guard here is also advisable.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission evaluates permissions per group resource in a loop, causing N permission evaluations per request

GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 106-128) iterates all group resources via resourceStore.findByType and calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) for each, which triggers a full policy evaluation (root.evaluatePermission) per group. For realms with many groups, this is O(N) policy evaluations on every user search/count request that goes through UsersResource.searchForUser or getUsersCount (when the admin lacks global view-users). The V1 implementation (GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission) has the same pattern, so this is not a regression, but the V2 implementation could batch-evaluate permissions for all resources in one call (the evaluation engine supports evaluating multiple ResourcePermissions). Given that this runs on the hot path of user listing, the performance impact for large realms should be assessed; at minimum, the per-resource evaluation should be short-circuited or cached per request.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission javadoc says 'If UserPermissionEvaluator#canView() evaluates to true, returns empty set' but implementation also checks canManage in V1

The javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 142-147) states: 'If UserPermissionEvaluator#canView() evaluates to true, returns empty set.' However, the V1 implementation (GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, line 298) checks `root.users().canView()` only (the canManage check was removed in this PR; previously getGroupsWithViewPermission checked canView() || canManage()). The V2 implementation (GroupPermissionsV2 line 107) also checks only canView(). The javadoc is accurate for the new implementation but the semantics changed from the old method (which returned empty for canView || canManage). The javadoc should also mention that an empty set means 'no group-based filtering' and that callers interpret it as 'see all users', to make the contract clear.

getGroups non-hierarchy path drops the global canView bypass, changing V1 behavior for admins with global view

In GroupsResource.getGroups (line 113), the non-hierarchy path filter was changed from `g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g)` to `groupsEvaluator::canView`. In V1, GroupPermissions.canView(group) already includes the global canView()/canManage() check, so V1 behavior is preserved. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.canView(group) checks admin roles (MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS) or per-group permission; an admin with a fine-grained 'view' permission on the all-groups resource (Groups resource type) but no per-group resource for a specific group will fail canView(group) because hasPermission(group.getId(), ...) finds no per-group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource only when the per-group resource is null — which it does (line 141-150 of GroupPermissionsV2), so the fallback works. However, the fallback only applies when the per-group resource does not exist; if a per-group resource exists (created by a previous permission) but has no policies granting this admin, hasPermission returns false without falling back to the all-groups resource. This means: once any permission is created for a specific group, admins with only all-groups view permission lose visibility of that group in the listing. This 'specific overrides global' behavior may be intended, but combined with the removal of the explicit global bypass it creates an inconsistency with the hierarchy path (populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups), which uses the evaluator differently. The behavior should be verified and ideally the fallback to the all-groups resource should also occur when the per-group resource exists but yields no permission.

getOrCreateResource throws IllegalStateException for unknown resource type, but callers may expect null return

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 107-112), the switch on resourceType throws IllegalStateException for unknown types. Previously, the code returned null name for unknown types and then threw IllegalStateException at line 114-116 ('Could not map resource object...'). The behavior is similar (exception), but the exception type/message changed. Callers that catch IllegalStateException with the old message or that expected a null return for unsupported types (e.g. when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false, the method returns null at line 93-95) may now get an unexpected exception for a resource type that is simply not yet supported (e.g. 'Roles' if added later). This is a minor API contract change; the method should either return null for unknown types (consistent with the supportsAuthorizationSchema=false path) or the javadoc should document the exception.

getResourceName only handles Users resource type; Groups and Clients fall through to display name

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName (lines 328-350) resolves a human-readable name only for the USERS resource type ('All users' or the username). For GROUPS and CLIENTS resource types, it returns resource.getDisplayName(), which for schema-created resources is typically null or the raw id, so admin UIs listing permissions for groups/clients will show unhelpful names. Since this PR adds the Groups resource type, getResourceName should be extended to resolve group names (and ideally client names) the same way resolveGroup/resolveClient do, otherwise the permission management UI will display broken labels for group permissions.

getScope NPEs when resourceType is not in the schema

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope (line 238), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code calls `SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes()` without checking that getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) is non-null. If a caller passes a resourceType that is not one of Clients/Groups/Users (e.g. a legacy policy or a malformed request), this throws a NullPointerException instead of the intended ModelValidationException. The method should validate that the resource type exists and throw ModelValidationException('Resource type ... not found') similar to throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided (line 220-222).

getSubGroups filter change removes the canView-global bypass, but V2 canView(group) may not cover hierarchy semantics

In GroupResource.getSubGroups (line 176-180), the filter was changed from `g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g)` (where canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView()) to simply `auth.groups()::canView`. In V1, GroupPermissions.canView(group) returns true if canView() (global) OR canManage() OR per-group permission, so the behavior is equivalent. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.canView(group) returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS roles OR hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE). The subtle issue: in V2, an admin with a fine-grained 'view' permission on a parent group but not on child groups will not see the child groups in the children listing, whereas the previous code with canViewGlobal would show all children if the admin had global view. This is arguably correct for fine-grained permissions (per-group scoping), but it means the 'view' permission is no longer inherited down the group hierarchy — an admin with view on a parent group cannot see its subgroups unless they also have view on each subgroup or on all-groups. This is a significant semantic change for the subgroups listing endpoint that should be verified as intended; if hierarchy inheritance is expected, canView should walk up the parent chain like UserPermissions.evaluateHierarchy does for users.

grantIfNoPermission fallback grants both MANAGE and VIEW only when both scopes are expected; V2 does not honor this flag

In UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 500-502), when the Users resource does not exist (permissions not initialized), the method returns `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`. This is a legacy fallback: when fine-grained permissions are not configured for users, and the caller has set grantIfNoPermission=true (which UsersResource.toRepresentation does when group-based filtering is active), the admin is granted access. The condition requires BOTH manage and view scopes to be in the expected scopes, which is unusual (most callers check one or the other). This means the fallback rarely triggers as intended. In V2, UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission does not implement this fallback at all (returns false when resource server is null or resource is null and no all-users permission exists). The consequence: in V2, when an admin has group-based view permissions (session attribute set) but no user permissions configured, canView(user) returns false for users not in the admin's groups, which is correct, but for users in the admin's groups, canViewByGroup(user) should return true — this works. The grantIfNoPermission flag is a V1 mechanism to handle the case where permissions are not initialized; its absence in V2 means V2 relies on the all-users resource existing (created by AdminPermissionsSchema.init). If init was not called (e.g. admin permissions enabled but schema not initialized), V2 denies everything, which is safe but may break flows that worked in V1. This should be verified as intended.

groups() returns GroupPermissionsV2 but the field type and superclass method signature use GroupPermissions, hiding V2-specific UnsupportedOperationException methods

MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() (line 58-62) returns GroupPermissions (the superclass type), instantiated as GroupPermissionsV2. Callers that need V2-specific behavior must cast. More importantly, the AdminPermissionEvaluator interface (and AdminPermissionManagement) declare groups() returning GroupPermissionEvaluator / GroupPermissionManagement; the V2 implementation throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods. This is a design smell: the V2 evaluator implements the full management interface but throws for most methods, which is error-prone. A separate V2 management interface (or null-returning defaults) would be cleaner. Not a functional bug per se, but it means any code path that calls management methods on the evaluator (rather than on a management-specific instance) will crash in V2. The GroupResource/UserResource management endpoints are the concrete victims (see separate findings).

hasPermission NPE when all-groups resource does not exist — denial of service / 500 error

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 141-150), when groupId is null or the per-group resource is not found, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` (line 144) and then immediately `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 147) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource does not exist (line 133-151 of AdminPermissionsSchema: returns null if type is null or resource not found). This happens when: (1) admin permissions are enabled but AdminPermissionsSchema.init was not called (e.g. realm created before feature, or init failed), (2) the 'Groups' resource was deleted manually, (3) the resource server exists but schema resources were not created. The NPE propagates as a 500 error to the admin API caller. Every group permission check (canView, canManage, canViewMembers, etc.) goes through hasPermission, so a missing all-groups resource breaks all group admin endpoints with 500 errors. The fix: add `if (resource == null) return false;` after line 144.

hasPermission NPE when all-users resource does not exist — denial of service / 500 error

In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 105-114), when the per-user resource is not found, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` (line 109) and then `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 111) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the 'Users' resource does not exist. This NPE breaks all user permission checks (canView, canManage, canMapRoles, etc.) with a 500 error when the all-users resource is missing. The fix: add `if (resource == null) return false;` after line 109.

hasPermission filters evaluated permissions by resource id, dropping permissions granted via the all-users resource

In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission(UserModel, EvaluationContext, String...) (lines 116-130), after evaluating `new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server)`, the code only accepts a permission if `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())` (line 123). When the per-user resource does not exist, `resource` is the 'Users' all-resource (line 109), and the evaluation engine returns permissions whose resourceId is the id of the resource the permission is actually attached to. Scope permissions created for the all-users resource evaluate against that resource, so this filter is consistent for the all-users case; however, when a per-user resource exists, permissions defined on the all-users resource (the documented fallback: 'check if there is permission for all-users') are evaluated by the engine but then discarded by this filter because their resourceId differs from the per-user resource id. This breaks the intended fallback semantics (a realm-wide 'view all users' permission no longer applies to a user that has its own resource), causing denial of access that admins configured. The filter should accept permissions matching either the per-user resource or the all-users resource type resource, or the evaluation should be performed per resource.

hasPermission looks up group resource by raw group id instead of schema resource name, and NPEs when the all-groups resource is missing

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission(String groupId, ...) resolves the per-group resource with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` (line 141). In the V2 schema (AdminPermissionsSchema), per-group resources are created with the group id as their name (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and getOrCreateResource uses that as the resource name), so findByName works only if the resource was already created; however, when no per-group resource exists, the code falls back to the 'Groups' all-resource via `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` (line 144) and then immediately calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 147) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource does not exist (e.g. admin permissions were enabled but the schema resources were not initialized, or the feature was toggled), causing a NullPointerException instead of a clean 'false' denial. A null check (return false when resource == null) is required. Additionally, relying on findByName(groupId) means a group whose resource was never created silently falls back to the all-groups permission, which may grant unintended access if a broad all-groups permission exists while the intent was per-group scoping; the fallback should be explicit and safe.

hasPermission method name overloaded with different semantics from parent class

GroupPermissionsV2 defines a private hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes) (line 130) that has completely different semantics from the parent GroupPermissions.hasPermission(GroupModel, String...) and hasPermission(Resource, EvaluationContext, String...). The parent methods are still inherited and used by V1 code paths (e.g. canView(group) in the parent is overridden, but getGroupIdsWithViewPermission in the parent uses the parent's hasPermission). The overloading with different parameter types (String vs GroupModel/Resource) is confusing and error-prone. The V2 method should be renamed (e.g. hasGroupPermission or evaluateGroupPermission) to avoid confusion.

hasPermission method name overloaded with different semantics from parent class

UserPermissionsV2 defines a private hasPermission(UserModel, EvaluationContext, String...) (line 94) that differs from the parent's protected hasPermission(String...) and private hasPermission(EvaluationContext, String...). The V2 method takes a UserModel as the first parameter, making it distinct, but the naming overlap is confusing. Rename to evaluateUserPermission for clarity.

hasPermission(String...) lost the EvaluationContext overload visibility needed by subclasses

UserPermissions.hasPermission(String... scopes) (line 486) delegates to a private hasPermission(EvaluationContext, String...) (line 490). UserPermissionsV2 defines its own private hasPermission(UserModel, EvaluationContext, String...) and does not reuse the parent's context-aware evaluation, which is fine, but the parent's `hasPermission(EvaluationContext, String...)` being private means V2 cannot reuse the grantIfNoPermission fallback logic (line 501: `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`). In V2, UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission returns false when the resource server is null (line 101-103), whereas V1's grantIfNoPermission mechanism (set via usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(...) in UsersResource.toRepresentation when group-based filtering is active) allowed access when no permissions are configured. This means in V2, when an admin has group-based view permissions (UserModel.GROUPS session attribute set) but no user permissions configured, canView(user) may return false where V1 granted access, breaking the group-membership-based visibility flow. The V2 evaluator should honor the grantIfNoPermission flag similarly.

isImpersonatable throws UnsupportedOperationException but is still called by V1 code paths (canClientImpersonate in UserPermissions)

UserPermissionsV2.isImpersonatable(UserModel, ClientModel) and isImpersonatable(UserModel) throw UnsupportedOperationException (lines 142-149). However, the base class UserPermissions.canClientImpersonate (line 340-353) calls `canImpersonate(context) && isImpersonatable(user)`, and UserPermissionsV2 overrides canClientImpersonate to delegate to canImpersonate(user, client) (line 137-139), so canClientImpersonate is safe. But any other caller of isImpersonatable (e.g. legacy code or the deprecated interface method) will crash in V2. The interface UserPermissionEvaluator still declares isImpersonatable as @Deprecated but not removed; if it is part of the public-ish contract used by extensions, throwing UnsupportedOperationException is a break. The method should either be implemented in V2 (e.g. return true, as V1 does when no user-impersonated permission is configured) or the interface should be cleaned up to remove the deprecated method and update all callers.

registerListener now checks feature flag at registration time instead of event time, changing behavior for dynamically enabled features

In AdminPermissions.registerListener (lines 73-99), the Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) check was moved from inside onEvent to the registration call itself. Previously, the listener was always registered and the feature check happened per event; now, if the feature is disabled at server startup (when registerListener is called), the listener is never registered, and enabling the feature later (e.g. via a restart-less config change or in tests that toggle the profile) will not register the cleanup listener. The consequence: when a group/role/client is removed, its permissions are not cleaned up (setPermissionsEnabled(false)), leaving orphaned authorization resources. The check should remain inside onEvent, or the listener should be registered unconditionally as before.

requireManageMembers javadoc incorrectly references canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers

In GroupPermissionEvaluator (line 132-135), the javadoc for requireManageMembers says 'Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} returns {@code false}.' It should reference #canManageMembers(GroupModel). This is a copy-paste error in the documentation that misleads readers about which permission is enforced.

testManageAllGroups creates a group with a blank name and expects FORBIDDEN, but the assertion may pass for the wrong reason

In testManageAllGroups (line 141), the test calls `groups().add(new GroupRepresentation())` (blank name) and expects 403 FORBIDDEN. The server-side GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup checks `auth.groups().requireManage()` before validating the group name (line 181-189), so the 403 is due to missing permission, which is the intent. However, if the permission check were accidentally reordered after name validation, the test would get 400 and fail — so the test does guard the order. But the test does not verify that after granting MANAGE, creating a group with a blank name returns 400 (validation still works). More importantly, the test at line 146 adds a child with a blank name and expects 403; same reasoning. These are acceptable, but the test would be more robust using a named group to avoid conflating validation errors with permission errors. Not a blocking issue.

testManageAllGroups expects NO_CONTENT for subGroup with an existing group id, but the server returns 204 only when moving an existing group; the test may be asserting move semantics unintentionally

In testManageAllGroups (line 174), after creating 'testGroup' (which gets id testGroupId), the test calls `groups().group(topGroup.getId()).subGroup(group)` where group has an id set. GroupResource.addChild with a non-null rep.getId() moves the existing group under topGroup and returns 204 (builder initialized to 204, only set to 201 in the create branch). The test asserts NO_CONTENT (204), which matches the move path. This is intentional per the comment 'it should be possible to add the child to the group now', but the test name and flow suggest testing child creation; using an existing group id tests the move path, not creation. The permission check exercised is requireManage(group) on the parent, which is the same for both paths, so the test is valid for permission coverage but misleadingly named. Consider adding a separate assertion for creating a new child with a fresh name (no id) to cover the create path under the all-groups manage permission.

testManageGroupMembership does not verify the negative case after granting permissions (no assertion that joinGroup with invalid group fails with NotFound rather than Forbidden)

In testManageGroupMembership (line 306), after granting MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP on all-users and MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP on topGroup, the test calls `users().get(bobId).joinGroup(topGroup.getId())` and expects success (no exception). It does not verify that joining a non-existent group now returns NotFoundException (proving the permission check passed and the failure moved to group lookup), nor does it verify that myadmin still cannot manage membership of a group without MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP. The test would pass even if the permission check were silently bypassed (e.g. if the evaluator always returned true), because no negative control is present after the grant. Add an assertion that joining a different group without permission still throws ForbiddenException.

'Illegal HTML' message includes the full File object (toString) which may be an absolute path

The message at line 111 uses `"... for file " + file` where `file` is a `File` object. `File.toString()` returns the path string, which is whatever was passed to the constructor — if the Mojo passes an absolute path, the message contains the absolute path. Same concern as the duplicate-keys message. Should use a relative path or file name for consistency and to avoid leaking build paths.

ANCHOR_PATTERN `</?a[^>]*>` matches any tag starting with 'a' (e.g. `<article>`, `<abbr>`), not just anchor tags

The pattern `</?a[^>]*>` matches `<a...>` and `</a...>` but also matches `<article>`, `<abbr>`, `<address>`, etc., because `[^>]*` allows any characters after the initial `a`. If a translation legitimately contains an `<article>` or `<abbr>` tag (unlikely in Keycloak messages, but possible in future), the anchor sanitization would treat it as an anchor and try to match it against English anchors, producing a false 'Didn't find anchor tag' error. The pattern should be `</?a(\s[^>]*)?>` or `</?a[\s>]` to ensure the tag name is exactly `a`.

Account UI error-invalid-multivalued-size changed from {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} (i18next interpolation) to {0}/{1}/{2} with a MessageFormat choice pattern, which i18next will not interpolate correctly

The account UI (React/i18next) message changed from `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` The account UI uses i18next, which interpolates `{{0}}` (double curly braces), not `{0}` (single braces), and does not understand Java `MessageFormat` choice patterns (`{2,choice,...}`). With the new value, i18next will render the literal text `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` instead of the attribute name and counts, so users will see a broken error message. The account UI file should keep the i18next `{{0}}`/`{{1}}`/`{{2}}` syntax (and plural handling via i18next's own `_one`/`_other` suffixes if needed), not the Java MessageFormat syntax used by the FreeMarker themes.

The admin UI (React) uses its own i18n (react-i18next) with `{{0}}` interpolation and ICU-style plurals, not Java `MessageFormat`. The new value will be displayed literally with `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2} {2,choice,...}` un-interpolated, breaking the error message shown to administrators. The admin UI bundle must keep the `{{0}}`/`{{1}}`/`{{2}}` syntax (or the project's ICU plural syntax), not the server-side MessageFormat syntax.

Admin theme (FreeMarker) error-invalid-multivalued-size changed to MessageFormat choice syntax — verify the admin theme actually uses MessageFormat and not a different interpolation

The admin theme's `messages_en.properties` changed `error-invalid-multivalued-size` from `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The admin theme is server-rendered (FreeMarker) and Keycloak's message resolution uses `java.text.MessageFormat`, so the choice pattern is correct for this theme. However, the same key is also consumed by the admin UI (React) via `js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties`, which uses i18next and does NOT understand MessageFormat (see the admin UI finding). The two bundles now have the same MessageFormat value, but the admin UI bundle should use i18next syntax. The admin theme (FreeMarker) change is correct; the admin UI bundle change is wrong.

Anchor mismatch message 'Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string' is unclear — 'original string' should be 'English source'

The message `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string"` uses 'original string' to refer to the English source value. This is unclear; it should say 'in English source' or 'in the English message' to be unambiguous.

Anchor mismatch message does not include the file name, making it hard to locate the problem

When `santizeAnchors` finds an anchor in the translation that doesn't match the English source, it adds the message `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string"` (line 157). Unlike the 'Illegal HTML' message (line 111) which includes the key and file, this message does not include the key or the file name. In a build with hundreds of files, the developer would have to search for the anchor text across all files to find the offending translation. The message should include the key and file, e.g. `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string for key " + key + " in file " + file`.

Anchor sanitization removes the English anchor from the translated value at the wrong position and can loop forever / corrupt the value

`santizeAnchors` iterates over anchors in the translated value and, for each match, calls `value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. `replaceFirst` removes the first occurrence of the English anchor text anywhere in the translated string, not the occurrence at the translated matcher's position. If the translated value contains the same anchor text earlier (e.g. repeated links, or text identical to the tag), the wrong occurrence is removed and the remaining anchors shift, so subsequent iterations compare mismatched anchors and report false 'Didn't find anchor tag' errors. It also mutates `value` while iterating with a Matcher created from the original string, which can cause the loop to never terminate or to skip anchors when the removal shortens the string (Matcher indices become stale). The method should rebuild the string by removing the exact matched region (e.g. using `matcher.start()/end()` with a StringBuilder) instead of `replaceFirst` on the whole value.

Chinese admin templateHelp still contains a full-width space inside `<NAME >` that the verifier's templateHelp normalization does not strip

The diff changes `CLAIM.<NAME >` to `CLAIM.<NAME>` (removing a full-width/ideographic space U+3000 that was inside the angle brackets). The verifier's `normalizeValue` strips `CLAIM\.<[A-Z]*>` — a regex that only matches ASCII uppercase letters between `<` and `>`. The original zh_CN value had `CLAIM.<NAME\u3000>` (with an ideographic space before `>`), which the regex would not match, so the verifier would have flagged it. The PR fixes the message text, which is correct. However, the verifier's regex remains ASCII-only; any future translation using lowercase claim names or non-ASCII characters inside `CLAIM.<...>` will false-positive. This is a robustness gap in the verifier (see related finding on the templateHelp regex).

Choice-format normalization regex does not handle nested braces, breaking verification of messages with nested choice/format patterns

For keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit` and `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, the code replaces `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` with `...`. The character class `[^}]*` stops at the first `}`, so a choice pattern containing a nested brace (e.g. `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<{2,number}}` or the new `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` combined with other placeholders on the same line) will only be partially replaced, leaving a dangling `{` or `}` that the sanitizer treats as text and that will mismatch the sanitized output, producing false 'Illegal HTML' reports. The replacement should consume balanced braces or the whole `{n,choice,...}` construct including nested groups.

Czech error-invalid-multivalued-size choice pattern uses an incomplete set of plural forms

The Czech login file ends with `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Atribut {0} musí mít nejméně {1} {1,choice,0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot} a nejvíce {2} {2,choice,0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot}.` Czech has three plural forms (1 → hodnota/hodnotu, 2-4 → hodnoty, 0/5+ → hodnot). The choice pattern `0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot` maps: 0 → 'hodnot', 1 → 'hodnotu', 2-4 → 'hodnoty', 5+ → 'hodnot'. This is actually a reasonable Czech plural mapping (0 and 5+ use genitive plural 'hodnot', 1 uses accusative singular 'hodnotu', 2-4 use nominative plural 'hodnoty'). However, the English source uses `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` — the choice is on `{2}` (the maximum), not `{1}` (the minimum). The Czech translation attaches a choice to `{1}` as well, which diverges from the English structure and will produce grammatically correct but structurally different output. The Czech value should mirror the English: `Atribut {0} musí mít nejméně {1} a nejvíce {2} {2,choice,0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot}.` (choice only on `{2}`).

Difference-highlighting substring logic can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when one string is a prefix of the other

When `sanitized` and `value` differ, the code computes `start` as the length of the common prefix and `end` as the length of the common suffix, then calls `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` and `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)`. If one string is a strict prefix of the other (e.g. value = 'abc', sanitized = 'abcd'), then start = 3 and end = 0, and `value.substring(3, 3)` is fine, but if the strings share both a prefix and a suffix that overlap (e.g. value = 'aa', sanitized = 'a'), start can exceed `value.length() - end`, causing `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` (begin > end). Example: value = 'aba', sanitized = 'aa': common prefix 'a' (start=1), common suffix 'a' (end=1), then `value.substring(1, 3-1=2)` = 'b' and `sanitized.substring(1, 2-1=1)` → begin 1 > end 1 is OK (empty), but value='aa', sanitized='a': start=1, end=1, `sanitized.substring(1, 1-1=0)` → begin 1 > end 0 → StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The verifier would crash with an unhelpful exception instead of reporting the illegal HTML. The code should clamp `start`/`end` so that `start + end <= min(value.length(), sanitized.length())`.

Email RTL style stripping uses a hardcoded English attribute string that will not match translations that reorder or translate the style attribute

English reference file path is computed with a regex that does not match real locale suffixes, causing the verifier to fail or compare against the wrong file

The English bundle path is derived with `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. The character class `[a-zA-Z-_]` does not include digits, so locale suffixes containing digits such as `_zh_CN`, `_zh_TW`, `_pt_BR` are not matched and the path is left unchanged (pointing at the translated file itself). Additionally, for files already named `messages_en.properties` the regex matches `_en` and rewrites it to `_en.properties` (harmless), but for any file whose locale suffix contains a digit the verifier will read the translated file as the 'English' source. Consequence: the HTML policy decision (`containsHtml(englishValue)`) is made against the translated value instead of the English source, so translations can be wrongly allowed or wrongly rejected, and the anchor-tag comparison compares a translation against itself. The regex should be something like `_[a-zA-Z]{2}(_[A-Za-z0-9]+)?\\.properties` or, more robustly, the locale should be parsed from the file name.

PropertyResourceBundle is created with the platform default charset instead of UTF-8, which can misread non-ASCII translations

`new PropertyResourceBundle(fis)` uses the constructor `PropertyResourceBundle(InputStream)` which, per the JavaDoc, reads the stream as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1). Keycloak's message properties files are UTF-8 (the project sets `project.build.sourceEncoding=UTF-8` and modern Keycloak loads properties as UTF-8). Reading a UTF-8 file as ISO-8859-1 will mojibake all non-ASCII characters (e.g. Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic), which means the sanitizer operates on corrupted text and the comparison against the sanitized form may produce false 'Illegal HTML' reports for any translation containing non-ASCII characters (the mojibake bytes may include characters that look like HTML entities or tags after unescapeHtml4). The code should use `new PropertyResourceBundle(new InputStreamReader(fis, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))` to match Keycloak's actual loading behavior.

Unconditional unescapeHtml4 on the sanitized value corrupts legitimate HTML entities in message values

After sanitizing, the code unconditionally applies `StringEscapeUtils.unescapeHtml4(sanitized)` (line 95) and also unescapes the original value in `normalizeValue` (line 130). The OWASP sanitizer escapes text content (e.g. `&` becomes `&`, `'` becomes `'`), and the comparison then unescapes both sides. However, unescaping the sanitized output also unescapes entities that were present verbatim in the source value and were intentionally double-escaped by the sanitizer, and it will turn a literal `&amp;` in the source into `&` on both sides, masking real differences. More importantly, a value that legitimately contains the text `<script>` (escaped HTML shown to the user) is unescaped to `<script>` on the value side, then re-sanitized... actually the sanitize happens before unescape, so the unescape happens after sanitize and can reintroduce `<` characters into `sanitized` that are then compared against the unescaped original; any value whose sanitized form differs only by entity encoding will be compared after both sides are unescaped, which can both hide real differences (a translation that adds `<` where English has `<`) and create false positives. The unescape should only be applied to compensate for the sanitizer's own escaping of characters that were not entities in the source, not as a blanket unescape of the whole string.

Verifier does not detect translations that omit an anchor tag present in the English source

`santizeAnchors` only iterates over anchors found in the *translated* value (`matcher = ANCHOR_PATTERN.matcher(value)`) and checks each against the English anchors. If a translation simply omits an `<a>` tag that exists in the English source (e.g. the English has two links and the translation has only one), the loop runs once for the single translated anchor, matches it against the first English anchor, removes it, and returns without ever noticing that the second English anchor has no counterpart. The subsequent sanitization also passes because there is no extra HTML in the translation. The result is a silently broken translation (missing link) that the verifier — whose stated purpose is to catch changed anchors — does not report. The method should also iterate over the English anchors and verify each has a matching counterpart in the translation (i.e. compare counts and sequences in both directions).

VerifyMessageProperties instance fields (messages, file) are not thread-safe; if the Mojo runs verifications in parallel, shared state would be corrupted

The class has instance fields `file` and `messages` (line 39-40). `messages` is initialized in `verify()` (line 47) and appended to in `verifySafeHtml` and `verifyNoDuplicateKeys`. If a single `VerifyMessageProperties` instance is used from multiple threads (e.g. a parallel Maven build), the `messages` list would be corrupted. However, the class is instantiated per file (the test does `new VerifyMessageProperties(file)`), so each file has its own instance. If the Mojo creates one instance per file and processes files in parallel, each instance is independent and thread-safe. If the Mojo reuses a single instance for multiple files, `messages` would accumulate across files and `file` would be overwritten. The class should either be immutable (pass file to constructor, return messages from verify) or documented as not thread-safe. Currently `file` is final but `messages` is mutable instance state, which is a code smell.

This asymmetry means: (a) the English value's anchors are not stripped before `containsHtml`, so if the English value contains ONLY anchors (e.g. `link`), `containsHtml` returns true (the regex `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` matches ``), and `POLICY_SOME_HTML` is selected — which allows `br/p/strong/b` but NOT `a`. So a translation that mirrors the English anchors would have its anchors stripped by `santizeAnchors` (matching the English anchors), and then the remaining text is sanitized with `POLICY_SOME_HTML` (which doesn't allow `a`, but there are no `a` tags left). This works by accident. But if the English value contains anchors AND other HTML (e.g. `

link

`), `containsHtml` returns true, `POLICY_SOME_HTML` is selected, the translation's anchors are stripped, and the remaining `

` tags are allowed. This is correct. The asymmetry is intentional (only the translation's anchors need to be removed for the sanitizer), but it means the English value's anchors are never validated by the sanitizer — if the English source itself contains a malicious anchor (e.g. ``), the verifier would not catch it because the English value is never sanitized. The verifier should also sanitize the English value (or at least validate its anchors) to catch malicious English source messages.

`normalizeValue` special-cases the key `templateHelp` with `value.replaceAll("CLAIM\\.<[A-Z]*>", "")`. The comment says it allows `CLAIM.<NAME>`, but the regex only matches uppercase letters. A translation using `CLAIM.<name>` or `CLAIM.<sub>` (lowercase claim names are common, e.g. the zh_CN admin message references `${CLAIM.sub}`) will not be stripped, the `<name>` will be treated as an HTML tag by the sanitizer, and the verifier will report a false 'Illegal HTML' error. The regex should be case-insensitive or match any non-`>` characters: `CLAIM\\.<[^>]*>`.

verify() catches only IOException from Files.readString but verifySafeHtml() throws RuntimeException for file read errors, breaking the declared exception contract

`verify()` declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and wraps `IOException` from `Files.readString` into `MojoExecutionException`. However, `verifySafeHtml()` (called inside the try block) catches `IOException` from the two `FileInputStream` constructions and rethrows them as `RuntimeException` (lines 70 and 79). These RuntimeExceptions are not caught by the `catch (IOException e)` block and propagate out of `verify()` as unchecked exceptions. The caller (presumably a Maven Mojo) expects `MojoExecutionException` for verification failures; a `RuntimeException` will produce an unhandled stack trace. The `verifySafeHtml` method should either declare `throws MojoExecutionException` and throw that, or `verify()` should catch `RuntimeException` from `verifySafeHtml` and wrap it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant-shortcut comparison

In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the check `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (match failure) when the grant shortcut MATCHES the expected value, and falls through to `return isUUID().matches(items[1])` when it does NOT match. The logic is inverted: the matcher will reject tokens whose grant shortcut equals the expected one and accept tokens with any other (or missing) grant shortcut as long as the suffix is a UUID. Additionally, `substring(3, 5)` is off by one: the encoded prefix is 6 chars (2 session + 2 token type + 2 grant), so the grant shortcut occupies indices 4-5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`. As written, every test using `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` will fail against correctly encoded token IDs (or worse, pass against wrong ones), making the test assertions meaningless. Fix: `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

false_positives.candidate:
Duplicate-shortcut validation compares wrong map sizes and cannot detect collisions

In `postInit`, the duplicate-detection check `if (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size())` is intended to catch two different grant types sharing the same shortcut (or same ID). However, `grantsByShortcuts` is keyed by shortcut and `grantsToShortcuts` is keyed by grant ID. If two grants share the same shortcut, `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantName)` silently overwrites the first entry, shrinking `grantsByShortcuts` by one while `grantsToShortcuts` keeps both IDs — the sizes then differ and the check fires, which is correct. But if two grants share the same ID (impossible for distinct factories) or, more importantly, if a shortcut collides with the reserved `UNKNOWN` shortcut "na", the overwrite happens at line 78 AFTER the loop, again changing sizes — still detected. The real gap: the check only detects size differences, so a collision that is later overwritten by an equal-size map change would be missed, and more practically the error message and detection are fragile. A more robust approach is to detect the overwrite during insertion (e.g., check `grantsByShortcuts.put(...) != null` inside the loop and throw immediately). As written, the validation is indirect and can produce a confusing failure or, in edge cases where a custom provider registers grants dynamically via `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut`, silently accept a colliding shortcut, which would corrupt the token-ID encoding (two grant types mapping to the same 2-char code).

Grant type attribute set on a freshly-created DefaultClientSessionContext may not propagate to token creation

`PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process` builds `sessionContext` via `DefaultClientSessionContext.fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter(...)` and then sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` on that context (line 82) before calling `tokenManager.createClientAccessToken(..., sessionContext)`. Whether the attribute is visible during `initToken` depends on `DefaultClientSessionContext` storing attributes in-memory vs. reading from the underlying client session notes; if `fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter` returns a wrapper whose `setAttribute` writes to a transient map that `initToken` later re-reads through a different context instance, the grant type may be lost and the token ID would be encoded with the "na" shortcut. This is the only grant that sets the attribute on a locally-constructed context rather than through `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse` or the client session itself, so it is the most likely to silently produce `pc`-less (i.e., `na`) token IDs. Worth verifying with an integration test for the pre-authorized-code flow.

Lightweight-token detection reads client attribute from the wrong client context

`getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` determines the token type via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads `session.getContext().getClient()`. During token issuance in `TokenManager.initToken`, the session context client is the client for which the token is being issued, which is normally correct. However, for flows where the session context client differs from the client session's client (e.g., token exchange where `StandardTokenExchangeProvider.setClientToContext` sets the requesting client, or admin/service-account flows), the lightweight flag could be evaluated against the wrong client, encoding `lt` (lightweight) for a regular token or `rt` for a lightweight one. The PR's stated goal is to "recognize more reliably if access-token is lightweight or not"; deriving it from `session.getContext().getClient()` rather than from `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` undermines that reliability. Prefer `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` (the client the token is actually issued for) when deciding the token type.

Potential NPE when client session has no user session

`getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and service accounts, Keycloak can create client sessions without a user session (transient service-account sessions may have a user session, but some code paths create client sessions with a null user session). If `getUserSession()` returns null, this throws a NullPointerException inside `initToken`, failing token issuance. The method should handle a null user session (e.g., treat as TRANSIENT, which matches how service-account/client-credentials tokens behave) instead of dereferencing blindly.

Refresh grant type is hardcoded to REFRESH_TOKEN constant instead of the actual grant type used

In the refresh-token path (`refreshAccessToken` / the code around line 248), the PR sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)`. `OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN` is the string "refresh_token", which matches `RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.getId()`, so the encoding will produce the `rt` shortcut — but note this collides conceptually with the token-type shortcut `rt` (regular token) used in the token-type position; they are in different positions so encoding is unambiguous, but it is confusing. More importantly, hardcoding the constant here bypasses the `OAuth2GrantType.Context.getGrantType()` mechanism used everywhere else; if the refresh flow is ever entered via a different grant type (e.g., a custom refresh-like grant), the encoded ID would incorrectly claim `refresh_token`. Using the actual grant type from the request context would be more consistent.

Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for the SPI

`OAuth2GrantType.Context` is a public class in `server-spi-private` and previously exposed a public copy constructor `Context(Context context)`. The PR removes it (the diff shows the copy constructor body deleted and replaced by the `grantType` initialization in the main constructor). Any third-party `OAuth2GrantType` implementation that relied on the copy constructor (a common pattern for wrapping/decorating contexts) will fail to compile against the new version. Since this is an SPI in `server-spi-private` that the PR explicitly wants to be extensible ("provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), removing a public constructor without a deprecation cycle is an API break. Either keep the copy constructor (initializing `grantType` from `context.grantType`) or document the break.

Unit test bypasses factory.postInit and hand-builds maps, missing coverage of duplicate-shortcut validation

The test's `@Before` constructs `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory`, calls `init(null)`, and then directly assigns `factory.grantsByShortcuts` / `factory.grantsToShortcuts` (package-private fields) instead of calling `postInit(...)`. This means the production initialization path — including the duplicate-shortcut validation in `postInit` (lines 70-86) and the population of maps from real `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` instances — is never exercised by this test. A regression in `postInit` (e.g., the broken size-comparison check, or a shortcut collision between two real grant factories) would not be caught. Add a test that runs `postInit` against a real/mock `KeycloakSessionFactory` with the actual grant factories, and a test that a duplicate shortcut causes startup failure.

getTokenContextFromTokenId uses indexOf(':') which breaks if raw ID contains a colon

`getTokenContextFromTokenId` splits the encoded ID with `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` and takes everything after the first colon as `rawId`. `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()` produces UUIDs (no colons), so for newly issued tokens this is fine. However, the method is a public SPI entry point (`TokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId`) meant to decode token IDs that may come from external/custom encoders or older/foreign formats; any raw ID containing a colon (or a legacy ID that happens to contain a colon) would be mis-parsed: the prefix check `encodedContext.length() != 6` would throw `IllegalArgumentException` for a legacy ID like `ab:cd:uuid`, and even a well-formed custom encoding with a colon in the raw part would be split at the wrong position. Using `lastIndexOf(':')` would be more robust, or better, `split(":", 2)` semantics with an explicit prefix-length check. At minimum the parsing should use the LAST colon or validate that the prefix is exactly 6 chars before the first colon and document the constraint.

In `initToken`, the access token ID is now built via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)` where `tokenCtx` comes from `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`. That method sets `grantType = UNKNOWN` ("na") when `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is not set on the client session context, and `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` maps "na" back to "na" via the factory maps (line 78-79 of the factory put UNKNOWN->UNKNOWN), so the common path works. However, `encodeTokenId` throws `IllegalStateException("Cannot encode token with unknown grantType: ...")` when `factory.getShortcutByGrantType(...)` returns null. The factory's lazy-refresh path (`getShortcutByGrantType`, lines 106-119) only refreshes when the grant type is not found AND a provider factory exists for it; for any grant type string that is set on the client session context but has no registered `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` (e.g., a custom grant type implemented without the new SPI, or a code path that sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` to a value with no factory), `getShortcutByGrantType` returns null and `encodeTokenId` throws. Since `initToken` is on the critical path of every access-token issuance (authorization code, refresh, client credentials, CIBA, device, token exchange, etc.), any such gap turns into a 500 error at token issuance instead of degrading to the "na" shortcut. The PR sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` in several grant types but the fallback to UNKNOWN only happens when the attribute is absent — a present-but-unmapped value is fatal. Consider falling back to the UNKNOWN shortcut in `encodeTokenId` (or in `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` validating against known grants) rather than throwing.

Recovery codes are bearer credentials equivalent to passwords; storing them unhashed in an external user storage is a serious data-integrity/security issue, and it also breaks the validation contract: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates input by hashing the input and comparing to the stored hash, while a federated provider receiving raw codes must compare raw-to-raw (as the test provider does at line 340), meaning the same code validates differently depending on where it is stored. The recovery-codes branch of updateCredential builds a CredentialModel with only id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON) and createdDate. This is a race: 0.1 seconds may not be enough on a loaded CI machine, causing the test to fail intermittently when `step.join()` is called before the flusher thread has produced the message. The test should poll in a loop with a timeout (e.g. wait up to 5 seconds for `messages` to be non-empty) rather than relying on a fixed sleep. The `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top also patches `time.sleep` globally, but the explicit `time.sleep(0.1)` call at line 62 uses the real `time.sleep` because it was imported as `import time` and the monkeypatch patches the `time` module's `sleep` attribute — actually this does patch it, making the sleep a no-op, which means the test relies entirely on `step.poll()` and `step.join()` timing, making the race even worse. The test needs a proper wait condition.
