The script now caps each segment set at 1000 members with `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`. Because the buffer is now a sorted set scored by end_timestamp_precise (see buffer.py zadd), ZPOPMIN evicts the spans with the *earliest* end timestamps — i.e., it silently discards real span data whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Previously the Python side enforced max_segment_spans=1001 only at flush time (logging an error and skipping the oversized segment); now data is destroyed at insert time with no metric, no log, and no signal. Consequences: (1) silently incomplete traces shipped downstream — a correctness/data-integrity regression; (2) the eviction happens inside the Lua script where the Python-side `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric can no longer fire; (3) the eviction count is computed from `span_count`, which is only set when a ZUNIONSTORE ran — when neither union branch executes (e.g., root span arriving first, or set_span_id == parent_span_id with no existing set), span_count is recomputed via zcard (line 58-60), but when a union *did* run, ZUNIONSTORE's return value is the cardinality *after* the union, which is correct — however if both unions run, the second assignment overwrites with the post-second-union count, which is also correct; the real issue is the silent data loss itself. Also note the eviction threshold (1000) is hardcoded in Lua while SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (1001) still exists in Python, creating two divergent limits.

Redirect-chain traversal limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling the overflow case

The loop `for i = 0, 1000 do` follows redirect mappings in the `span-buf:sr:` hash. The original code used 10000 with an explicit comment that the limit means segment trees deeper than 10k may not be joined correctly. The new limit of 1000 silently exits the loop after 1001 iterations *without* breaking — when the loop exhausts, `set_span_id` still holds an intermediate (non-root) span id, and the script proceeds to merge into that intermediate set and write a redirect from span_id to it. This is functionally the same failure mode as before but at a 10x lower depth, and the returned `redirect_depth` (1000) is indistinguishable from a legitimate depth-1000 chain, so the Python metrics (min/max_redirect_depth gauges) cannot alert on truncation. Deep chains (e.g., from long-running traces or pathological redirect accumulation) will now be split into multiple segments more often, producing duplicate/partial segments downstream.

ZADD keyed by raw payload bytes makes duplicate spans overwrite each other and breaks set semantics for identical payloads

process_spans now writes spans with `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise for span in subsegment})`. In a Redis sorted set, the *member* is the payload bytes and the score is the timestamp. Two consequences: (1) If the same span payload is processed twice (at-least-once Kafka delivery, consumer rebalance replay, or the same span appearing in two batches), the second ZADD silently overwrites the first — previously SADD also deduplicated, so this is not a regression per se, but combined with the score it means the *latest* end_timestamp wins, which is fine; (2) more importantly, the dict comprehension `{span.payload: ... for span in subsegment}` collapses multiple spans with identical payload bytes within the same batch into a single entry *before* Redis is involved — if a batch legitimately contains two distinct Span objects whose serialized payloads are byte-identical (possible when end_timestamp_precise differs but... actually payload includes the timestamp, so identical payload implies identical span), this is mostly benign. The real issue: the member being the full payload means ZSCAN in _load_segment_data returns (payload, score) tuples — handled — but ZUNIONSTORE in the Lua script aggregates scores with SUM by default across the two source sets, so a span present in both set_key and span_key gets its end_timestamp *doubled* as its score after merge. Since scores now drive ZPOPMIN eviction order (see add-buffer.lua finding), merged segments have corrupted eviction ordering: spans that participated in a merge are ranked as if they had ~2x their end timestamp and will be evicted last / retained incorrectly, and the flush ordering semantics change. The score is no longer a pure end_timestamp.

max_segment_spans limit silently removed from flush path while Lua now evicts at 1000 — the Python-side guard and metric are dead code

The diff removes the `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans:` check (and its `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric + error log) from _load_segment_data, on the assumption that the Lua script now caps segments at 1000 spans. But the constructor still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` (line 150), which is now unused — dead configuration that misleads operators into thinking the flush path enforces a span-count limit. Worse, the two limits disagree (Lua 1000 vs Python 1001), and the Python-side metric that alerted on oversized segments no longer exists, so dashboards/alerts on `segment_span_count_exceeded` silently stop firing. Either remove the unused parameter or keep a defensive check in Python.

__reduce__ drops segment_page_size and max_segment_bytes/max_segment_spans when pickling SpansBuffer for multiprocessing

SpansBuffer.__reduce__ returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))` — it omits segment_page_size, max_segment_bytes, and max_segment_spans. This is pre-existing (not introduced by this diff), but the diff makes it more impactful: since max_segment_spans is now only a constructor default and the Lua script hardcodes 1000, a pickled buffer (used by run_task_with_multiprocessing in factory.py) silently uses defaults for the byte-size limit too. Not introduced by this PR, but worth noting the pickle path now diverges further from configured behavior. (Reporting as low since it's pre-existing; flagging because the PR touches this class's limits.)

process_batch assumes end_timestamp_precise is always present in the span payload — KeyError on older Relay payloads

process_batch now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` (direct indexing, line 141). The ingest-spans schema may mark this field optional or older Relay versions may omit it; direct [] indexing raises KeyError, which would crash the consumer task and block offset commits for the entire batch (poison-pill message). The neighboring fields use .get() with defaults (parent_span_id, is_remote). If the field can be absent, this should be `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` or the schema must be verified to guarantee presence. A missing field would halt span ingestion for affected partitions until the message is skipped/dead-lettered.

Pre-existing typo `queryset.query.order_b` (should be `order_by`) in BasePaginator.build_queryset, now reachable via OptimizedCursorPaginator

Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — a typo for `order_by`. This is pre-existing, but it means that when the queryset is already ordered by `-key` and an ascending traversal is requested, the re-ordering is silently dropped (the attribute assignment creates a new unused attribute), so the queryset keeps its original descending order and pagination returns wrongly-ordered/duplicated rows. OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits build_queryset unchanged, so the new paginator inherits this latent bug. Worth fixing while touching this code, since the new paginator is presented as an 'optimized' path.

Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but Cursor.from_string and all paginators either reject or mishandle them

The added comment on Cursor.__init__ says 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios'. In reality, Cursor.from_string will parse a negative offset from a client-supplied cursor string (int(bits[1]) accepts '-5'), and the only consumer that 'supports' it is OptimizedCursorPaginator's broken negative-slicing path (which crashes on Django's assertion), while BasePaginator now silently clamps it to 0 and OffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator raise BadPaginationError. The comment documents an intent that the codebase does not safely implement; it should be removed or the behavior made consistent (reject negative offsets at parse time).

No test covers the new 1000-span eviction behavior or the sorted-set migration of existing buffer keys

The PR changes the buffer from Redis sets (SADD/SSCAN/SUNIONSTORE) to sorted sets (ZADD/ZSCAN/ZUNIONSTORE) with eviction at 1000 spans. The test suite updates Span construction for the new end_timestamp_precise field but adds no test that: (1) a segment exceeding 1000 spans is truncated by the Lua script (data loss is untested and unasserted); (2) ZUNIONSTORE score aggregation (SUM across merged sets) doesn't corrupt eviction order; (3) mixed old-format (set) and new-format (zset) keys during a rolling deploy are handled — the Lua script calls ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE on keys that may still be plain sets from before the deploy, which returns a WRONGTYPE error and fails the whole EVALSHA pipeline for that batch. A rolling deploy of this consumer will hit WRONGTYPE errors on any segment key created by the old code until its TTL (redis_ttl=3600s) expires. There is no migration/compatibility handling and no test for it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python's randomized hash(), causing cache misses and cross-process inconsistency

The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's `hash()` for tuples of ints is deterministic within a process but the string representation is embedded in a cache key shared across processes/workers (and potentially a shared Redis/memcached backend via `sentry.utils.cache`). More importantly, `hash()` output can differ between processes when `PYTHONHASHSEED` randomization affects str/bytes hashing (tuple hash of ints is stable, but relying on `hash()` for a persistent cache key is fragile and non-portable), and the key is not human-inspectable. Consequence: cache entries may never be hit across workers, silently defeating the stated 60-second caching optimization, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73) computes the same key so invalidation works only within the same process/seed. Use a stable serialization such as `":".join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: using Python's built-in `hash()` for generating cache keys from `project_ids` causes cross-process inconsistency and breaks `invalidate_upsampling_cache`, recommending a deterministic string serialization instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the outer `dataset` variable instead of the actually-scoped dataset, breaking dashboard split queries

Inside `_get_event_stats`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using `dataset` captured from the enclosing `get()` scope. However `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `scoped_dataset` (line 210), which the dashboard-widget factory (lines 372-435) sets to `discover` for split error/transaction sub-queries even when the outer `dataset` is `metrics_enhanced_performance`. Consequence: for a metrics-enhanced widget, the error sub-query executed against `discover` will be evaluated with `dataset=metrics_enhanced_performance`, which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` treats as "other dataset" and returns False — so upsampling is silently skipped for exactly the error queries the feature targets (or conversely applied based on the wrong dataset). The check must use `scoped_dataset`, not `dataset`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset`, causing upsampling to be skipped in dashboard split queries where the outer dataset is metrics and the actual query dataset is discover.

false_positives.candidate:
Allowlist check compares project IDs against an option that may contain project slugs, and ignores the organization

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` reads `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` and checks `project_id in allowlist`. Sentry options of this kind are typically configured with project slugs or a mixed list, not numeric IDs; if the allowlist contains slugs (or org-scoped values), the membership test will always fail or, worse, could accidentally match if the option is keyed differently. Additionally, the `organization` parameter is accepted but never used, so an allowlist configured per-organization cannot be honored, and a global allowlist would incorrectly apply to every organization. Consequence: upsampling may be silently disabled (safe) or incorrectly enabled for organizations whose projects coincidentally match IDs from another org's allowlist (unsafe — wrong counts). The option value's expected type/scope must be validated and the organization must be part of the check.

Upsampled count assumes sample_weight is populated for every event, producing wrong counts when it is not

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count`, which the discover dataset (src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py, added SnQLFunction `upsampled_count`) implements as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. The docstrings claim "we rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed". In ClickHouse/Snuba, `sum()` over a column with NULL/missing values yields NULL (or 0 with default settings), and events ingested before the allowlist was enabled, events from Relay configs that don't set sample_weight, or non-sampled error events will not have a meaningful sample_weight. Consequence: `count()` silently returns 0 or NULL instead of the true event count for allowlisted projects — a data-integrity bug that under-reports error volumes in the events-stats API. The transformation must use `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))` (or equivalent) or the eligibility check must guarantee sample_weight presence per event.

Column transformation only matches the exact string "count()" and misses equivalent forms

The transform lowercases and strips the column, then compares `column_lower == "count()"`. Real queries produce columns such as `count() as count`, `count()` with an alias, `count_unique(...)` is fine, but also `count()` embedded in equations or with different spacing like `count( )`, or the API's `yAxis=count()` may arrive as `count()` — however any aliasing (`count() as cnt`), whitespace inside the parens, or a trailing alias will not match and will be passed through untransformed. Consequence: mixed queries (e.g. `yAxis=count()&yAxis=count() as total`) would upsample one series and not the other, producing inconsistent, incomparable counts within a single response. The matcher should parse the aggregation (e.g. regex `^count\(\s*\)(\s+as\s+\w+)?$`) and preserve the alias.

Discover-dataset eligibility is decided by naive substring match on the raw query string

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the substring `event.type:error` appears anywhere in `request.GET["query"]`. This is trivially bypassed and also produces false positives: a query like `event.type:transaction AND message:"event.type:error"`, or `!event.type:error`, or a negated/quoted occurrence, will be treated as error-focused. Consequence: transaction events (which have no `sample_weight`) get their `count()` rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, yielding wrong/zero counts for transaction series on the discover dataset. Eligibility must be based on the parsed search query (the resolved event-type filter), not substring matching.

Errors dataset is unconditionally upsampled even for queries that include non-error or transaction events

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for the entire `errors` dataset module without inspecting the query. The errors dataset can still be queried with filters that exclude error events or with `event.type:transaction` (the endpoint itself supports dataset=errors with arbitrary queries, and the dashboard split logic in organization_events_stats.py issues `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction` and `event.type:transaction` sub-queries against `discover`). If any non-error rows can appear in the result set, `sum(sample_weight)` will miscount them. Consequence: incorrect counts whenever the errors dataset query is not strictly error-only. The check should apply the same parsed-query validation used for discover, or at minimum exclude transaction event types.

Upsampling transformation is applied only to y-axis columns, not to `selected_columns`/group-by or equations, producing inconsistent results

The transformation rewrites `query_columns` (the y-axes) but `top_events_timeseries` is still called with `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)` and `equations=self.get_equation_list(...)` untransformed. If a user requests `yAxis=count()` together with `field=count()` or an equation referencing `count()`, the equation/selected column will compute a plain `count()` while the timeseries computes `upsampled_count()`, and the two will disagree. Consequence: top-events responses can return a `count` in the series that does not match the per-item `count` in the selected columns, corrupting the API contract. All count() aggregations in the query (y-axes, equations, and any selected aggregate columns) must be transformed consistently.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called, so allowlist changes leave stale cache entries for up to 60s

The module provides `invalidate_upsampling_cache(organization_id, project_ids)` with a docstring saying it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes", but a search of the changed files shows no call sites (no option-change hook, signal, or admin action invokes it). Combined with the 60-second TTL, toggling a project in/out of `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` can leave upsampling enabled (or disabled) for up to 60 seconds across all workers. Consequence: stale, inconsistent counts after configuration changes; the invalidation helper is dead code. Either wire it to the option update path or remove it and document the TTL-based eventual consistency.

Test factory mutates normalized event data to set sample_rate, which can leak into stored event payloads and distort other tests

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` is called on `normalized_data` (the event manager's data dict) inside `Factories.store_event` and writes `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)`. `normalized_data` is the dict that gets serialized and stored as the event payload; `sample_rate` is a top-level event attribute that Snuba/event processing treats as the event's sample rate. Consequence: any test that stores an event with `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` will now also persist a top-level `sample_rate`, changing event serialization, grouping, and Snuba `sample_weight` computation for that event — this can silently alter results of unrelated tests that use such contexts, and makes the factory's behavior surprising. The sample weight should be applied at the Snuba/ingest level (or via a dedicated parameter), not by mutating the event payload in a shared factory.

New Snuba tests mock the options module globally, bypassing the real allowlist option and cache behavior

All four new tests use `@mock.patch("sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options")`, which replaces the entire `options` module object in the helper. This means the tests never exercise the real option lookup (`options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`), the default value, or the cache path in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled` (the cache is still real, but the eligibility computation is mocked away). Consequence: the tests would pass even if the option name were wrong, if the option returned slugs instead of IDs, or if the caching logic inverted the boolean — precisely the failure modes that matter for this feature. Tests should set the real option (e.g. via `self.options(...)` / `options.set` with override) and add coverage for the cache hit/miss and invalidation paths.

Unit tests never cover the public entry point or the cache, and SnubaParams is constructed with None start/end

The test file only tests the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`). The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the cache key construction, cache get/set, and the composition of the helpers — is never tested, so the `hash()`-based cache key bug and cache TTL behavior are uncovered. Additionally `SnubaParams(start=None, end=None, projects=...)` is created but never used in any test, suggesting intended coverage of the public function was abandoned. Consequence: the most fragile logic (caching and key construction) has no test protection.

Module identity comparison (`dataset == errors`) is fragile and imports modules inside the function on every call

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` compares dataset modules with `==` (module identity works, but is unusual and breaks if datasets are reloaded or proxied) and performs `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` / `transactions` inside the function body on every invocation. In the endpoint this function is called once per `_get_event_stats` invocation, including multiple times for dashboard split queries. Consequence: repeated import machinery overhead per request and brittle equality semantics; module imports should be top-level and comparison should use `is` or a dataset-name string.

A git submodule pointer file (`sentry-repo`) is added at the repository root

The PR adds a new top-level file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`. This is a git submodule gitlink accidentally committed as a regular file (or a submodule added without a `.gitmodules` entry). Consequence: it pollutes the repository root, will confuse tooling/CI that iterates over files, and indicates the submodule was not added correctly. It should be removed or properly registered via `.gitmodules` + `git submodule add`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cached permission check treats 'not allowed' as cache miss and re-queries, but denial is only cached after DB requery — TOCTOU window combined with stale allow cache

In Check(), when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cached permissions (line 123) and checkPermission returns allowed=false (line 125-135), the code does NOT write a denial-cache entry; it falls through to re-query the DB (line 139). This means a user repeatedly probing resources they cannot access will never populate the denial cache from the cached-permissions path — every request re-runs the full DB permission query (getUserPermissions), defeating the stated purpose of the denial cache and creating a DB load amplification vector for denied users. Additionally, because the positive permCache entry is only refreshed when getUserPermissions runs, a permission revocation is not reflected until the permCache TTL (30s) expires AND the denial path is taken; there is no invalidation of permCache or permDenialCache when permissions change, so a user whose permissions were just granted will be denied for up to shortCacheTTL (30s) via the denial cache, and a user whose permissions were revoked will be allowed for up to shortCacheTTL via permCache. The PR's stated goal (creator can access newly created dashboard) is undermined by the denial cache: if the creator's first check happens before the permission row is visible/committed, the denial is cached for 30s and the creator is locked out.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same asymmetric cache logic in the Check() operation as the golden comment: cached permission grants are trusted immediately (allowing stale access when permissions are revoked), whereas cached denials are ignored and fall through to a fresh database lookup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses raw name/parent strings without escaping, risking cache key collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators (cache.go line 30-32). None of these fields are escaped or length-delimited. A resource name or folder UID containing '_' (which is common for Grafana UIDs) can produce identical cache keys for different (name, parent) pairs — e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' and name='a', parent='b_c' both produce '..._a_b_c'. A denial cached for one combination will incorrectly deny a different resource. This is a correctness bug in the authorization decision cache.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys using simple string concatenation with underscore separators without escaping, leading to key collision risks when fields contain underscores and potentially causing incorrect authorization denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity authorization bypass

The denial cache key is built as userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) and does not include the identity type (user vs service account vs anonymous vs render). The same userUID string can be used with different identity types (e.g. 'user:test-uid' vs 'service-account:test-uid' both yield UserUID 'test-uid' after ParseTypeID). If a check for one identity type is denied and cached, a subsequent check for a different identity type with the same UID, action, name and parent will hit the denial cache at line 117 and be incorrectly denied — or conversely, the design invites key collisions between distinct principals. More importantly, the denial is cached for the raw subject UID without binding to the resolved internal user ID, so any future change in how subjects map to UIDs, or any two distinct principals sharing a UID string across identity types, produces wrong authorization decisions. The key must include checkReq.IdentityType (and ideally the resolved internal user ID from UserIdentifiers) to be safe.

Denial cache is populated even when the denial is due to a transient error or missing resource, locking out legitimate access

At line 153-155, whenever checkPermission returns allowed=false after a fresh DB query, the denial is cached unconditionally with s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true). checkPermission returns false not only for genuine lack of permission but also when the requested resource does not exist yet (e.g. a dashboard/folder being created, or a race where the permission row hasn't been committed). Because the PR's stated motivation is 'allow users to fetch newly created dashboards and folders', caching a denial for a resource that was just created (and whose permission grant may not yet be visible) will cause the creator to be denied for up to shortCacheTTL (30 seconds). There is no distinction between 'resource not found' and 'permission denied', and no cache invalidation hook when a new permission is created. This directly contradicts the PR's goal and introduces a user-facing lockout window.

permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented as 'false' (cache miss) even when the cache was hit but the permission check returned not-allowed

At line 137, s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc() is executed unconditionally after the cached-permissions block, including the case where getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeded (cache hit) but checkPermission returned allowed=false. In that case the permission cache WAS used (hit), but the metric records a miss. This misreports cache effectiveness and will mislead operators tuning cache TTLs. The metric should only be incremented as a miss when getCachedIdentityPermissions actually returned an error (cache.ErrNotFound).

Denial cache is keyed on request-supplied Name and ParentFolder before verifying the resource exists, enabling cache pollution / memory exhaustion

The denial cache key includes checkReq.Name and checkReq.ParentFolder, which are arbitrary attacker-controlled strings from the CheckRequest (validated only for non-empty namespace/subject/action). An attacker (or a misbehaving client) can issue Check requests with many distinct random Name values for an action they are denied, each generating a unique permDenialCache entry with shortCacheTTL (30s). With an unbounded local cache (cache.NewLocalCache with no size limit configured in rbac.go line 88), this allows unbounded memory growth in the authz service — a denial-of-service vector. The cache implementation (authlib cache.NewLocalCache) has no max-entries bound, so this is a real memory exhaustion risk.

In-proc authz client uses NoopCache, silently disabling client-side caching and changing behavior vs remote mode

In ProvideAuthZClient, the in-proc path now constructs the authzlib client with authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}) (line 103), replacing the previous newRBACClient which used a real 30s local cache. NoopCache.Get always returns cache.ErrNotFound and Set is a no-op. This means the in-proc client never caches Check responses client-side. While the PR description says this is intentional ('remove the use of authLib cache when running authZ service in-proc'), the consequence is that every Check/List call from Grafana's own API server now goes through the full gRPC in-proc round trip plus the server-side cache logic, with no client-side short-circuit. Combined with the server-side denial cache issues above, this changes the latency and load profile of the in-proc path. More critically, if the server-side caches are cold or bypassed (e.g. for render service identity which always returns cache.ErrNotFound from getCachedIdentityPermissions), every request hits the DB. This is a performance regression that should be acknowledged and the NoopCache behavior documented, or a bounded cache should be used instead.

Denial cache Set is not protected by singleflight, allowing stampede and inconsistent state

The positive permission path uses singleflight (s.sf.Do) to deduplicate concurrent DB queries for the same userPermKey (line 380). However, the denial cache write at line 154 (s.permDenialCache.Set) and the denial cache read at line 117 are not coordinated with singleflight or with the positive cache population. Two concurrent Check requests for the same denied resource can both miss the denial cache, both query the DB, and both write denial entries — a minor stampede. More significantly, there is a race between the positive permCache.Set inside getUserPermissions (line 406) and the denial cache: a request that queries the DB and finds no permission writes a denial entry, while a concurrent request that queried slightly earlier may have populated permCache with a scope map; subsequent requests will hit the denial cache and be denied even though permCache contains a (possibly stale) allow. The two caches can hold contradictory state with no reconciliation, and the denial cache takes precedence (checked first at line 117), so a stale denial can override a fresh allow.

Denial cache test does not verify that a denial is actually cached after a DB denial, nor that the denial expires / is invalidated

TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest (line 973) manually seeds the denial cache and verifies a deny, but there is no test that verifies the production code path at service.go line 153-155 actually writes a denial entry when a DB query returns not-allowed. The existing 'should deny user without permission' test in TestService_Check (line 756) checks the response but does not assert that s.permDenialCache now contains an entry. Without this assertion, a regression that removes or breaks the denial-cache write would not be caught. Additionally, there is no test covering the cross-identity-type key collision issue (same UID, different identity types) or the cache-key collision issue from unescaped '_' in names.

false_positives.candidate:
OAuth token exchange failure is not handled, causing unhandled exception instead of user-facing error

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called without any exception handling. If GitHub's token endpoint returns a non-2xx status (e.g., invalid/expired/replayed `code`, rate limiting, or network error), `safe_urlopen` raises an exception that propagates up as a 500 error rather than the intended user-facing 'Invalid installation request' error page. The PR description explicitly states the pipeline should fail gracefully when 'GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code (wrong or attempt of re-use of code)', but a GitHub error response (which is the normal way GitHub signals a bad code) will crash instead of rendering the error template. The subsequent try/except only wraps `safe_urlread(req).decode('utf-8')` and `parse_qsl`, not the `safe_urlopen` call itself, so HTTP error statuses from the token endpoint are unhandled.

OAuth authorize redirect URL parameters are not URL-encoded

The redirect to GitHub's authorize endpoint is built via f-string interpolation: `f"{ghip.get_oauth_authorize_url()}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. The `redirect_uri` value (produced by `absolute_uri(reverse(...))`) and potentially `state` are not URL-encoded with `urlencode`. If `redirect_uri` contains characters like `&`, `=`, `+`, or spaces (e.g., from a customer-domain URL prefix or unusual host configuration), the query string will be malformed — parameters can be injected or truncated, potentially causing the OAuth flow to use an incorrect redirect_uri or allowing parameter manipulation. This should use `urllib.parse.urlencode` to safely construct the query string.

get_user_info API failure is unhandled, causing 500 instead of graceful error

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called without exception handling. `get_user_info` makes an HTTP request to GitHub's `/user` endpoint (as evidenced by the test stub at tests line 123). If that request fails (network error, GitHub 401/403 because the token is invalid or lacks `user` scope, rate limiting, or returns a non-JSON body), the exception propagates as an unhandled 500 error rather than the intended 'Invalid installation request' error page. The very next line defensively checks `if "login" not in authenticated_user_info`, showing the author intended to handle bad responses gracefully, but only handles the case where the response parses successfully yet lacks a `login` field — not the case where the request itself fails. This should be wrapped in try/except and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

OAuth state comparison is not constant-time, allowing timing side-channel

The pipeline signature (a security token acting as OAuth `state`) is validated with a plain string equality check: `if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature:`. String comparison in Python short-circuits on the first differing character, creating a timing side-channel that could theoretically allow an attacker to recover the signature byte-by-byte. Since `pipeline.signature` is a secret used to authenticate the OAuth callback (and the pipeline state in Redis is keyed by it), it should be compared using `hmac.compare_digest()` (or `secrets.compare_digest()`). This is a defense-in-depth issue — the signature is high-entropy so practical exploitation is difficult — but comparing secrets with `==` is a recognized anti-pattern for exactly this reason.

GitHubInstallation reads installation_id from request.GET without validating pipeline state, allowing cross-pipeline state confusion

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, `installation_id = request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))` prefers a request-supplied `installation_id` over the pipeline-bound state. Because `PipelineAdvancerView` has `auth_required = False` and `csrf_protect = False` (src/sentry/web/frontend/pipeline_advancer.py lines 25-27), and the pipeline is looked up from a cookie/Redis keyed by pipeline name, an attacker who knows (or guesses) a valid pipeline identifier could craft a request to `sentry-extension-setup` with an arbitrary `installation_id` query parameter. The OAuthLoginView step binds `github_authenticated_user` to the pipeline, but GitHubInstallation then trusts a fresh `installation_id` from GET — meaning the user-mismatch check at line 501 compares the OAuth-authenticated user against the `sender` of a *different* installation than the one whose OAuth flow was completed. While the mismatch check still requires the authenticated user to match the sender of whatever installation_id is supplied, this breaks the intended binding between the OAuth step and the installation step: the `installation_id` validated in OAuthLoginView (line 397-399) is not necessarily the one checked in GitHubInstallation. The installation_id should come exclusively from pipeline state (`pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id")`), with the GET parameter only used to *initialize* the pipeline on the first entry, not to override it on subsequent steps.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path

The test `test_installation_not_found` stubs a 404 for `GET /app/installations/{installation_id}` (line 381-383), but then makes requests that never reach `build_integration`/`get_installation_info`. The first request (line 385-387) hits `setup_path` with only `installation_id` — this enters GitHubInstallation (the second pipeline view) which redirects to the GitHub app URL because... actually with the new pipeline, the first view is OAuthLoginView which redirects to GitHub authorize (no state param). The second request (line 388-395) supplies a `state` value of `"ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` which does NOT match the pipeline signature (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` used elsewhere), so OAuthLoginView returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error at the state-mismatch check (integration.py line 412-413) — before any call to `get_installation_info`. The assertion `assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content` (line 396) passes, but the test name and the 404 stub are now misleading: the test no longer exercises the 'GitHub installation could not be found' code path in `build_integration` (integration.py lines 352-357). The original assertion `assert b"The GitHub installation could not be found." in resp.content` was removed. A proper test for the 404 path would need to complete the OAuth step first (with the correct state signature) and then trigger `build_integration` with the 404-stubbed installation_id.

assert_setup_flow hardcodes response call index, making it brittle to unrelated stub changes

In `assert_setup_flow`, the assertion `auth_header = responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` (line 257) relies on the exact ordering and count of HTTP requests made by `responses`. The index was changed from `calls[0]` to `calls[2]` to account for the two new requests made by OAuthLoginView (the token exchange POST and the `/user` GET). This is brittle: any future change that adds or reorders a stubbed HTTP call (e.g., adding a rate-limit check, changing the order of operations in OAuthLoginView, or adding a request in `determine_active_organization`) will silently break this assertion or, worse, assert against the wrong request's headers. A more robust approach would be to find the relevant call by URL (e.g., `next(c for c in responses.calls if "/app/installations/" in c.request.url and c.request.method == "POST")`) rather than by positional index.

OAuth access token may be logged or leaked via exception traces

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the `access_token` obtained from GitHub's token endpoint (line 431-434) is passed to `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])`. If `get_user_info` raises an exception (unhandled, per the related finding), the exception traceback — and potentially the request URL or headers containing the token — could be logged by Sentry's error reporting or appear in server logs. Additionally, the token is stored in the pipeline state only as the derived `login` string (line 438), which is good, but the raw token exists in local variables (`payload`, `data`) for the duration of the request. While this is largely unavoidable in an OAuth flow, the lack of exception handling around `get_user_info` increases the risk that the token-bearing request context is captured in an error report. Wrapping the token-exchange and user-info calls in try/except (returning the generic error page) would prevent token leakage through unhandled exception traces.

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated) decides whether to invalidate the getForLogin caches by comparing only the login predicate (enabled, not link-only, not hidden) and the organizationId. It does NOT compare the IDP's config, specifically the OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC flag. The login predicate added in IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getLoginPredicate() (line 254) now includes 'idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))', meaning an org-linked IDP qualifies for login only when BROKER_PUBLIC is true. If an admin updates an org-linked IDP and flips BROKER_PUBLIC from true to false (or vice versa) while keeping it enabled/not-link-only/not-hidden and keeping the same organizationId, both original and updated pass getLoginPredicate() only if the flag is true in both — but when flipping true→false, original passes and updated fails, so invalidation does happen. The real gap: an org-linked IDP with BROKER_PUBLIC=false (not a login IDP) updated to BROKER_PUBLIC=true becomes a login IDP — handled. But what about an org-linked IDP where BROKER_PUBLIC stays true and organizationId stays the same, yet some other config relevant to login display changes? The actual bug: when organizationId is unchanged and both pass the predicate, the method returns without invalidating — but the predicate itself depends on config (BROKER_PUBLIC). The subtle break is: the predicate test on the 'updated' model uses the in-memory model passed to update(), but the JPA delegate may normalize config (e.g. missing keys). More concretely, the method's second guard requires Objects.equals(original.getOrganizationId(), updated.getOrganizationId()) — but it does not verify that the BROKER_PUBLIC config value is unchanged. If an org-linked IDP has BROKER_PUBLIC absent (null → parseBoolean(null)=false → not a login IDP) and the update sets BROKER_PUBLIC=true, original fails predicate, updated passes → invalidates (correct). If BROKER_PUBLIC=true → absent: original passes, updated fails → invalidates (correct). So the predicate comparison does cover BROKER_PUBLIC transitions. The remaining hole: the predicate does not include the organization's enabled state or the organization provider's enabled state, but those are checked at read time via createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel, not cached. After deeper analysis, the concrete defect is different: the method compares original.getOrganizationId() with updated.getOrganizationId(), but when an IDP is linked to an org via OrganizationProvider.addIdentityProvider (as in the test at line 505), that operation may not go through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update() — it may directly set the organizationId on the IDP through a different code path, meaning registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is never invoked for org-link changes done via the organization API, leaving the login caches stale. By collecting into a HashSet, the cached path loses any ordering guarantee, so the stream returned to callers (e.g. login page rendering in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean, which sorts afterwards, but other callers may not) has non-deterministic iteration order. The same pattern exists in getByOrganization (line 200), but for getForLogin the ordering matters more because the login page displays IDPs and the sorting in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean uses IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE which sorts by display name/alias — however, if two IDPs have the same display name, the tie-breaking order becomes non-deterministic across cache hits vs misses, causing inconsistent UI ordering and potentially flaky tests. The new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` replaces the real DuckDB-backed implementation (`github.com/scottlepp/go-duck/duck`) with a stub `DB` type whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` methods all return `errors.New("not implemented")`. `TablesList` is called from `NewSQLCommand` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go line 30) and `QueryFramesInto` from `SQLCommand.Execute` (line 100). This means that even if the `enableSqlExpressions` gate in `pkg/expr/reader.go` were corrected to allow SQL expressions when the feature flag is enabled, any SQL expression query would fail at runtime: `NewSQLCommand` would return a BadRequest error ("error reading SQL command") because `sql.TablesList` returns "not implemented", and `Execute` would set `rsp.Error` to "not implemented". The PR description says the goal is to move the security fix into the repo while keeping the feature flag functional, but this stub makes the feature completely non-functional rather than gated. Either the DuckDB dependency should be retained behind the flag, or the stub should be clearly documented as permanently disabling the feature (in which case the flag check in reader.go should be removed entirely rather than kept as dead code).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: the removal of the go-duck dependency in `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` and the replacement of `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` with stubs that return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Results overwritten when frame has zero rows: NoData result is immediately replaced by empty TableData

In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values` to a `mathexp.NoData{Frame: frame}` (lines 110-114), but then unconditionally overwrites `rsp.Values` with `mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}` at lines 116-118. The `NoData` branch is therefore dead code and the intended "no data" semantics (which typically signal to the frontend/alerting that the query returned no data points, distinct from an empty table) are lost. This is a pre-existing bug in the file (not introduced by this diff), but it is in the direct path of the SQL expression feature being modified by this PR, and it means the `if frame.Rows() == 0` block should either be removed or the unconditional assignment should be made conditional (`else`).

SQL string escaping by doubling single quotes is insufficient and leaves an injection path if TablesList is ever reachable

`TablesList` builds a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only replacing single quotes with doubled single quotes (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`). This escaping does not account for backslash escapes (DuckDB/SQL string literals interpret `\'` as an escaped quote, so a payload ending in a backslash can break out of the string literal), and it is applied to user-controlled SQL before it is passed to `RunCommands`. In the current state this code path is unreachable in production because `NewSQLCommand` is gated off in `pkg/expr/reader.go` and the stub `DB.RunCommands` returns "not implemented", but the function remains exported and callable, and the escaping is a classic SQL-injection anti-pattern. If the feature flag gate is fixed (see related finding) or if this function is called from any other path, an attacker-controlled `rawSQL` value could inject arbitrary DuckDB commands (which, per CVE-2024-9264, can lead to RCE/LFI via DuckDB extensions and file access). The correct fix is to not build SQL by string concatenation at all — use a parameterized query or pass the SQL text via a bound parameter — and to ensure this code is unreachable unless the feature is explicitly enabled.

Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading — the feature exists but is disabled

When SQL expressions are rejected, the error returned to the caller is `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message is inaccurate: the SQL expression feature is implemented (see `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` and `pkg/expr/sql/`), it is deliberately disabled/gated as a security measure (CVE-2024-9264). Telling users it is "not implemented" will cause confusion and incorrect troubleshooting (users may believe the query type is unsupported rather than disabled by configuration). The message should say something like "SQL expressions are disabled" or "sqlExpressions feature is disabled" so that operators understand they need to enable the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle (and accept the security implications) to use it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race: cache check and cache write are not atomic, allowing duplicate work and stale reads in dev mode

The fast-path read (lines 41-43) and the write (line 69) are protected by separate lock acquisitions, so the check-then-act sequence is not atomic. In dev mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), the fast path is skipped entirely and every concurrent caller acquires the write lock and re-reads the manifest from disk, which is wasteful but not incorrect. More importantly, in non-dev mode, two goroutines can both observe ret == nil, both take the write lock sequentially, and both perform the file read; the second overwrites the first result. This is not a data race (the mutex does protect the variable), but it is a TOCTOU logic flaw: the double-checked locking pattern is incomplete because the second check of entryPointAssetsCache inside the write lock is missing. The consequence is redundant disk I/O and CDN requests under concurrency, and in dev mode every request hits the filesystem. The fix is to re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock (standard double-checked locking), or use sync.Once for the non-dev path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the cache is checked under a read lock, and if empty, a write lock is acquired to populate it, but the code fails to re-check if the cache was populated by another goroutine after acquiring the write lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is populated even when reading the manifest fails, poisoning the cache with nil and a non-nil error

Line 69 unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result` before returning, even when `result` is nil due to an error from readWebAssetsFromFile (line 60) or readWebAssetsFromCDN (line 56). On the next call in non-dev mode, the fast path at line 45 checks `ret != nil`, so a nil cache entry means the error is not cached and the read is retried — that part is benign. However, if `err != nil` but `result != nil` (which cannot happen with the current code paths, but the contract is fragile), a partially-initialized or error-associated result would be cached. More concretely, the function returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err` (line 70) rather than `result, err`; this is equivalent today but couples the return value to the global, making the function's behavior depend on global state mutation order. If a future change makes readWebAssetsFromFile return a non-nil result alongside an error, that broken result would be permanently cached for the process lifetime in non-dev mode, causing all subsequent requests to receive invalid assets with no error. The cache assignment should be conditional on err == nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug on line 69: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, even when an error occurs during asset fetching, rather than only caching the result when `err == nil`.

false_positives.candidate:
HTTP response status code is never checked in readWebAssetsFromCDN

readWebAssetsFromCDN (line 85) performs an HTTP GET via http.DefaultClient.Do (line 90) but never checks response.StatusCode. If the CDN returns a 404, 500, or any non-2xx status, the body is still passed to readWebAssets (line 97), which will attempt to JSON-decode an HTML error page or empty body. This will produce a confusing 'failed to read assets-manifest.json' error rather than a clear 'CDN returned status 404' error, making production debugging difficult. Additionally, the response body is closed but the error from Close is ignored (acceptable), and there is no limit on response body size, which could allow a malicious or misconfigured CDN to exhaust memory. A status check like `if response.StatusCode != http.StatusOK { return nil, fmt.Errorf(...) }` should be added before reading the body.

Typo in error message: 'asssets-manifest' should be 'assets-manifest'

The error message at line 119 reads 'could not find entrypoints in asssets-manifest' — 'asssets' is a typo (three s's). This message is returned to callers and may appear in logs or API responses when the manifest file is malformed. It should read 'assets-manifest' to match the actual filename referenced elsewhere in the file (e.g., line 60, line 77).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug-level log statements left in production cleanup path, logging full ID lists at Error level

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error(...) on every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) with the full list of annotation/tag IDs and the SQL condition. true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation

The diff changes the cleanup ticker from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. The PR description says nothing about changing the schedule; it only claims to split the annotation cleanup queries to avoid deadlocks. Running the entire cleanup suite (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history — including two EnforceRowLimitInQueryHistory passes over up to 200k/150k rows) every minute instead of every 10 minutes is a 10x increase in background database load and directly contradicts the PR's stated goal of reducing lock contention on MySQL. If this change is intentional it must be called out and justified in the PR description; if it is accidental (e.g., leftover from local testing), it must be reverted. Either way it is a real behavioral change a maintainer must consciously approve.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: the cleanup job ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which will significantly increase database load and contention, and should be reviewed.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite large-batch path interpolates IDs into SQL and keys the decision off configured batch size, not actual ID count

In deleteByIDs, when the database is SQLite and cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, the IDs are string-interpolated directly into the DELETE statement instead of being bound as parameters. Two problems: (1) the decision is based on the configured batch size, but the actual number of IDs in a batch is what matters — a batch size of 1000 with only 500 matching rows still takes the interpolation path unnecessarily, and conversely the guard only protects when the config exceeds 999, while SQLite's real limit (SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER) can be lower on older builds or when other statements in the same connection consume variables; the safe check is len(ids) > limit, not cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > limit. (2) Although the values are int64s fetched from the database itself (so not attacker-controlled), building SQL by string concatenation is a fragile pattern that will break or become a SQL-injection vector if this helper is ever reused with non-integer IDs. The condition should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit` and the interpolation should be replaced by chunking the DELETE into multiple statements of at most 999 bound parameters each.

Cleanup by MaxCount no longer deletes annotation_tag rows, orphaning tags

The old implementation deleted from the annotation table with a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ...), and the annotation_tag rows were removed by CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags in a separate pass. The new implementation has the same structure (delete annotations by IDs, then CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags cleans tags), so tags are still eventually removed — but only if CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags runs. More importantly, the MaxAge and MaxCount loops in CleanAnnotations now delete annotation rows in one session and rely on a later, separate job invocation for tag cleanup; between the two, annotation_tag rows reference deleted annotations. The test asserts affectedAnnotationTags == affectedAnnotations*2, which only passes because the test's ProvideCleanupService.Run presumably calls both cleaners. This is acceptable only if the caller always runs CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags after CleanAnnotations; the repository API does not enforce or document this ordering, so any caller that invokes CleanAnnotations alone (the method is exported on xormRepositoryImpl and used directly in TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst) leaves orphaned tag rows. The tag deletion should be coupled to the annotation deletion (delete tags for the fetched IDs in the same batch loop) rather than relying on a separate sweep.

MaxCount cleanup condition is not idempotent across batches: OFFSET-based selection re-selects already-kept rows and can loop forever or delete the wrong rows

The MaxCount branch builds its condition as `annotationType ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT/OFFSET(batchSize, MaxCount)` — i.e., it selects rows at offset MaxCount, keeping the newest MaxCount rows overall. After deleting that batch, the next iteration re-runs the same query; the rows just deleted are gone, so the query now returns the next batchSize rows past the new MaxCount-th row — this part is correct. However, the loop termination relies on deleteByIDs returning 0 affected rows. If a concurrent insert adds a new annotation between the SELECT and the DELETE, the next iteration's SELECT returns a non-empty ID set whose DELETE still affects rows, which is fine; but if the DELETE affects 0 rows (e.g., rows were deleted by another process between SELECT and DELETE), untilDoneOrCancelled sees affected == 0 and stops — correct. The real issue: the OFFSET is applied to a table whose contents change between iterations, and the ORDER BY id DESC with OFFSET MaxCount is only correct if no rows with id greater than the current MaxCount-th row are inserted concurrently; a concurrent insert of a newer annotation shifts the window and causes older-than-necessary rows to be kept or, combined with the fetch-then-delete race, can cause the loop to keep selecting a non-empty batch that deletes 0 rows only if IDs collide — which cannot happen. The concrete defect is subtler: because fetchIDs and deleteByIDs are separate statements, a concurrent insert between them does not cause incorrect deletion, but a concurrent DELETE of the selected IDs causes the loop to terminate early (affected == 0) even though more excess annotations remain, silently under-deleting. The previous single-statement DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ...) was atomic per batch and did not have this early-termination-on-race behavior. The loop should distinguish 'no rows matched the SELECT' (done) from 'rows matched but DELETE affected 0' (retry or continue), e.g., by returning len(ids) == 0 as the termination signal rather than affected == 0.

New large-batch SQLite test inserts 40003 rows with hard-coded IDs, which will collide across subtests sharing the same test database

createTestAnnotations now assigns explicit IDs (ID: int64(i + 1)) and each subtest in TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp calls it against the same fakeSQL database, relying on t.Cleanup to delete all rows after each subtest. The cleanup deletes from annotation and annotation_tag, so IDs are reset between subtests — but the cleanup runs after the subtest, and if a subtest fails mid-way (require.NoError aborts), t.Cleanup still runs, so this is mostly safe. The actual gap: the new test case with 40003 annotations and batch size 32767 exercises the SQLite interpolation path in deleteByIDs, but it only runs on SQLite (db.InitTestDB default) and is skipped in -short mode; there is no test covering the fetch-then-delete race, the early-termination-on-zero-affected case, or the MaxCount OFFSET window behavior under concurrent inserts. More importantly, the test asserts affectedAnnotations == 40000 but with MaxCount=1 and 40003 rows, the loop must run ceil((40003-1)/32767) = 2 iterations; the second iteration selects OFFSET 1 LIMIT 32767 from the remaining 32768 rows, deleting 32767, leaving 1 — the math works, but the test does not verify that the surviving annotation is the newest one (highest ID), which is the actual contract of MaxCount cleanup. TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst covers ordering for MaxCount=1 with 3 rows, but not at batch scale.

fetchIDs interpolates table name and condition into SQL via fmt.Sprintf

fetchIDs builds its query with fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT id FROM %s WHERE %s`, table, condition). The table name and condition are currently only called with hard-coded literals from within this file, so there is no exploitable injection today, but the function is a general-purpose helper whose signature invites future callers to pass user-influenced values. The condition strings themselves embed cutoffDate via %v and annotationType (a caller-supplied string parameter to CleanAnnotations) directly into SQL. annotationType is passed from the cleanup service as a constant (alertAnnotationType etc.), but CleanAnnotations is an exported method and nothing validates annotationType against a whitelist; a future caller passing user input would get SQL injection. At minimum, annotationType should be validated against a known set, and fetchIDs/deleteByIDs should not accept raw SQL fragments as parameters.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage duration with the object name instead of the kind

In Delete, the success-path metric is recorded as d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) (line 106), passing the object name as the 'kind' label, whereas every other method (Create line 48, Get line 73, List line 89, Update line 132, DeleteCollection line 159) passes options.Kind. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: `name` is used instead of `options.Kind` when recording metrics, which is inconsistent with other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes capture the request context, which is cancelled when the HTTP request returns

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine that performs the asynchronous legacy write derives its context from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). In Kubernetes apiserver handlers, the request context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns. Since the legacy write is launched in a goroutine and the function returns immediately after, the parent ctx is almost certainly already cancelled (or will be cancelled within microseconds) by the time d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection runs. The 10-second timeout is therefore meaningless: the derived context is dead on arrival, so every asynchronous legacy write will fail immediately with context.Canceled. This defeats the entire purpose of mode 3 (writing to legacy 'just as a safe measure') — legacy will silently never receive any writes, and because errors are only recorded as metrics (recordLegacyDuration) and never logged, the divergence between unified storage and legacy will be invisible. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to preserve values, or context.Background() with the logger re-attached) so the legacy write actually executes.

Create records a legacy-duration metric on a storage failure path

In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) (line 45). This records a 'legacy' operation duration/error even though no legacy operation was attempted — the failure was in unified storage. This corrupts the legacy-write error/duration metrics that operators would use to detect legacy divergence, making storage failures appear as legacy failures. The correct call is d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...) (as done in Delete at line 103 and DeleteCollection at line 156). The same copy-paste mistake exists in Update at line 129, where a storage update failure is recorded via d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

Unbounded goroutine creation with no backpressure for async legacy writes

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each spawn a fire-and-forget goroutine per request to write to legacy storage, with no worker pool, queue, or concurrency limit. Under load (e.g. a bulk import or a delete-collection storm), every request spawns a goroutine that holds the request's object, options, and validation closures and performs a legacy DB write with a 10s timeout. This can exhaust goroutine/memory/DB-connection resources and, combined with the context-cancellation bug above, leaves large numbers of doomed goroutines. At minimum the legacy write should be dispatched through a bounded worker queue (or the mode should document/limit this), and the goroutines should not retain request-scoped objects longer than necessary.

Async legacy Create reuses the caller's object, which the storage layer may have mutated (resourceVersion/uid set)

In Create, the same obj pointer passed to d.Storage.Create is later passed to d.Legacy.Create in the goroutine (line 55). Unified storage Create typically mutates the object in place to set metadata such as resourceVersion, uid, and creationTimestamp before returning. The legacy store generally expects the original client-supplied object (legacy SQL stores assign their own ids/resource versions, and some legacy implementations reject or misbehave when resourceVersion is set on create). Writing the storage-mutated object to legacy can cause spurious conflicts, wrong uid mapping between the two stores, or legacy-side validation errors — and because the write is asynchronous and its error is only counted in a metric, the two stores will silently diverge. The legacy write should receive a deep copy of the object as it was before the storage Create mutated it (or the storage-mutated fields should be reset), so both stores persist equivalent but independently-versioned objects.

Async legacy Update replays the request's UpdatedObjectInfo, which may re-run create/update validation against a stale or already-applied object

In Update, the same objInfo (a rest.UpdatedObjectInfo closure supplied by the apiserver handler) is passed both to d.Storage.Update and, asynchronously, to d.Legacy.Update (line 139). UpdatedObjectInfo is typically single-use: the apiserver's update handler resolves it once (often caching the resolved object and the pre-update 'old' object for updateValidation). Calling UpdatedObject a second time — later, in a goroutine, after the storage update has already changed the stored object — can return a different/stale object, re-run createValidation/updateValidation against the post-storage-update state, or fail outright (many UpdatedObjectInfo implementations are not safe to invoke twice or concurrently). The previous (pre-async) implementation in this file resolved the object once via objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) and wrapped it in an updateWrapper precisely to avoid this. The async version should capture the resolved object once (as the old code did with updateWrapper) and pass that to legacy, not the raw objInfo.

Mode 3 tests never assert that the asynchronous legacy write actually happens, and would pass even if it never runs

All Mode 3 unit tests (TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) exercise the dual writer and assert only on the unified-storage result. Because the legacy write now runs in a detached goroutine, the tests return before (or regardless of whether) d.Legacy.* is invoked; the mocks' legacy expectations are set up but never asserted with m.AssertCalled / AssertExpectations, and there is no synchronization (e.g. waiting on a channel or Eventually) to observe the async call. Consequently the tests cannot detect the critical regression where the legacy write never executes (e.g. due to the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go): they would still pass. Each test that sets up setupLegacyFn should wait for and assert the legacy call (e.g. assert.Eventually on a mock call count, or a WaitGroup/channel in the mock), and there should be a test asserting that a legacy failure does not affect the returned result (the intended mode-3 semantics).

TestMode3_Get creates a fresh prometheus registry, unlike the other Mode 3 tests which share the package-level registry

TestMode3_Get declares a local p := prometheus.NewRegistry() (line 119) while every other Mode 3 test (and the Mode 1 tests) use the shared package-level var p = prometheus.NewRegistry() declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go. This inconsistency is harmless today only because NewDualWriter presumably tolerates an already-registered/unregistered registry, but it means the metrics asserted or scraped in the Get test come from a different registry than the rest of the suite, and if any test ever registered collectors on p it would behave differently. For consistency and to avoid future double-registration panics, the local declaration should be removed and the shared p used (this is the same cleanup that was applied to dualwriter_mode1_test.go in this PR, where the duplicate local registry was deleted).

Mode 3 integration tests cannot detect divergence because legacy writes are asynchronous and the legacy API is checked immediately

The new 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtests (lines 132-144 and 191-204) run the shared doPlaylistTests helper, which performs CRUD via the k8s API and then immediately reads via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (e.g. getFromBothAPIs at line 610, and the legacy search at line 523). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a background goroutine after the k8s response is returned, so the legacy read can race ahead of the legacy write and observe a missing/stale playlist, producing flaky failures — or, worse, if the async write is broken (see the context-cancellation finding), the test may still pass intermittently because nothing waits for the legacy write to land. The mode-3 subtests need synchronization: after each k8s write, poll the legacy API (require.Eventually) until the legacy write is visible before asserting equality, so the test both (a) tolerates the intended async delay and (b) actually verifies that the legacy write eventually happens.

Grafana rule list key has a stray trailing '}' and omits rule type
