Summary content rendered without null check — can render 'null' or crash

The component renders <SummaryContent>{summary}</SummaryContent> where summary is string | null. If the API returns success=true with summary=null (or the hook returns summary: null in a non-error, non-pending state), React renders nothing for null (safe), but if summary is undefined (e.g., data.summary missing from response), it also renders nothing. However, the hook's return type says summary: string | null, and the component doesn't guard against null before rendering the whole summary box. If summary is null but tooFewFeedbacks is false and isError is false, the component renders a "Feedback Summary" header with empty content — a broken UI state. Should check `if (!summary) return null;` before rendering.

request.user.id accessed without null check — crashes for unauthenticated requests

The endpoint uses ProjectEndpoint with permission_classes = (ProjectReleasePermission,). If authentication fails, DRF would normally return 401/403 before reaching post(). However, analytics.record uses request.user.id directly. If request.user is an AnonymousUser (id is None), this passes user_id=None to analytics. More importantly, if the endpoint is ever accessed with an auth token that authenticates but request.user is somehow unset, this crashes. The analytics Attribute for user_id is required=False, so passing None is acceptable, but accessing .id on AnonymousUser returns None (not a crash). This is a minor robustness note; the main issue is the ordering relative to the feature check (see related finding).

Removing ParameterizationRegexExperiment is a breaking API change for any external consumers

The PR removes the ParameterizationRegexExperiment class entirely and changes ParameterizationExperiment from a union type (ParameterizationCallableExperiment | ParameterizationRegexExperiment) to just ParameterizationCallableExperiment. This is a public API break: any code (including getsentry or plugins) that imports ParameterizationRegexExperiment or passes regex-based experiments to Parameterizer will fail at import/runtime. The __all__ export was also updated. If this class is used outside this repo (e.g., in getsentry), this will break. At minimum, a deprecation shim should be left, or this should be coordinated with downstream consumers.

Dead _handle_regex_match function in parametrize_w_experiments

parametrize_w_experiments defines a nested _handle_regex_match function (lines 335-343) that is identical to the one in parametrize_w_regex, but after the removal of ParameterizationRegexExperiment, the experiments loop only calls experiment.run(content, _incr_counter) and never uses _handle_regex_match. This is dead code that should be removed.

Migration body replaced with no-op return — data migration silently does nothing

The migration function convert_org_saved_searches_to_views previously contained the actual data migration logic (iterating SavedSearch objects with Visibility.ORGANIZATION and creating GroupSearchView entries). It has been replaced with a bare `return` and a comment saying "This migration had an error and was never run. See 0921...". If this migration has already been applied in any environment (recorded in django_migrations), replacing its body with a no-op is fine for that environment. But if there are environments where it has NOT yet run (e.g., fresh installs running all migrations, or environments that skipped it), the no-op means organization-level saved searches will never be converted to GroupSearchView, causing data loss for those users. The comment claims it "was never run" but this cannot be guaranteed across all deployments. The safer approach is to keep the original logic (or fix it) rather than no-op it, OR ensure 0921 supersedes it with proper dependencies. Since 0920 was also no-op'd and both depend on different predecessors (0916 vs 0919), there may be environments where neither the original nor the revised migration runs correctly.

Second migration also no-op'd — no working migration converts org saved searches

Same issue as 0917: this migration's body was replaced with a bare `return` and a comment pointing to 0921. Combined with 0917 also being no-op'd, there are now TWO no-op migrations in the chain. If 0921 (the "rerevised" migration) is not present in this PR's changed files (it is not listed), then NO migration actually performs the conversion. The changed files list shows 0917 and 0920 modified but no 0921 added. This means the data migration is completely missing from this PR — organization saved searches will not be converted to views. This is a critical data integrity gap.

Changing DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT from 'low' to 'off' changes behavior for all existing projects

DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT is changed from "low" to "off", and the corresponding project option default in src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py is also changed from "low" to "off". Project options with a default value apply to all projects that have not explicitly set the option. This means every existing project that has not explicitly configured sentry:autofix_automation_tuning will silently change from "low" (autofix runs at low automation level) to "off" (autofix does not run automatically). This is a significant behavior change affecting auto-fix automation for potentially all customers. This should be a deliberate, communicated rollout (e.g., via a migration that sets the option explicitly for existing projects, or a feature flag), not a silent default change. The tests were updated to expect "off" but no migration or rollout mechanism is provided.

Log message references event_data but logs workflow_event_data — potential NameError or wrong variable

In fire_actions_for_groups, the logger.info call at line ~580 uses extra={"workflow_ids": ..., "actions": ..., "event_data": workflow_event_data, "event_id": workflow_event_data.event.event_id}. The diff shows the change from "event_data": event_data to "event_data": workflow_event_data. If workflow_event_data is defined in the loop scope (it likely is, since it's used for workflow_event_data.event.event_id on the next line), this is fine. But the diff context suggests this was changed from event_data to workflow_event_data, which is correct if workflow_event_data is the per-workflow event data. However, if workflow_event_data is only defined inside a conditional branch and the logger call is outside that branch, this would be a NameError. Without seeing the full function, this is a potential bug — the variable rename should be verified to be in scope at the log call site.

useQuery result is used with isFetching for previous-data fallback but error state is not handled in return

The hook returns {attributes: isFetching ? previous : data, error, isLoading: isFetching}. When the query errors, isFetching becomes false and data is undefined, so attributes becomes undefined (not previous). The error is returned but callers must check it. More importantly, usePrevious(data, isFetching) — the second argument to usePrevious is typically a boolean indicating whether to skip updating. If isFetching is true, previous retains the last non-fetching value. But on error, isFetching is false, so previous would update to undefined (the errored data). This means after an error, attributes becomes undefined rather than retaining the last good data. The error handling pattern is fragile; callers get undefined attributes on error with no fallback to previous good data.

API request uses queryKey[0] and queryKey[1]?.query instead of the structured queryKey

The hook builds a queryKey via traceItemAttributeValuesQueryKey which returns [url, {query}], then calls api.requestPromise(queryKey[0], {method: 'GET', query: {...queryKey[1]?.query}}). This works but is awkward — it reconstructs the options from the queryKey tuple rather than just passing the url and options directly. The spread {...queryKey[1]?.query} creates a new object, which is fine. This is a code smell but not a bug. The queryKey is built but not used for caching (no useApiQuery), so building an ApiQueryKey is unnecessary overhead. Minor.

Body cell renderer returns raw value without field renderer when tableData.meta is missing, but head cell still uses fieldAlignment

In renderDefaultBodyCell, when tableData?.meta is missing, it returns dataRow[column.key] directly (raw value, no formatting). But renderDefaultHeadCell always calls fieldAlignment(column.name, column.type as ColumnValueType) regardless of whether meta exists. This inconsistency means headers are aligned based on column.type but body cells are unformatted raw values when meta is missing. More importantly, when meta IS present, getFieldRenderer is called with tableData.meta.fields, but if column.key is not in meta.fields (e.g., a custom column not present in the data), getFieldRenderer may return a fallback or throw. The renderer should handle the case where column.key is not in meta.fields gracefully.

Fallback column extraction crashes when tableData.meta.fields is undefined

When columns prop is not provided, the component does Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields).map(...). If tableData.meta is undefined or tableData.meta.fields is undefined, Object.keys(undefined) throws a TypeError, crashing the component. The TabularData type says meta is required, but the component uses tableData?.meta.fields with optional chaining on tableData but NOT on .meta.fields — so if tableData exists but meta.fields is undefined (e.g., empty API response), this crashes. Should be Object.keys(tableData?.meta?.fields ?? {}).

useApiQuery enabled condition uses replayRecord?.id and project?.slug but query key uses replayRecord?.id ?? '' — query fires with empty replayId

createAISummaryQueryKey(organization.slug, project?.slug, replayRecord?.id ?? '') is called unconditionally to build the query key. If replayRecord is undefined, the query key becomes `/projects/org-slug/undefined/replays//summarize/breadcrumbs/` (with empty replayId). The enabled condition checks Boolean(replayRecord?.id && project?.slug && feature), so the query won't fire when replayRecord is undefined. However, the query key is still constructed with undefined/empty values, which could cause React Query cache collisions if multiple components mount with undefined replayRecord. More importantly, if project is undefined (project_id set but project not loaded yet), project?.slug is undefined and the query key contains 'undefined' as a string segment. The enabled check prevents firing, but the key construction with undefined values is sloppy and could cause cache issues.

chapterData maps over summaryData?.data.time_ranges but summaryData could be undefined after the null check

After the `if (!summaryData) return ...` check, the code accesses summaryData.data.summary and summaryData?.data.time_ranges.map(...). The optional chaining on summaryData?.data.time_ranges is inconsistent with the earlier non-optional summaryData.data.summary access. If summaryData.data is undefined (response has no data field), summaryData.data.summary throws. The SummaryResponse type says data is required, but runtime responses may not match. The optional chaining on time_ranges suggests defensive coding, but summaryData.data.summary on line 150 is not defensive. Inconsistent null handling.

Entire request payload is buffered in memory as a JSON string before sending to Seer

analyze_recording_segments builds the entire request_data via json.dumps({"logs": get_request_data(...)}) which materializes ALL log messages into a list in memory (get_request_data returns list(gen_request_data(...))), then json.dumps the whole thing, then json.loads the Seer response. For long replays with many breadcrumbs and errors, this can consume significant memory. The code comments acknowledge this: "XXX: Request isn't streaming. Limitation of Seer authentication." and "XXX: I have to deserialize this request so it can be 'automatically' reserialized by the paginate method. This is less than ideal." The double serialization (json.dumps then json.loads) is also wasteful. While acknowledged as a known limitation, this is a real performance concern for large replays and should be tracked as a follow-up.

make_seer_request has no timeout — request can hang indefinitely

requests.post(f"{settings.SEER_AUTOFIX_URL}/v1/automation/summarize/replay/breadcrumbs", data=request_data, headers={...}) is called without a timeout parameter. If the Seer service is slow or unresponsive, the request (and thus the API endpoint) will hang indefinitely, tying up worker threads and potentially causing cascading failures. All outbound HTTP requests should have an explicit timeout. This is especially important since the request body can be large (all breadcrumbs + errors for a replay).

Error log includes full response content which may be large or contain sensitive data

On non-200 status, the code logs extra={"status_code": ..., "response": response.text, "content": response.content}. Logging both response.text and response.content is redundant (content is bytes, text is str of the same body). If the Seer error response is large, this floods logs. The response body from an internal service is unlikely to contain user-sensitive data, but logging the full body at warning level for every failed request is excessive. Should log status_code and a truncated response.

get_slow_conditions_for_groups is now called once per process_delayed_workflows batch instead of per-function, but the no_slow_condition_groups logging may be noisy

The refactor moves get_slow_conditions_for_groups from being called inside get_condition_query_groups and get_groups_to_fire (potentially multiple times) to once in process_delayed_workflows. This is a good change. However, the new logging block logs "delayed_workflow.no_slow_condition_groups" at info level whenever any DCG has no slow conditions. In a batch with many DCGs, if most have no slow conditions (which may be common), this logs a potentially large sorted list at info level on every batch, causing log noise. The comment says "that's interesting enough to log" but info-level logging of potentially many IDs per batch is excessive; debug or a metric would be more appropriate.

processing_deadline_duration added to schedule_webhook_delivery without explanation

A processing_deadline_duration=30 is added to schedule_webhook_delivery's TaskworkerConfig. This is a behavior change: tasks will now be killed/timed out after 30 seconds. If schedule_webhook_delivery legitimately takes longer than 30 seconds (e.g., processing a large batch of webhooks), it will be terminated mid-execution, potentially leaving webhooks undelivered. The PR description doesn't explain why this deadline is needed. Similar additions (300 for drain_mailbox, 120 for drain_mailbox_parallel) should be justified. Without context, these deadlines could cause silent task failures.

processing_deadline_duration=60 added to check_auth_identities may truncate large batches

check_auth_identities processes a list of auth_identity_ids (default chunk_size=100) and then reschedules check_auth. With processing_deadline_duration=60, if processing 100 identities takes longer than 60 seconds (e.g., slow identity provider refreshes), the task will be killed mid-batch. Identities already processed have last_synced updated, but the rescheduling call check_auth.apply_async at the end may not execute if the task is killed, potentially leaving remaining identities unprocessed until the next scheduled run. The deadline should be generous enough to handle the chunk size, or the task should checkpoint progress.

Visualize.fromJSON return type changed from Visualize to Visualize[] — breaking change for callers

Visualize.fromJSON previously returned a single Visualize; now it returns Visualize[] (an array, mapping over yAxes). This is a breaking API change. Callers that did `const v = Visualize.fromJSON(json)` and used v directly (e.g., v.yAxis, v.chartType) will now get an array and break. The diff shows callers were updated (aggregateFields.tsx uses Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField) and maps over the result), but any external/downstream callers (getsentry, plugins) will break. This should be a new method name (e.g., fromJSONMany) or the old single-return behavior preserved.

updateLocationWithAggregateFields uses Visualize.fromJSON which now returns an array — flatMap handles it but the semantics changed

updateLocationWithAggregateFields calls Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField) and now does visualizes.map(visualize => JSON.stringify(visualize.toJSON())) inside a flatMap. Previously fromJSON returned a single Visualize and the code did JSON.stringify(Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField).toJSON()). The new code correctly handles the array return. However, this means a single BaseVisualize with multiple yAxes now expands into multiple URL query params (one per yAxis), each with its own chartType. Previously it was a single param. This changes the URL format for multi-yAxis visualizes — existing bookmarks/shared URLs with multi-yAxis visualize params will be parsed differently (each yAxis becomes a separate visualize param with the same chartType, losing the grouping). This is a URL contract change.

Analytics visualizes field changed from raw Visualize objects to toJSON() — but the analytics schema may expect the old format

The trackAnalytics calls changed visualizes: visualizes to visualizes: visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.toJSON()). Previously, Visualize objects were passed directly (which would serialize via their properties). Now toJSON() returns {yAxes: [yAxis], chartType?}. The analytics event schema for trace.explorer.metadata may expect a specific format for the visualizes field. If the analytics pipeline expects the old format (e.g., array of Visualize instances serialized differently), this changes the data shape. The change is likely correct (toJSON is the intended serialization), but the analytics event schema should be verified to accept the new format.

Sentry logger info call uses String(String(search.tokens).length) — double String() is a bug

In the info() log call: user_queries_count: ${String(String(search.tokens).length)}. search.tokens is an array; String(search.tokens) converts it to a string, then .length gets the string length (character count of the stringified array), then String() wraps it. This is wrong — it should be search.tokens.length (the number of tokens), not the character length of the stringified array. The double String() is clearly a mistake. Compare with the trackAnalytics call which correctly uses search.tokens.length. The log output will show a meaningless number (character count of the string representation of the tokens array).

visualizes_count log uses String(String(visualizes).length) — meaningless value

In the info() log call: visualizes_count: ${String(String(visualizes).length)}. visualizes is an array of Visualize objects; String(visualizes) produces something like "[object Object],[object Object]", and .length gives the character count of that string. This is completely wrong — it should be visualizes.length (the number of visualizes). The trackAnalytics call correctly uses visualizes.length. The log output is a meaningless number.

Log visualizes field uses v.chartType but should use visualize.toJSON() for consistency with analytics

The info() log call uses visualizes: ${visualizes.map(v => v.chartType).join(', ')} which only logs chart types, while the trackAnalytics call logs visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.toJSON()). This inconsistency means the Sentry log and the analytics event have different granularity for the visualizes field. The log is less useful (only chart types, no yAxis info). Should use the same toJSON() format for consistency, or at least include yAxis.

DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION pushed to yAxes array then deduped and sorted — mutates the visualizes-derived array

The yAxes useMemo does: const allYAxes = visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.yAxis); allYAxes.push(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION); return dedupeArray(allYAxes).sort(). The push mutates allYAxes which is a fresh array from map, so no external mutation. This is fine. However, the comment says "injects DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION here as it can be used to populate the confidence footer as a fallback" — this means the timeseries query always includes an extra yAxis (DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) even when not needed, adding an extra series to every query. This is a performance overhead (extra data fetched) that is intentional but should be documented. Not a bug per se.

dedupeArray import still used but could be simplified since each visualize now has single yAxis

dedupeArray is still imported and used on line 103: dedupeArray(allYAxes).sort(). Since each Visualize now has a single yAxis, allYAxes is a flat list of strings. dedupeArray is still needed to remove duplicates (multiple visualizes could have the same yAxis, plus DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION could duplicate). So the import is still needed. Not a bug.

Removed multi-yAxis check changes top events behavior — now returns 5 even when multiple visualizes exist

The hook previously checked `if (visualizes.some(visualize => visualize.yAxes.length > 1)) return undefined;` to disable top events when any visualize had multiple y-axes. This check was removed because Visualize now always has a single yAxis. However, the original intent was to disable top events when there are multiple y-axes IN A SINGLE CHART (overlaid series). With the new model, each Visualize is a separate chart with one yAxis, so multiple visualizes = multiple charts, and top events should still work per-chart. But the hook now returns TOP_EVENTS_LIMIT (5) whenever there's at least one groupBy and mode is AGGREGATE, regardless of how many visualizes/charts exist. If there are 4 visualizes (4 separate charts), top events=5 is applied to the timeseries query, which may produce unexpected results (top 5 series across all charts). The hook's comment acknowledges this limitation but the behavior change (removing the multi-yAxis guard) means top events is now enabled in cases where it previously wasn't. This should be verified against the backend's top events handling for multi-visualize queries.

addChart creates new Visualize without label — labels may be missing or duplicated

addChart does: [...visualizes, new Visualize(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)].map(visualize => visualize.toJSON()). The new Visualize is created without a label option, so its label defaults to '' (empty string). Existing visualizes have labels 'A', 'B', etc. (assigned by getVisualizesFromLocation). The new chart gets label '' instead of the next letter (e.g., 'C'). This means the new chart won't have a proper label badge. The shouldRenderLabel check (visualizes.length > 1) will be true, but the new chart's label is empty, so no badge renders for it. The label should be assigned as String.fromCharCode(65 + visualizes.length) to continue the sequence.

setYAxis uses visualizes[group]!.replace({yAxis: newYAxis}) but loses the label

setYAxis does: visualizes.toSpliced(group, 1, visualizes[group]!.replace({yAxis: newYAxis})). The replace method creates a new Visualize with the new yAxis but preserves the label (replace passes label: this.label). So the label is preserved. This is fine. Not a bug.

Compare Queries link uses yAxes: [visualizeYAxes[0]!] — only first visualize is included in comparison

The Compare Queries LinkButton navigates to generateExploreCompareRoute with queries: [{query, groupBys, sortBys, yAxes: [visualizeYAxes[0]!], chartType: visualizes[0]!.chartType}]. This only includes the FIRST visualize's yAxis. If the user has multiple visualizes (charts), only the first is carried into the comparison view. The other visualizes are silently dropped. The comparison feature may only support a single query/visualize, but if so, the UI should indicate this (e.g., disable the button when multiple visualizes exist) rather than silently dropping data.

visualizeYAxes computed but only [0] is used in compare — dead computation for multi-visualize case

visualizeYAxes = visualizes.map(v => v.yAxis) is computed, used for alertsUrls (all yAxes) and chartOptions (all visualizes), but the Compare link only uses visualizeYAxes[0]!. If there's only one visualize, visualizeYAxes[0] is fine. The computation of the full array is needed for alertsUrls. Not a bug, just noting the compare limitation (see related finding).

getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) called inside map for each visualize — redundant computation

Inside the chartInfos useMemo, for each visualize, if sampleCount === 0 && !defined(isSampled), it calls getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) to get fallback sampling metadata. If multiple visualizes hit this fallback condition, getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) is called multiple times (once per visualize), each time re-querying the same data. This is redundant computation. The fallback chartInfo for DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION should be computed once outside the map and reused. Performance issue for queries with multiple visualizes that all lack sampling metadata.

Fallback series lookup uses timeseriesResult.data[yAxis] directly instead of getSeries result

In the fallback block: const series = dedupedYAxes.flatMap(yAxis => timeseriesResult.data[yAxis]).filter(defined). This accesses timeseriesResult.data directly, bypassing the shouldUsePreviousResults logic in getSeries. If previous results should be used (timeseriesResult.isPending && canUsePreviousResults), the fallback confidence computation uses the current (pending) data instead of previous data, producing incorrect confidence values during loading states. Should use the same data source as getSeries.

handleApply converts Visualize to toJSON() but the onColumnsChange type expects BaseAggregateField[] — GroupBy objects pass through unchanged

handleApply does: onColumnsChange(tempColumns.map(col => (isVisualize(col) ? col.toJSON() : col))). The onColumnsChange prop type is (columns: BaseAggregateField[]) => void. BaseAggregateField = GroupBy | BaseVisualize. isVisualize(col) returns true for Visualize instances, converting them to BaseVisualize (toJSON). GroupBy objects pass through as-is. This is correct. But the test expects onColumnsChange to be called with [{groupBy: 'geo.region'}, {yAxes: ['avg(span.self_time)']}] — the Visualize is converted to {yAxes: [...]} which matches BaseVisualize. This is correct behavior. Not a bug.

insertColumn(new Visualize(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)) — new column has empty label

When adding a new visualize column via the dropdown, insertColumn(new Visualize(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)) creates a Visualize with default label '' (empty string). Existing columns may have labels 'A', 'B', etc. The new column gets no label. When applied, the labels are not reassigned (handleApply just converts to JSON). This means the new column has an empty label in the URL/state, which may cause issues downstream (e.g., chart labels, analytics). Labels should be reassigned sequentially after add/delete operations.

FeedbackSummary rendered inside SummaryListContainer but the container has no defined height — layout may collapse

The FeedbackSummary component is placed inside SummaryListContainer (a flex column with gap) above the Container (FluidHeight) that wraps FeedbackList. The SummaryListContainer has style={{gridArea: 'list'}}. The grid row for 'list' is '1fr' (from grid-template-rows: max-content 1fr). The SummaryListContainer is a flex column containing FeedbackSummary (which may render null, a Placeholder, or the summary box) and Container (FluidHeight). If FeedbackSummary renders null (feature disabled, error, or too few feedbacks), the SummaryListContainer just contains the Container. If it renders content, the summary box appears above the list. The layout should work, but the SummaryListContainer doesn't have overflow handling — if the summary is very long (55 words max per the prompt), it could push the list down. Minor layout concern.

referrer added to getAlertsUrl but not to exploreUrl — inconsistent analytics tracking

The diff adds referrer to getAlertsUrl({..., referrer}) but the exploreUrl (getExploreUrl) already had referrer passed (it was in the original code at line 56). So the change adds referrer to the alert URL generation. This is correct — the alert creation URL now includes the referrer for analytics. The exploreUrl already had it. Not a bug, just confirming the change is intentional and correct.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filtering only applied when searchQuery is non-empty — hidden attributes shown when search is empty

The sortedAndFilteredAttributes useMemo: if (!searchQuery.trim()) return sorted; — returns ALL sorted attributes without filtering HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES when there's no search query. The HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter (!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)) is only applied in the search branch. This means when the search box is empty (the default state), hidden attributes (is_segment, project_id, received) ARE displayed. They are only hidden when the user types a search query. This is backwards — hidden attributes should always be hidden, regardless of search state. The filter should be applied unconditionally, with the search filter applied additionally when searchQuery is non-empty.

getTraceAttributesTreeActions uses findSpanAttributeValue(attributes, 'project_id') but project_id is in HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES

The component hides 'project_id' from display (HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES) but still uses findSpanAttributeValue(attributes, 'project_id') to get project IDs for getTraceAttributesTreeActions. This is fine — the attribute is hidden from the UI but still used internally for actions. Not a bug, just noting the attribute is used despite being hidden.

PercentInput disabled when bulk edit enabled but not active — but onBlur still fires onBulkEditChange(false)

The PercentInput is disabled when !hasAccess || (isBulkEditEnabled && !isBulkEditActive). When disabled, the input can't be focused or blurred normally, so onBlur={() => onBulkEditChange?.(false)} won't fire from user interaction. However, if the input was active (isBulkEditActive=true) and then isBulkEditActive becomes false (e.g., parent state change), the input becomes disabled while focused — the blur event may or may not fire depending on browser behavior. If it doesn't fire, onBulkEditChange(false) is never called, leaving the parent in a stale bulk-edit-active state. The disabled logic and blur handler interaction is fragile.

Enter key handler only works when isBulkEditActive — but input may not be in bulk edit mode

The onKeyDown handler checks if (event.key === 'Enter' && isBulkEditActive) before blurring. If the input is not in bulk edit mode (isBulkEditActive is false), pressing Enter does nothing (no blur, no submit). This may be intentional (Enter only confirms bulk edit), but if the input is used in non-bulk-edit mode, Enter should still trigger blur or form submission. The handler is a no-op for non-bulk-edit usage.

Removal of 'Type' rows from grouping variant display — information loss

The diff removes the 'Type' data rows for COMPONENT, CUSTOM_FINGERPRINT, BUILT_IN_FINGERPRINT, SALTED_COMPONENT, and PERFORMANCE_PROBLEM variant types. These rows displayed the variant.type value with a QuestionTooltip explaining what each type means (e.g., 'Uses a complex grouping algorithm taking event data into account'). Removing them loses educational context for users trying to understand how their events are grouped. If this is intentional (UI simplification), it should be confirmed; otherwise it's a regression in user-facing documentation.

serverSidePct uses toFixed() without radix — returns string, then Number() conversion for clientSidePct

const serverSidePct = ((httpDuration / totalDuration) * 100).toFixed(); — toFixed() without arguments defaults to 0 decimal places, returning a string like "75". Then const clientSidePct = 100 - Number(serverSidePct); — converts back to number. This works but is convoluted. More importantly, toFixed() rounds, so serverSidePct and clientSidePct may not sum to exactly 100 (e.g., 75.5 rounds to "76", clientSidePct = 100 - 76 = 24, but actual client is 24.5). The displayed percentages may be off by 1 and won't sum to 100. Should use toFixed(0) consistently or Math.round for both, or display one decimal place.

totalDuration could be zero or negative — division by zero produces Infinity/NaN percentages

const totalDuration = rootEvent.endTimestamp - rootEvent.startTimestamp; If endTimestamp equals startTimestamp (zero-duration transaction) or is less (clock skew), totalDuration is 0 or negative. Then ((httpDuration / totalDuration) * 100) produces Infinity, -Infinity, or NaN. toFixed() on Infinity returns "Infinity", on NaN returns "NaN". These would be displayed as percentages in the UI. Should guard against totalDuration <= 0.

Flex wrapper without gap — icon and text spacing relies on StyledIconClock margin

The Flex component wraps the icon and TimeSince components. The StyledIconClock has margin-right: ${space(0.5)} for spacing. But the separator span ( — ) and the second TextOverflow don't have explicit gap handling. determineDefaultChartType reduce starts with ChartType.AREA as initial accumulator — ties broken toward AREA

return [ChartType.AREA, ChartType.BAR, ChartType.LINE].reduce((acc, ct) => (counts[ct] >= counts[acc] ? ct : acc), ChartType.AREA); — the reduce starts with AREA as the initial value. So if all counts are 0 (no recognized functions), acc stays AREA (initial). If BAR and LINE tie, LINE wins (>=). If AREA and BAR tie, BAR wins. The initial AREA is effectively overridden by the first iteration (AREA >= AREA is true, so acc stays AREA). The logic is correct but the initial value is redundant since the first element is AREA. owasp-java-html-sanitizer 20240325.1 is used without a stated policy for URL schemes on allowed elements; combined with the anchor-stripping logic this leaves anchor validation entirely to string comparison

The PR adds `com.googlecode.owasp-java-html-sanitizer:owasp-java-html-sanitizer:20240325.1` to verify message HTML. The `POLICY_SOME_HTML` policy allows `br`, `p`, `strong`, `b` with no attributes and no URL policy, and `POLICY_NO_HTML` allows nothing. If a translation's anchor matches the English anchor textually, its `href` is never checked by the sanitizer. Difference-highlighting substring logic can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when one string is a prefix of the other

When `sanitized` and `value` differ, the code computes `start` as the length of the common prefix and `end` as the length of the common suffix, then calls `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` and `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)`. If one string is a strict prefix of the other (e.g. value = 'abc', sanitized = 'abcd'), then start = 3 and end = 0, and `value.substring(3, 3)` is fine, but if the strings share both a prefix and a suffix that overlap (e.g. value = 'aa', sanitized = 'a'), start can exceed `value.length() - end`, causing `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` (begin > end). Example: value = 'aba', sanitized = 'aa': common prefix 'a' (start=1), common suffix 'a' (end=1), then `value.substring(1, 3-1=2)` = 'b' and `sanitized.substring(1, 2-1=1)` → begin 1 > end 1 is OK (empty), but value='aa', sanitized='a': start=1, end=1, `sanitized.substring(1, 1-1=0)` → begin 1 > end 0 → StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The verifier would crash with an unhelpful exception instead of reporting the illegal HTML. The code should clamp `start`/`end` so that `start + end <= min(value.length(), sanitized.length())`.

Email RTL style stripping uses a hardcoded English attribute string that will not match translations that reorder or translate the style attribute

`normalizeValue` strips ` style="direction: rtl;"` (with an English attribute name and value) from values in files whose path contains 'email'. The OWASP sanitizer would otherwise escape or strip the `style` attribute (it is not allowed by either policy), causing a false 'Illegal HTML' report for RTL email templates. However, the strip is a literal string match: any translation that writes the attribute differently (e.g. `style='direction: rtl;'`, `style="direction:rtl;"`, or with extra spaces) will not be stripped and will false-positive. More importantly, the check `file.getAbsolutePath().contains("email")` is a heuristic on the path; the same RTL style may legitimately appear in non-email themes. The normalization should use a regex tolerant of quoting/spacing, or better, the policy should allow the `style` attribute with a strict `direction: rtl` value matcher for email templates.

The `changedAnchor_de.properties` fixture ends without a newline (`\ No newline at end of file`) while `changedAnchor_en.properties` also has no trailing newline. The test `verifyNoChangedAnchors` checks that a translation with `<a href="http://malicious.com">` against an English `<a href="http://example.com">` produces 'Didn't find anchor tag'. It does not cover: (a) a translation with an extra anchor not present in English, (b) a translation missing an anchor present in English, (c) a translation with a self-closing or differently-structured anchor. The `santizeAnchors` loop breaks on the first mismatch, so case (a) with multiple anchors where the first matches but the second doesn't is partially covered, but case (b) (missing anchor) is not tested at all — a translation that drops an anchor entirely will pass `santizeAnchors` silently (the while loop simply doesn't execute for the missing anchor) and then the sanitizer will not complain because there is no extra HTML. Verifier does not detect translations that omit an anchor tag present in the English source

`santizeAnchors` only iterates over anchors found in the *translated* value (`matcher = ANCHOR_PATTERN.matcher(value)`) and checks each against the English anchors. If a translation simply omits an `<a>` tag that exists in the English source (e.g. the English has two links and the translation has only one), the loop runs once for the single translated anchor, matches it against the first English anchor, removes it, and returns without ever noticing that the second English anchor has no counterpart. The subsequent sanitization also passes because there is no extra HTML in the translation. The result is a silently broken translation (missing link) that the verifier — whose stated purpose is to catch changed anchors — does not report. The method should also iterate over the English anchors and verify each has a matching counterpart in the translation (i.e. compare counts and sequences in both directions).

PropertyResourceBundle is created with the platform default charset instead of UTF-8, which can misread non-ASCII translations

Keycloak's message properties files are UTF-8 (the project sets `project.build.sourceEncoding=UTF-8` and modern Keycloak loads properties as UTF-8). Reading a UTF-8 file as ISO-8859-1 will mojibake all non-ASCII characters (e.g. Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic), which means the sanitizer operates on corrupted text and the comparison against the sanitized form may produce false 'Illegal HTML' reports for any translation containing non-ASCII characters (the mojibake bytes may include characters that look like HTML entities or tags after unescapeHtml4). The code should use `new PropertyResourceBundle(new InputStreamReader(fis, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))` to match Keycloak's actual loading behavior.

The pattern should be `</?a(\s[^>]*)?>` or `</?a[\s>]` to ensure the tag name is exactly `a`.

This is the intended behavior (translations should not add HTML that English doesn't have). However, if the English source contains HTML that the regex misses (uppercase tags, tags with digits like `

VerifyMessageProperties instance fields (messages, file) are not thread-safe; if the Mojo runs verifications in parallel, shared state would be corrupted

The class has instance fields `file` and `messages` (line 39-40). `messages` is initialized in `verify()` (line 47) and appended to in `verifySafeHtml` and `verifyNoDuplicateKeys`. If a single `VerifyMessageProperties` instance is used from multiple threads (e.g. a parallel Maven build), the `messages` list would be corrupted. However, the class is instantiated per file (the test does `new VerifyMessageProperties(file)`), so each file has its own instance. If the Mojo creates one instance per file and processes files in parallel, each instance is independent and thread-safe. If the Mojo reuses a single instance for multiple files, `messages` would accumulate across files and `file` would be overwritten. The class should either be immutable (pass file to constructor, return messages from verify) or documented as not thread-safe. Currently `file` is final but `messages` is mutable instance state, which is a code smell.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Wrong null-check message for rawTokenId

The constructor validates `grantType` twice: line 72 checks `grantType` with message "Null grantType not allowed" and line 73 checks `grantType` again with message "Null rawTokenId not allowed". The second check was clearly intended to validate `rawTokenId` (which is never null-checked), so a null `rawTokenId` would pass validation silently and later cause a NullPointerException in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` when concatenating `':' + tokenContext.getRawTokenId()` (actually producing "null" string) or in `getTokenContextFromTokenId`. Fix: change line 73 to `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: the constructor checks grantType twice instead of checking rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values through. Its speculative downstream effects do not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant-shortcut comparison

In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the check `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (match failure) when the grant shortcut MATCHES the expected value, and falls through to `return isUUID().matches(items[1])` when it does NOT match. The logic is inverted: the matcher will reject tokens whose grant shortcut equals the expected one and accept tokens with any other (or missing) grant shortcut as long as the suffix is a UUID. Additionally, `substring(3, 5)` is off by one: the encoded prefix is 6 chars (2 session + 2 token type + 2 grant), so the grant shortcut occupies indices 4-5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`. As written, every test using `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` will fail against correctly encoded token IDs (or worse, pass against wrong ones), making the test assertions meaningless. Fix: `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies both issues in the golden comment: the grant shortcut should use substring(4, 6), and a matching shortcut should succeed when combined with the UUID check rather than return false.

false_positives.candidate:
Duplicate-shortcut validation compares wrong map sizes and cannot detect collisions

In `postInit`, the duplicate-detection check `if (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size())` is intended to catch two different grant types sharing the same shortcut (or same ID). However, `grantsByShortcuts` is keyed by shortcut and `grantsToShortcuts` is keyed by grant ID. If two grants share the same shortcut, `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantName)` silently overwrites the first entry, shrinking `grantsByShortcuts` by one while `grantsToShortcuts` keeps both IDs — the sizes then differ and the check fires, which is correct. But if two grants share the same ID (impossible for distinct factories) or, more importantly, if a shortcut collides with the reserved `UNKNOWN` shortcut "na", the overwrite happens at line 78 AFTER the loop, again changing sizes — still detected. The real gap: the check only detects size differences, so a collision that is later overwritten by an equal-size map change would be missed, and more practically the error message and detection are fragile. A more robust approach is to detect the overwrite during insertion (e.g., check `grantsByShortcuts.put(...) != null` inside the loop and throw immediately). As written, the validation is indirect and can produce a confusing failure or, in edge cases where a custom provider registers grants dynamically via `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut`, silently accept a colliding shortcut, which would corrupt the token-ID encoding (two grant types mapping to the same 2-char code).

getTokenContextFromTokenId uses indexOf(':') which breaks if raw ID contains a colon

`getTokenContextFromTokenId` splits the encoded ID with `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` and takes everything after the first colon as `rawId`. `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()` produces UUIDs (no colons), so for newly issued tokens this is fine. However, the method is a public SPI entry point (`TokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId`) meant to decode token IDs that may come from external/custom encoders or older/foreign formats; any raw ID containing a colon (or a legacy ID that happens to contain a colon) would be mis-parsed: the prefix check `encodedContext.length() != 6` would throw `IllegalArgumentException` for a legacy ID like `ab:cd:uuid`, and even a well-formed custom encoding with a colon in the raw part would be split at the wrong position. Using `lastIndexOf(':')` would be more robust, or better, `split(":", 2)` semantics with an explicit prefix-length check. At minimum the parsing should use the LAST colon or validate that the prefix is exactly 6 chars before the first colon and document the constraint.

initToken can throw IllegalStateException for unknown grant type, breaking token issuance

In `initToken`, the access token ID is now built via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)` where `tokenCtx` comes from `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`. That method sets `grantType = UNKNOWN` ("na") when `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is not set on the client session context, and `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` maps "na" back to "na" via the factory maps (line 78-79 of the factory put UNKNOWN->UNKNOWN), so the common path works. However, `encodeTokenId` throws `IllegalStateException("Cannot encode token with unknown grantType: ...")` when `factory.getShortcutByGrantType(...)` returns null. The factory's lazy-refresh path (`getShortcutByGrantType`, lines 106-119) only refreshes when the grant type is not found AND a provider factory exists for it; for any grant type string that is set on the client session context but has no registered `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` (e.g., a custom grant type implemented without the new SPI, or a code path that sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` to a value with no factory), `getShortcutByGrantType` returns null and `encodeTokenId` throws. Since `initToken` is on the critical path of every access-token issuance (authorization code, refresh, client credentials, CIBA, device, token exchange, etc.), any such gap turns into a 500 error at token issuance instead of degrading to the "na" shortcut. The PR sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` in several grant types but the fallback to UNKNOWN only happens when the attribute is absent — a present-but-unmapped value is fatal. Consider falling back to the UNKNOWN shortcut in `encodeTokenId` (or in `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` validating against known grants) rather than throwing.

Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for the SPI

`OAuth2GrantType.Context` is a public class in `server-spi-private` and previously exposed a public copy constructor `Context(Context context)`. The PR removes it (the diff shows the copy constructor body deleted and replaced by the `grantType` initialization in the main constructor). Any third-party `OAuth2GrantType` implementation that relied on the copy constructor (a common pattern for wrapping/decorating contexts) will fail to compile against the new version. Since this is an SPI in `server-spi-private` that the PR explicitly wants to be extensible ("provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), removing a public constructor without a deprecation cycle is an API break. Either keep the copy constructor (initializing `grantType` from `context.grantType`) or document the break.

Lightweight-token detection reads client attribute from the wrong client context

`getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` determines the token type via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads `session.getContext().getClient()`. During token issuance in `TokenManager.initToken`, the session context client is the client for which the token is being issued, which is normally correct. However, for flows where the session context client differs from the client session's client (e.g., token exchange where `StandardTokenExchangeProvider.setClientToContext` sets the requesting client, or admin/service-account flows), the lightweight flag could be evaluated against the wrong client, encoding `lt` (lightweight) for a regular token or `rt` for a lightweight one. The PR's stated goal is to "recognize more reliably if access-token is lightweight or not"; deriving it from `session.getContext().getClient()` rather than from `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` undermines that reliability. Prefer `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` (the client the token is actually issued for) when deciding the token type.

Potential NPE when client session has no user session

`getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and service accounts, Keycloak can create client sessions without a user session (transient service-account sessions may have a user session, but some code paths create client sessions with a null user session). If `getUserSession()` returns null, this throws a NullPointerException inside `initToken`, failing token issuance. The method should handle a null user session (e.g., treat as TRANSIENT, which matches how service-account/client-credentials tokens behave) instead of dereferencing blindly.

Grant type attribute set on a freshly-created DefaultClientSessionContext may not propagate to token creation

`PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process` builds `sessionContext` via `DefaultClientSessionContext.fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter(...)` and then sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` on that context (line 82) before calling `tokenManager.createClientAccessToken(..., sessionContext)`. Whether the attribute is visible during `initToken` depends on `DefaultClientSessionContext` storing attributes in-memory vs. reading from the underlying client session notes; if `fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter` returns a wrapper whose `setAttribute` writes to a transient map that `initToken` later re-reads through a different context instance, the grant type may be lost and the token ID would be encoded with the "na" shortcut. This is the only grant that sets the attribute on a locally-constructed context rather than through `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse` or the client session itself, so it is the most likely to silently produce `pc`-less (i.e., `na`) token IDs. Worth verifying with an integration test for the pre-authorized-code flow.

Refresh grant type is hardcoded to REFRESH_TOKEN constant instead of the actual grant type used

In the refresh-token path (`refreshAccessToken` / the code around line 248), the PR sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)`. `OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN` is the string "refresh_token", which matches `RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.getId()`, so the encoding will produce the `rt` shortcut — but note this collides conceptually with the token-type shortcut `rt` (regular token) used in the token-type position; they are in different positions so encoding is unambiguous, but it is confusing. More importantly, hardcoding the constant here bypasses the `OAuth2GrantType.Context.getGrantType()` mechanism used everywhere else; if the refresh flow is ever entered via a different grant type (e.g., a custom refresh-like grant), the encoded ID would incorrectly claim `refresh_token`. Using the actual grant type from the request context would be more consistent.

Unit test bypasses factory.postInit and hand-builds maps, missing coverage of duplicate-shortcut validation

The test's `@Before` constructs `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory`, calls `init(null)`, and then directly assigns `factory.grantsByShortcuts` / `factory.grantsToShortcuts` (package-private fields) instead of calling `postInit(...)`. This means the production initialization path — including the duplicate-shortcut validation in `postInit` (lines 70-86) and the population of maps from real `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` instances — is never exercised by this test. A regression in `postInit` (e.g., the broken size-comparison check, or a shortcut collision between two real grant factories) would not be caught. Add a test that runs `postInit` against a real/mock `KeycloakSessionFactory` with the actual grant factories, and a test that a duplicate shortcut causes startup failure.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optional.get() without isPresent() check will throw NoSuchElementException when user has no recovery codes credential

The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) which returns an Optional that is empty when the user has neither a federated nor a local recovery-authn-codes credential, then immediately calls credentialModelOpt.get() on line 19. Previously the code called getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get() which had the same latent problem, but the new helper makes the empty case more reachable: getCredential checks federated credentials first and falls back to local, and a user can legitimately reach the recovery-code input page (e.g. via a misconfigured flow, or a race where the credential was removed after the page was rendered, or all codes used and credential deleted) without any credential present. This will throw NoSuchElementException and produce a 500 error instead of a graceful login page. The code should handle the empty Optional (e.g. render the form without a code number or fail the authentication gracefully).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unchecked Optional.get() call on the result of RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user), which can throw NoSuchElementException when no credential exists. Although it does not mention raw List deserialization, it directly matches the concrete bug described in the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
createRecoveryCodesCredential stores raw recovery codes in user storage instead of hashed codes

The new method createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (generatedCodes) to JSON and passes that JSON as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). For local (Keycloak DB) storage, the recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel) path is used, and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes each raw code before persisting. But when the credential is stored in federated user storage, the raw, unhashed codes are handed to the storage provider verbatim. Any user storage provider that persists the credential data as-is (as the test provider BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does at line 197 with recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())) will store the recovery codes in plaintext. Recovery codes are bearer credentials equivalent to passwords; storing them unhashed in an external user storage is a serious data-integrity/security issue, and it also breaks the validation contract: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates input by hashing the input and comparing to the stored hash, while a federated provider receiving raw codes must compare raw-to-raw (as the test provider does at line 340), meaning the same code validates differently depending on where it is stored. The fix is to hash the codes (e.g. via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) before building the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential, and to construct the credential model consistently for both storage paths.

UserCredentialModel for federated recovery codes storage is missing userLabel and createdDate metadata

When the credential is stored in federated user storage, the code builds new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson) and calls updateCredential. The credentialModel parameter (a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel) carries the generatedAt timestamp and userLabel, but these are not transferred to the UserCredentialModel — only type and challengeResponse (the JSON) are set. The id is empty and createdDate is unset. A federated storage provider that reconstructs the credential from the CredentialInput (as BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials does, reading getCreatedDate() and getUserLabel()) will get a null/zero createdDate and null userLabel, so the stored federated credential loses the generatedAt metadata that the UI displays and that RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues expects. The OTP equivalent (createOTPCredential) similarly builds a minimal UserCredentialModel, but for OTP the secret is the only data. For recovery codes the createdDate/userLabel should be propagated (e.g. via UserCredentialModel.setUserLabel / credential data or by passing the full model) so federated storage round-trips the credential faithfully.

removeStoredCredentialById only removes local credential; federated recovery codes credential is never removed when all codes are used

After a successful recovery-code login, when all codes are used the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). For a user whose recovery codes live in federated user storage, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns the federated credential (from getFederatedCredentialsStream), and removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB — it does not call the federated storage's disableCredentialType. As a result, the spent recovery-codes credential remains in the user storage. The subsequent isConfiguredFor check (line 149) and the required-action re-trigger logic (lines 90-92) then operate on stale data: the federated credential still reports all codes used, but it is never deleted, so the credential lingers in the external storage indefinitely (a data-hygiene issue and potentially confusing state for the storage provider). The code should remove the credential through the credential manager in a way that also disables/deletes it in federated storage (e.g. credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById for local plus disableCredentialType for federated, or use the credential's storageId to route the removal).

Test user storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing raw input to raw stored codes (plaintext comparison)

In isValid, the recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data (which, due to CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential passing the raw codes JSON to updateCredential, contains plaintext codes) and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). This is a plaintext equality comparison of a bearer credential against stored plaintext — no hashing, no constant-time comparison. While this is test-suite code, it both (a) demonstrates and enshrines the insecure contract that federated providers receive raw codes, and (b) uses a non-constant-time equals comparison for a credential check. Combined with the production-side issue of storing raw codes in federated storage, this provider will keep plaintext recovery codes in memory and on disk. The provider should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) and compare against hashed stored values, matching the local-storage validation semantics.

updateCredential for recovery codes drops userLabel and does not set secretData

The recovery-codes branch of updateCredential builds a CredentialModel with only id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON) and createdDate. It does not set userLabel (available on the incoming UserCredentialModel via getUserLabel()) nor secretData. Later, getCredentials reconstructs the model via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(..., myUser.recoveryCodes.getUserLabel()) — which will be null — so the user label chosen during setup is lost for federated users. The OTP branch in the same method has the same pattern of dropping fields, but for recovery codes the userLabel is user-visible metadata that the account console and setup flow display. The provider should copy input.getUserLabel() (and createdDate from the input if present) into the stored CredentialModel.

Recovery codes test only exercises the first code and never verifies code consumption / all-codes-used behavior in user storage

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin enters recovery code index 0 once and asserts login succeeds. It never verifies that (a) the used code is marked as consumed in the federated storage, (b) reusing the same code fails, or (c) after all 12 codes are consumed the credential is removed from user storage and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-added. Given that the production change specifically alters how the credential is created and looked up in federated storage (and that removeStoredCredentialById does not touch federated storage), the test gap means the most important behavioral consequences of the PR in the federated path are unverified. A test that consumes codes and asserts the federated credential state (and the re-triggered required action) would be needed.

Misspelled config alias 'delayed-suthenticator-config' in test flow setup

In configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes the delayed-authenticator config alias is set to "delayed-suthenticator-config" (missing 'n' in "authenticator"). The alias is only used as a label for the execution config and the test passes delay=0, so it is functionally harmless, but it is a typo in test configuration text that will show up in the admin console/flow listing and could confuse anyone copying this setup. It should be "delayed-authenticator-config".

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code change from 4 to 3 for recreate upgrade breaks documented contract and existing automation

The PR changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 (and introduces FEATURE_DISABLED = 4). This is a breaking change to the exit-code contract of the `update-compatibility check` command: any existing CI/CD pipeline or script that was written against the already-released behavior (where exit code 4 meant 'rolling upgrade not possible') will now misinterpret the result. Exit code 3 previously had no meaning for this command, and 4 is now reused for a different condition (feature disabled). The docs in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc are updated to match the new values, but the change silently invalidates automation built against the previous release. If this command has already shipped in a released version, the exit code for 'recreate upgrade' must not be changed; a new code should be added instead (e.g., keep 4 for recreate and use 5 for feature-disabled), or the change must be clearly called out as breaking in release notes.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same undocumented breaking exit-code change and explicitly calls for release notes. Its discussion of affected automation and preserving or updating exit-code handling aligns with the golden comment's migration-guidance concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Feature check runs before config validation, so --features=rolling-updates is never actually honored for the check itself

In `run()`, the code checks `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES)` before `validateConfig()` is called. The `--features` option is a runtime configuration option that is only applied to the Profile during configuration processing (which happens in validateConfig()/the Quarkus config phase). At the point of the check, the Profile reflects only the persisted/optimized build-time configuration, not the `--features=rolling-updates` CLI flag passed on the command line. This means a user running `kc.sh update-compatibility check --file=x.json --features=rolling-updates` on a server where the feature is not enabled in the build will still get 'feature not enabled' and exit code 4, even though they explicitly passed the flag — contradicting the documentation (docs/guides/templates/kc.adoc) which shows the command being run with `--features=rolling-updates` appended. The feature gate therefore cannot be satisfied via CLI at all for non-optimized invocations, making the documented usage in kc.adoc and update-compatibility.adoc incorrect. The check should either be performed after configuration is applied, or the feature flag should be read from the parsed CLI options directly.

Same premature feature check: --features=rolling-updates passed on the CLI is ignored by the gate

Identical issue to UpdateCompatibilityCheck: `run()` checks `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES)` before `validateConfig()` processes the `--features` CLI option. Since the Profile is only updated with CLI-provided feature flags during configuration processing, a user who runs `kc.sh update-compatibility metadata --features=rolling-updates` (exactly as documented in docs/guides/templates/kc.adoc line 53 and docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc line 63) on a default build will always be rejected with 'The preview feature rolling-updates is not enabled' and exit code 4. The documented command therefore cannot work as written unless the feature was enabled at build time, which contradicts the purpose of the docs showing the flag being passed at invocation time.

No test verifies the exit code for the feature-disabled path (exit code 4)

The new test `testFeatureNotEnabled` asserts only the error message via `cliResult.assertError(...)`, but never asserts the exit code. The whole point of introducing `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED = 4` is to give automation a machine-readable signal (documented in update-compatibility.adoc exit-code table). Without asserting `cliResult.exitCode() == 4`, a regression that returns a different code (e.g., the generic picocli error code 1 or 2) would not be caught. The test should assert the exit code equals `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` for both the `metadata` and `check` subcommands. Additionally, there is no test asserting exit code 3 for the recreate/incompatible path (testWrongVersions only asserts the error message), leaving the changed exit-code contract untested.

Test parameterization with null strategy no longer exercises the feature-disabled path, and the feature is now always enabled

In `createInitialDeployment`, when `updateStrategy == null` the method returns early (line 105-107) before the `ROLLING_UPDATES` feature is enabled (lines 112-115). Previously the null-strategy case configured the update spec via the `unsupported` stanza; now the null case gets neither an update spec nor the feature. The test names (`testImageChange-{0}`, `testCacheMaxCount-{0}`) and the comment on line 64 ('changing the image to non-existing will always use the recreate upgrade type') suggest the null case is meant to represent the default/legacy behavior, but with the feature flag now being a hard requirement for the operator's update strategies (per the new CAUTION in advanced-configuration.adoc: 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail'), the null-strategy deployment may fail outright rather than exercise the intended default path. The test does not assert that the initial deployment actually becomes ready before the upgrade is triggered, so a failure of the initial deployment would surface as a confusing timeout. Either the null case should also enable the feature (to test default strategy behavior with the feature on), or a separate test should verify the operator fails when the feature is missing — currently neither is covered.

However, the NOTE block immediately below (lines 461-466) says 'During this preview stage, the update strategy defaults to mimicking Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior' and the table lists `<not set>` (default) as a valid value that 'Mimics Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior'. These two statements are contradictory: if the operator fails without the feature, there is no default behavior to mimic; if there is a working default, the operator does not fail. The docs need to clarify whether existing deployments without the feature continue to work (legacy behavior) or are rejected, and the example YAML (lines 468-482) only shows the feature enabled together with a strategy, giving no example of a CR without the feature. This ambiguity will cause users to either unnecessarily enable a preview feature or, conversely, hit unexpected failures.

CAUTION says commands fail without the feature, but the documented command examples pass --features=rolling-updates which (per the code) does not satisfy the gate

The guide's CAUTION block (lines 12-16) states the feature 'must be enabled. Otherwise, the commands will fail.' Yet every command example in the guide (via the kc.adoc macro, line 63 and 83) appends `--features=rolling-updates` at invocation time. As implemented in UpdateCompatibilityCheck/UpdateCompatibilityMetadata, the feature check reads the Profile before CLI options are applied, so passing `--features=rolling-updates` on the command line does not enable the feature for the check — the command will still fail with exit code 4. The documentation therefore instructs users to do something that does not work. The docs should state that the feature must be enabled at build time (e.g., `kc.sh build --features=rolling-updates`) or the code should be fixed so the CLI flag is honored (see related finding). Until one or the other is resolved, the guide is incorrect.

ROLLING_UPDATES is declared as Type.PREVIEW, which means it is automatically enabled for all users running with `--profile=preview` (see isEnabledByDefault, line 316-325). This feature gates significant operational behavior: the Keycloak Operator's update strategies (documented as causing the operator to fail if not enabled) and the update-compatibility CLI commands. Auto-enabling an operator-affecting feature for every preview-profile user is a broad blast radius for a preview feature; users who enable the preview profile for unrelated features (there are many other PREVIEW features) will silently get the rolling-updates behavior change in the operator. Consider whether this should be PREVIEW_DISABLED_BY_DEFAULT (which exists in the Type enum precisely for 'Preview features, which are not automatically enabled even with enabled preview profile') so that it must be explicitly enabled, matching the docs' emphasis that it 'must be enabled'.

In the V2 schema (AdminPermissionsSchema), per-group resources are created with the group id as their name (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and getOrCreateResource uses that as the resource name), so findByName works only if the resource was already created; however, when no per-group resource exists, the code falls back to the 'Groups' all-resource via `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` (line 144) and then immediately calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 147) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource does not exist (e.g. admin permissions were enabled but the schema resources were not initialized, or the feature was toggled), causing a NullPointerException instead of a clean 'false' denial. GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (lines 313-317) iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Group", ...)` and strips the 'group.resource.' prefix from resource names to recover group ids. This is the V1 evaluator, but MgmtPermissionsV2 now overrides groups() to return GroupPermissionsV2, so this V1 method is only used in V1 mode; however, the type string 'Group' (singular) versus the V2 schema's GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE ('Groups') shows the two evaluators use different resource type conventions, and any code path that mixes them (e.g. a realm migrated from V1 to V2 where resources were created with type 'Group') will silently return an empty set, breaking the group-based user visibility filter. The consequence is that admins lose visibility of users in groups they can view members of. The resource type lookup should be consistent (use AdminPermissionsSchema constants) or both types should be handled.

V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set when user can manage but not view, changing semantics from previous getGroupsWithViewPermission

The old V1 method getGroupsWithViewPermission() returned an empty set when `root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()` (i.e. full access). The new getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (line 298) only checks `root.users().canView()`, omitting the canManage() case. An admin with manage-users but not view-users would previously get an empty set (meaning 'no group filter, see all users'), but now gets a set of group ids derived from view-members/manage-members permissions, which is likely empty — and an empty set is treated by callers (UsersResource.searchForUser: `if (!groupIds.isEmpty()) session.setAttribute(...)`) as 'no filter', so the outcome may be the same by accident, but the intermediate semantics differ and any future caller that distinguishes empty-set from null will misbehave. More importantly, in V1, canViewMembers(group) was true when `root.users().canView()`; the new canViewMembers also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE, which is a deliberate change, but getGroupIdsWithViewPermission's guard should mirror the old condition (canView() || canManage()) to preserve behavior for manage-only admins.

In GroupPermissions.canViewMembers(GroupModel) (line 340), the permission check was changed from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)`. Whether this is intended is unclear — the V2 GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers does the same — but it is a behavioral change to the V1 evaluator that widens access: manage-members was previously not sufficient to view the member list. If the intent is that manage implies view, it should be documented; otherwise this is an unintended privilege widening in the legacy (non-V2) permission path.
